Duration: 6 months Excluding the outlier cases, it seems fair to expect a typical accession process, from decision to implementation, to take somewhere around six years. Assessing the starting point: CPI is OK-ish It is clear that, as of today, Hungary would not meet the adop- tion criteria: inflation is too high, the deficit is too wide, debt is too large, long-term yields are too elevated and the Forint is too volatile. But there’s nothing inherently unique about that - most countries aren’t ready this early in the process. It is the political decision to adopt the Euro that emboldens reform and brings fundamental and legal alignment. So how far are Hungary’s fundamentals from the objective? Starting with inflation, Hungary’s CPI has on average been more than 4%-pts over the Euro area’s best performers, which is far above the 1.5%-pt reference (Figure 2). Only on isolat- ed occasions has the gap shrunk to 1.5% or below. Instead, they will hope that voter support picks up if the spending and reforms result in noticeable improvements over time. Energy support package crumbles The government’s recent energy support package illustrates some of the internal problems. The package had three compo- nents. First, a €0.17 reduction in taxes on petrol and diesel during May and June. Second, a €1000 tax-free bonus that companies can pay to their employees to help with their increased energy expenditures. Third, steps to address energy companies’ windfall profits. All three measures face challenges. The pass-through of reduced petrol/diesel taxes on pump prices has looked partial as the last observation in Figure 1 should have seen a clearer decoupling of petrol prices from oil prices. The competition authority is saying that pass-through by energy firms is becoming more complete, but the initial impression may be hard to shake off. More dramatically, the €1000 tax-free bonus failed to get through the Bundesrat (upper house) last week, with some CDU-led and SPD-led states opposing it and the government misjudging the likely vote. records.text: Today, we expect the macroeconomic backdrop and the outlook for AI will be the key determinants of the trajectory of Momentum. In general, Momentum as a factor performs best in periods of stasis. A downturn in the outlook for AI investment would cause a “catch down” Momentum reversal, as would a severe deterioration in the macroeconomic outlook that triggers a sharp increase in equity market or bond volatility and causes investors to trim risk exposures. A sharp improvement in the macro outlook would also likely trigger a Momentum reversal as laggards “catch up.” For the broad market, sharp Momentum rallies near equity market highs have generally signaled below-average near-term S&P 500 returns. Several of the sharpest Momentum rallies in the past have occurred during equity market downturns, such as in September 1990 and March 2020. In these episodes, the Momentum rallies preceded strong average S&P 500 returns in the subsequent 3-6 months. In contrast, sharp Momentum rallies that have occurred with the S&P 500 at or near a high have generally preceded weaker subsequent equity market returns. These episodes included mid-1998, late 1999, and late 2021. records.text: US Daily Data Recap14 May 2026 ab 5 Initial claims rise to 211K Initial claims rose 12K to 211K in the week ending May 9, a bit above consensus (205K) and our estimate (204K). That brought the four-week moving average up 1K to 204K. The recent ups and downs in the claims data — which appeared to be more artifacts of mistimed seasonal adjustment than reflective of labor market fundamentals — have not materially changed our assessment that initial claims remain stable, with little evidence right now of accelerated loosening or tightening in the labor market. We noted in our preview (link here) that seasonally-adjusted initial claims in New York appeared to have some normalization yet to come, following a spate of volatility associated with seasonal factors that looked mistimed with New York City spring break. Some normalization materialized in today's data, as Empire State claims rose 3K to 15K, seasonally adjusted, within the range prior to the spring break swings. The increase in New York accounted for about a quarter of the overall increase in claims in the week ending May 9. Seasonally-adjusted initial claims also rose 3K to 4K in Kentucky, 2K to 18K in Texas, 1K to 7K in Florida, and 1K to 6K in Michigan. Continuing claims rose 24K to 1782K in the week ending May 2, below our expectation for 1790K and in line with the 1780K expected by consensus. We assess supply not just in current terms, but also relative to past issuance and potential future issuance. An issuer that has raised a large amount of debt recently is increasing its debt and is less likely to face a supply shortage of its bonds. Furthermore, an issuer that frequently comes to the primary market may need to offer a bigger discount to incentivize investors to purchase the current issue instead of waiting for its next offering. We measure past supply as the dollar amount issued by the issuer in the trailing 12-month period. We define a frequent issuer by an indicator variable if the issuer has conducted four or more issuances during the trailing 12-month period. While we hypothesize that the supply curve is upward-sloping, we note that certain factors can also suggest alternative influences on concessions. For instance, frequent issuers are more well- known by market participants (better information transparency) and have better relationships with syndicates, suggesting a lower concession. This tension implies that the regression estimate can be ex-ante positive or negative. We let the empirical evidence reveal which influence has been stronger. But the focus on elevated Gilt yields needs to be put in the context of a global repricing of long-end yields and risk premium. 30y JGB yields are at multi-decade highs, 30y Bund yields are at the highest levels post-sovereign crisis, and 30y UST yields are near the highs of the cycle. On other measures of relative bond pricing, such as swap spreads (Exhibit 6) and the 10s30s curve (Exhibit 7), Gilts are currently comparable to other curves, and have actually shown improvement in recent quarters on a relative basis. But, as we have shown (see here and here), the risk premium in Gilts has not increased much in recent months, despite Gilt yields rising more than in other bond markets. This is because the drivers of Gilt yields in recent months have been the shift in the fundamental outlook for inflation and central bank policy. First, we think that the recent decline in risk premium (HUF appreciation and declining yields) has allowed the MNB to consider resuming its cutting cycle, as comments by Deputy Governor Kurali earlier in the month also indicated. Second, there is likely some resistance to a sharp currency move that is not accompanied by inflows into local bonds, rather than pushback against the direction itself. Alignment with Europe: VZ's 32NC7 structure is aligned with European corporate hybrid market standards. Under S&P's methodology, standard European-style hybrids, that have 25bp (five years after the first call date or in year 10) and 75bp (20 years after the first call date) step- ups, are structured to lose their 50% equity content at first call date as long as the issuer is investment grade. As a result, as long as senior spreads do not exceed hybrid reset spread (181bp for VZ 32NC7), the issuer's economic incentive is in favor of calling and replacing hybrids at their first call dates because of S&P's equity content loss. Heading to a global standardized corporate hybrid market? In our view, the VZ 32NC7 paves the way for a potential harmonization of the US and European corporate hybrids markets. Indeed, instead of coupon floors, introducing step-ups would reduce potential extension risk on 30NC5/32NC7 structures in the US would allow hybrid curve spread renormalization. In addition, it likely would expand the US investor base for 30NC5/32NC7 instruments and encourage European investors' involvement. 15 May 2026 30 Barclays | US Credit Alpha: Selective listening

While all of our European coverage offer low-carbon solutions, we would highlight Heidelberg Materials (OW) as the group remains the only player to operate an industrial scale CCUS cement plant (Brevik, Norway), which allows the Heidelberg to sell zero-carbon cement (EvoZero). Meanwhile, Holcim (OW) offers exposure to DCs via low-carbon concrete offerings as well as its high-performance flooring and roofing systems, which is part of the DC that other heavyside peers cannot service. In addition to direct cooling, the fall-out of AI data centers with higher compute power and subsequent heat generation, is an increased focus on fire protection in the construction of DCs. For insulation manufacturers, this translates into growing demand for non-combustible, high temperature resistant materials, which should be supportive for mineral wool, and stone wool in particular. records.text: Japan Outlook Growing support for early rate hike at the BoJ The BoJ's emphasis on upside inflation risk over downside growth risk and its growing support for an early hike, including in June, was clear this week. We stick to our June rate hike call, while noting that political pressure at home and abroad still appears key. Hawkish stance emphasizing upside inflation risks increasingly shared At the 27-28 April MPM, the BoJ revised down its FY26 real GDP growth forecast to +0.5%, roughly in line with potential growth, while significantly revising up its inflation forecasts for FY26-27, including for the CPI excluding perishables and energy (aka “BoJ core”). In addition, policy guidance was revised so that the Bank could continue on its rate-hike path even if turmoil in the Middle East exerts downward pressure on the economy. The Summary of Opinions from that meeting, released 12 May, confirmed this hawkish tilt. The view that upside inflation risks deserve more attention than downside growth risks appeared to be shared broadly across the Policy Board, not just among the three members who dissented in favor of a rate hike. On the economy, the discussion acknowledged deteriorating terms of trade caused by higher crude oil prices, as well as risks of supply constraints in crude oil and petrochemical products. How have domestic retail flows changed since implementation of RIA accounts? Reshoring investment accounts (RIAs), available since 23 March, offer a waiver on capital gains tax on sales of overseas equities if residents buy KOSPI-listed stocks with the proceeds and hold them for a year. Retail investors will get 100% relief if they repatriate those investments by the end of May, 80% if they can get it done by end-July and 50% between August and December (capital gains tax is 22% including a 2% local income tax). Since the launch, RIA account balances have steadily climbed to reach KRW1.6trn (~USD 1bn) as of 8 May, equating to KRW7.5mn on average per account. Meanwhile, we note that retail outbound investments have moderated meaningfully since early 2026 (especially compared to 2025, Figure 14). We attribute this both to government efforts to encourage repatriation and the strong KOSPI outperformance against US equities. Equity investment fund AUM has climbed substantially since 2025 (Figure 2). records.text: 15 May 2026 Euro Weekly Digest Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG Week in review ECB's reaction function Our baseline ECB view is a measured tightening this summer, with quarter-point hikes in June and September. This would raise policy rates to 2.50%, the upper end of the range of neutral. This is good risk management. It signals the commitment to price stability without overly burdening economic growth. President Lagarde’s description of the ECB reaction function links a large but not too persistent rise in inflation to a ‘measured’ tightening of monetary policy. Our view is this can be justified. On our latest forecasts, HICP is estimated at 3.1% in 2026 and 2.5% in 2027 – cumulatively almost 2pp higher than the pre-conflict forecast (core estimated at 2.4% in both years, cumulatively 1pp above pre- conflict). Surveys show strong evidence of passthrough , household inflation expectations have increased , and tightening supply chains could amplify the inflation shock. However, uncertainties are high and we describe the policy outlook as measured tightening at most. This is especially the case given the downside concerns about growth: a cooling labour market, tightening financial conditions and the potential for non-linear activity dynamics from fuel shortages. An agreed order for 200 Boeing jets is being sold as a large win by the US, but is below hopes. Market access to China and Chinese investment in US industries are likely to progress. We expect the talks to continue under the status quo, while a comprehensive “grand deal” may only come when President Xi comes to Washing- ton DC on September 24. The backdrop for the summit is a Chinese economy that is expanding but remains increasingly imbalanced—heavily reliant on exports and investments in strategically important industries while the rest of the economy struggles under the weight of over-capacity and a still-contracting housing mar- ket. The imbalance was underscored this week as exports sur- prised to the upside in April while weaker-than-expected loan creation points to soft domestic demand from households and corporates. Hard activity data for April are due next Monday. We look for a 0.5%m/m sa gain in IP, a 0.1% uptick in retail sales, and broadly stable FAI growth at 1.8%oya, ytd. In the event, global core consumer price increases outside China have remained elevated around 3%ar since 2H23. This has come alongside sustained above-potential growth and tight labor markets that have fueled pressure on both goods and services prices. Two recent developments are upending the debate about inflation inertia and the monetary policy path. The energy price spike is now raising inflation and generating a sharp squeeze on household purchasing power that could intensify if the Middle East conflict keeps the Strait of Hormuz closed. The risk of a negative growth shock raising unemployment rates is thus high, an outcome that would ultimately prove disinflationary and warrant lower policy rates. However, incoming news also points to strong global growth momentum lifting global core goods inflation. The expected signs are intuitive: higher reserves should be associated with lower repo spreads, while faster reserve runoff should push spreads wider. 2) APF gilt holdings. APF gilt holdings capture collateral scarcity. A higher APF holding ratio means a larger share of the gilt market is held inside the APF, reducing the free float available for repo transactions. We therefore use APF holdings as a percentage of total nominal gilts outstanding, rather than the APF stock alone. 3) Treasury bill supply. Treasury bill supply captures the short-collateral channel. More bills outstanding should increase the available stock of safe, short-dated collateral and should therefore be associated with wider repo spreads versus SONIA. We tested both the level of bills outstanding and bills outstanding relative to reserves, in levels and changes. 4) Composition of BoE liquidity provision. The UK is undergoing a regime shift in the way reserves are supplied. Since the GFC, and especially during QE and TFSME, reserves were largely provided through asset purchases and term funding schemes. UK: increasing risks In the UK, risks of a leadership challenge to the PM have increased, though a delay is looking increasingly possible. The risks have prompted questions from clients on the economic and fiscal policy implications of a potential leadership change. This can affect the economy through several channels. First, a leadership challenge in itself is likely to increase near-term policy uncertainty and lead to tighter financial conditions, which could weigh on growth. The process of electing a new leader could take months, keeping uncertainty on economic and fiscal policy elevated. Uncertainty can delay investment and consumption decisions, also weighing on growth. The latter is the risk we would worry more about very near term. Catalyst.Metric: Rubin GPU liquid cooling supply temperature

records.text: Air Cooling is NOT Going Away Air cooling is still going to be needed in AI data centers. Outside of full immersion cooling designs, data centers operate as hybrid thermal systems. Liquid cooling typically targets only the highest-heat-flux components—such as GPUs and, in some cases, CPUs—while networking equipment, memory, storage, power electronics, and ancillary systems remain well suited to air cooling from both a cost and serviceability perspective. Air cooling also supports facility-level operations by managing residual heat loads, maintaining ambient conditions, and providing flexibility, redundancy, and ease of maintenance across heterogeneous hardware fleets. In practice, the industry is not eliminating air cooling, but relegating it from a system-limiting constraint to a supporting role beneath liquid-dominant architectures optimized for AI workloads. Chillers Are NOT Being Displaced The Street overreacted to Nvidia's comments about chillers. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang drew significant attention in January 2026 when he stated that Nvidia’s next-generation Rubin GPU architecture would operate with a ~45 °C liquid cooling supply temperature, similar to its Blackwell-based systems, despite materially higher power density. Given the sensitivity of markets to unpredictable geopolitical developments and newsflow, we can turn to statistical methods in an attempt to identify trading opportunities that should be relatively insensitive to the aforementioned drivers. Last week, we noted how the price of oil has become the new principal component, the first PC of a PCA on the swap yield curve is now strongly correlated with the price of oil (Interest Rate Derivatives: Oil is the new principal component, US Fixed Income Markets Weekly, 5/8/2026). In a similar vein, doing a principal component analysis on SOFR futures (proxied by swaps), we see a similar story. PC1 continues to explain a large fraction of the moves in yields, ~80%, while other PCs explain much less (Figure 4). We can use these results to find trades that should be relatively insensitive to macro drivers, such as the price of oil. PC4 appears noise-like (Figure 5) and has very little correlation with the price of oil. We can thus construct trades that have a high correlation to PC4 and thus can be reasonably expected to be mean-reverting and relatively insensitive to macro factors. One such trade is a U6/Z6/ M7/M8 box spread using 3M SOFR futures (with risk weights of -0.6, +1, -0.63, and +0.28 respectively). As we have discussed in prior notes, much of the earlier premium embedded in the curve—partly reflecting Dutch pension fund (PF) transition dynamics and the associated receiving pressure in the long end—has been gradually absorbed, and the curve is no longer obviously dislocated in either direction. That said, the structural backdrop is not neutral: the Dutch PF transition process continues to generate episodic monthly rebal- ancing flows from schemes that have transitioned, and while funds have been mixed and opportunistic in their timing (which dampens the pace of any move), the medium-term bias is that further transitions over the next 6-12 months leans toward incremental paying pres- sure in the long end over time. Solvency II-related dynamics add a further layer, with long- end hedging behavior that can tilt toward steepening over a multi-quarter horizon. These structural forces are not powerful enough to drive a sharp near-term move, but they do pro- vide a medium-term steepening bias that we continue to hold. The practical implication is that we want to be positioned for steepening over the medium term but without being exposed to the near-term risk of a front-end-driven flattening. We decomposed the contribution of the different variables to the fitted model to understand what variables are more relevant for the curve premium. We highlight the relevant role of inflation expectations, strengthening the view that premium could sharply increase if the market prices in a scenario of BanRep’s independence being compromised (Fig 4 ). COP implied volatility: Risk premium for the election is high compared with typical daily volatility, and the daily implied breakeven for both the first and second round has risen as the vote approaches, Post - event one - week implied vol now prices a roughly 3.5% breakeven for both rounds (Figure 5); notably the first round has risen from previously pricing in a lower breakeven than the second round, which may reflect an increase in hedging of an outright Cepeda victory. Elections typically delivery binary outcomes, which means implied vol around the event settles down at a fair value equivalent to probability - weighted expected returns. In this case a straddle costing 3.5% means either a 50% change of USDCOP 3.5% higher or lower, or a small chance of a large move in one direction. That said, we do not expect USD/JPY to trade materially above 160 given the persistent risk of FX intervention.

In contrast to the US, Europe has moved rapidly toward a formal, standardized regulatory regime for data center water and energy use. The revised EU Energy Efficiency Directive (EED), adopted in 2023 and now being implemented by Member States, represents the first binding, EU-wide framework treating data center water use as a regulated efficiency metric rather than a voluntary ESG disclosure. Under the EED, data centers above 500 kW of installed IT capacity must disclose facility-level water withdrawals, water sources (potable vs. non-potable), cooling system type, and Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE) using standardized templates. These disclosures are public, location-specific, and designed to support benchmarking across operators and countries, materially raising transparency and reputational exposure. Several European countries had already imposed local caps or moratoria before EU-level action —most notably in the Netherlands, Ireland, and parts of Germany—driven by constraints on water, power, or both. The new EU framework effectively hard-codes water performance into permitting, incentives, and sustainable-finance claims, tightening the link between cooling design and regulatory approval. Europe also places greater emphasis on waste-heat reuse, particularly through district-heating systems in Northern Europe. There have been six types of FBs issued to date, depending on the legal basis: Ministry of Finance Bills, Fiscal Loan Fund Bills, Foreign Exchange Fund Bills, Petroleum Bills, Nuclear Damage Compen- sation Support Bills, and Food Bills. Previously, each was issued separately and mostly purchased by the BoJ, but in FY1999, the system shifted to a public auction format, and FBs began to be issued in an integrated man- ner. Furthermore, since February 2009, FBs have been issued together with Treasury Bills (TBs) as Treasury Discount Bills (T-bills), which is now the unified name for these short- term government securities. For contracts with negligible embedded option values, the relative value of the calendar spread can be determined by comparing the implied repo rate (IRR) of the calendar spread to the forward three-month funding rate. The relevant three-month Euro future is generally used as a proxy for the forward funding rate. The calendar spread IRR is the breakeven funding rate for going long the calendar spread, taking delivery in the front month and making delivery in the back month contract. If the calendar IRR is historically low compared to the three-month forward rate for a particular market, the calendar spread may be considered rich. For contracts where delivery options in the futures are valuable, such as U.S. Treasury bond futures, a simple IRR analysis is inadequate because it overlooks the potential impact of switches in the cheapest-to- deliver bond. In addition to the income test, a qualified low-income housing project must also satisfy the “gross rents test,” which requires that rents, adjusted for bedroom size, do not exceed 30% of either 50% or 60% of AMI, depending on which income test option the project elected. records.text: 214/05/2026 Electric vehicles: Crisis to catalyst KEY MESSAGES We expect a continued rise in global EV penetration as the Middle East conflict encourages reduced dependence on imported oil and stronger energy security. Global EV sales are likely to be led by robust momentum in Europe, with downside risks to absolute volumes in both the US and China. We forecast firm demand and supply constraints to keep battery metals prices high this year, but with limited pass-through to battery and EV prices, thanks to persistent overcapacity and increasing vertical integration across the EV supply chain. Elevated aluminium prices and premiums will bring significant input cost implications for automakers, in our view, with added pressure on US-based automakers from import duties. Advances in battery technologies, charging infrastructure and autonomous driving are likely to become key differentiators in an increasingly competitive EV market. records.text: educe energy efficiency and require greater chiller capacity. Favored in regions where water usage is restricted or where water sustainability is a priority. How it works: A CRAH unit functions as a large air handler equipped with chilled-water coils. Warm air from the server room is drawn into the CRAH, where it passes over the coils containing chilled water. The chilled water absorbs heat from the air, which is then recirculated back into the room as cooled air. The now-warmed water is pumped to outdoor air-cooled chiller. These mechanical chillers use a refrigeration cycle to remove the heat from the water, transferring it to a refrigerant. The refrigerant is then cooled by an integrated air-cooled condenser, which uses fans to blow cool ambient outside air across coils carrying the hot refrigerant. The cooled refrigerant is recirculated within the chiller, and the chilled water is returned to the CRAH units. This is a fully closed-loop system with no evaporative water loss. 'Free cooling' optional enhancement: The system is often paired with air-side economizers when ambient temperatures are low enough for extended periods to enable free cooling for a substantial portion of the year. This enables the system to bypass the mechanical air-cooled chillers by using filtered outside air to be used directly for cooling the data hall, improving energy efficiency and reducing wear on the mechanical chillers. 13 May 2026 34 Barclays | Thematic Investing

We expect SEK to catch up to these peers as energy stability allows for a broadening out of the USD weakening trend to cyclical currencies and a full compression in EUR-SEK interest rates bolsters the SEK rally into 2027. Key catalysts: Risk appetite, Riksbank and ECB rates, global growth expectations, commodity and energy prices, consumer spending SEK is noticeable among its risk-sensitive G10 peers for its underperformance YTD. Given SEK’s strong links to global growth and European cyclicality, we think this is understandable and reflects that the buoyancy of risk assets is not necessarily reflecting buoyancy in global growth expectations. But we think over time there is capacity for SEK to ‘catch up’ to its peers as energy prices stabilize. This is particularly true once the ECB begins cutting rates in 2027, which should see the carry on EUR/SEK shorts turn from modestly negative to flat. We think the combination of supportive rate differentials, supportive risk appetite, and, eventually, supportive cyclical growth expectations should see SEK lead G10 currency gains in the coming months. Given the sensitivity of markets to unpredictable geopolitical developments and newsflow, we can turn to statistical methods in an attempt to identify trading opportunities that should be relatively insensitive to the aforementioned drivers. Last week, we noted how the price of oil has become the new principal component, the first PC of a PCA on the swap yield curve is now strongly correlated with the price of oil (Interest Rate Derivatives: Oil is the new principal component, US Fixed Income Markets Weekly, 5/8/2026). In a similar vein, doing a principal component analysis on SOFR futures (proxied by swaps), we see a similar story. PC1 continues to explain a large fraction of the moves in yields, ~80%, while other PCs explain much less (Figure 4). We can use these results to find trades that should be relatively insensitive to macro drivers, such as the price of oil. PC4 appears noise-like (Figure 5) and has very little correlation with the price of oil. We can thus construct trades that have a high correlation to PC4 and thus can be reasonably expected to be mean-reverting and relatively insensitive to macro factors. One such trade is a U6/Z6/ M7/M8 box spread using 3M SOFR futures (with risk weights of -0.6, +1, -0.63, and +0.28 respectively). Since late‑2025, the FSR has been actively deployed against Chinese companies across the rail, clean‑tech, and digital sectors, marking a clear shift toward enforcement (Exhibit 10). The April 2026 decision in the Lisbon metro case – where a Chinese rail supplier (CRRC) was effectively excluded – represents the first binding remedy under the FSR procurement tool and signals a more interventionist stance. More broadly, the pattern of cases suggests that the FSR is evolving into a complementary instrument to trade defence, targeting subsidised competitive distortions that manifest inside the EU rather than at the border. Taken together, these measures point to a clear intensification of EU trade defence policy vis‑à‑vis China, extending from border measures to in‑market regulation in an effort to contain the impact of potential subsidised excess capacity.

records.text: This is where the conclusions of this thematic report reinforce our constructive European utility view. The positive angle is that liquid cooling is becoming an enabling technology for high-density AI data centers, supporting further deployment and, in many cases, improving overall efficiency. At the same time, the report makes clear that investor concerns are often misplaced: liquid cooling itself is not the primary driver of water use, and in some configurations can actually reduce water consumption by limiting reliance on evaporative cooling. That said, cooling and water are becoming more relevant variables for DC siting and execution. The key issue is not simply whether data centers use water, but the trade-off between power efficiency and water intensity. In water-stressed or highly regulated regions, cooling design, permitting timelines and local community acceptance may increasingly shape where projects get built and at what pace. For European utilities, that means the DC opportunity remains attractive, but the winners are likely to be those with the right combination of power availability, grid access, supportive regulation and, increasingly, credible water and cooling solutions. We see a "Magnificent Seven" of European utilities exposed to DC sensitivity: Drax (OW), Enel (OW), Engie (OW), Fortum (EW), Naturgy (EW), RWE (OW) and SSE (OW), with Drax, SSE and RWE most preferred. We are neutral on the very front of the curve though, and are therefore neutral. Repo risk and hedging: Bond futures prices are affected by repo rates through carry, which depends on the term repo rate to the delivery of the bond. Movements in the overall level of term repo rates can cause the roll to richen or cheapen, as repo carries a heavier weight in the price of the back contract, and changes in the spread between term repo for the front contract and term repo for the back contract can also impact the roll. To hedge against repo risk, we use the nearest 1-month and 3-month SOFR futures contracts for the front and back Treasury futures; rate expectations implied by SOFR futures can be used as a proxy for 1-month and 3-month term repo. In the current roll, these contracts are SERM6 for the front contract and SFRM6 for the back contract. To show the impact of repo on the roll, we examine past DV01-hedged rolls with and without hedges for repo and the hedge performance (Exhibit 6 and Exhibit 7 ). records.text: 4 Europe accelerates: The 2025–26 policy environment reflects a balancing act between measures to stabilise the auto market by easing short-term supply-side pressures and intensifying efforts to support medium-term EV adoption. At the national level, several countries are introducing initiatives to support EV adoption. Italy has allocated EUR600mn in funding, to be used by mid-2026, aiming to replace 39,000 ICE vehicles. Germany has reintroduced its tax-subsidy scheme, with a budget of EUR3bn, to support the purchase of around 800,000 vehicles between January 2026 and end-2029. France also plans to launch the third wave of its social leasing programme for EVs as early as June. Meanwhile, supply-side protection is becoming more prominent. The EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act envisages a requirement for EV manufacturers receiving state support to source at least 70% of their car components (excluding batteries) within the bloc. On batteries, the proposed act would introduce restrictions on foreign investments of more than EUR100mn (which would likely apply to most battery factories). The current draft sets out six requirements – related to local hiring, R&D spending, intellectual property sharing, sourcing, mandatory joint ventures, and a 49% cap on foreign ownership – with foreign investors having to comply with at least four of them. We start by assessing the impact of the 2025 US tariff wave on China’s exports to the EU (cross-checking against China’s exports to the US as a control) and any tariff-specificity attached to Chinese product baskets more heavily tariffed than EU goods. Our sample ranges from 2021 to January 2026. We classify HS2 sectors into three categories: product‑specific tariffs (Section 232), country‑specific tariffs (reciprocal), and a tariff- excluded group. We define the tariff implementation period as post April 2025. We first identify the tariff shock within each destination by running separate HS2 fixed‑effects regressions for the US and the EU, using a post‑April 2025 dummy to capture the introduction of the new tariffs. Across all HS2 sectors, the 2025 tariff episode is associated with a large and robust slowdown in Chinese export growth to the US. In our specifications, we find a statistically significant decline in Chinese export growth to the US of ca20-22% post April. The results also hold once year fixed effects are included. By contrast, Chinese export growth to the EU displays a mild – but not statistically significant – increase. Political steps, not all of them forwards After a febrile and fast-moving week of politics, at the time of writing the state of play is: (former) Health Secretary Wes Streeting has resigned his cabinet position and called for a change in leadership but has not triggered the challenge himself; Angela Rayner has been cleared of wrongdoing by HMRC following questions around her tax affairs but has confirmed she would not trigger a leadership challenge; and Mayor of Manchester Andy Burnham has found an MP to stand down from their seat and he will contest the seat as a Labour candidate in a by-election – if he is successful in winning the seat and becoming an MP , this could allow him to challenge for the leadership. However, until he is an MP he is unable to trigger that leadership challenge. In Possible political paths (12 May), we outlined the timing and process for a leadership challenge from MPs (Streeting/Rayner/others) and from non-MPs (Burnham). We think developments this week have shifted the probability towards the latter. On that basis, the 21-27 working day minimum timetable for a by-election to occur means we think it less likely that we see a leadership challenge of any sort over the next few weeks, and means the earliest feasible date - if the formal process is begun next week - is Thursday 18 June (by-elections are conducted on Thursdays in the UK). The present regime of compressed realized volatility, anchored policy expectations, and narrow trading ranges depends on energy markets remaining in a fragile but stable balance. Either a rapid normalization or a disorderly escalation would likely produce a sharp repricing in both rates and volatility markets. Bear case Our bear case is that the energy market successfully adapts to the disruption for much longer than currently expected. Under this scenario, inventory draws, higher US exports, rerouted trade flows, and weaker Chinese imports collectively offset the loss of Strait of Hormuz capacity sufficiently to prevent oil prices from reaching true demand destruction levels. Inflation pressure remains contained, central banks avoid a meaningful policy response, and the global economy gradually adjusts to a structurally tighter but manageable energy environment. In that world, realized volatility likely remains subdued, front-end implied volatility continues to decay, and the current calm in rates markets persists for longer than we expect. With investors continuing to debate the USD's long- run status, including its likely response to risk shocks and overall performance, we think a reduction in hedge costs will bolster hedging flows. That said, we see the window for EUR/USD strength as fundamentally limited in both magnitude and duration. The ECB's tolerance for a higher EUR remains finite; a stronger EUR may help offset the rise in imported inflation from energy prices, but it also amplifies growth weakness at a time where growth concerns are rising, not falling. We also see scope for EUR-negative risk premium to increase in the currency as we approach the French Presidential election in early 2027. More broadly, we think the outperformance of US asset returns versus Europe is likely to keep the long-term flow of capital into the US, not Europe, which limits EUR/USD's capacity to rally more. Indeed, we remain skeptical of longer-running arguments around 'dedollarization'; we see little evidence of a broad shift away from US assets and, without a credible alternative, think investor concerns over the USD’s reserve status are perhaps overblown. The result is EUR/USD has capacity to rally further amid a cyclical DXY weakening trend, but we continue to emphasize its limited scope to rally beyond 1.25 barring meaningful changes in the local outlook, and see EUR as more likely to return to funding currency status than asset currency status. Step 2: Heat rejection to the atmosphere. Once captured, the heat must be rejected outside the data center. This can occur via several pathways, including: • Fans exhausting hot air directly to the atmosphere; • Fans blowing cooler outside air across a condenser coil or heat exchanger containing warm refrigerant or liquid; • Or fans pulling outside air through water (via misting or wetted media), forcing heat and water vapor into the atmosphere—a process known as evaporative cooling, which involves direct water consumption. Between Step 1 and Step 2, heat may be transferred between air, water, or a refrigerant, or between multiple closed-loop systems using the same medium at different temperatures. The result is a wide range of cooling system permutations, which we detail in the Data Center Cooling Technology Overview section. Cooling system selection depends on numerous factors, including data center size and type (edge, colocation, enterprise, hyperscale), server power density, capital and operating costs, regional climate conditions (temperature and humidity), power and water availability, and broader sustainability objectives. records.text: M Global Insight 178 Investment strategy: Maintaining the 1y1y/1y4y SOFR/TONA basis curve flattener With the front-end USD/JPY basis expected to remain flat to tightening, while the medium- to long-term sector is expected to widen, we maintain the 1y1y/1y4y SOFR/ TONA basis flattener that we recommended in our 2026 outlook, noting that the medium- to long-term sector has a tendency to widen when reports on US-bound investments and loans emerge. More recently, as a result of the situation in Iran, the entire curve has tightened as a reaction to the earlier deterioration in risk sentiment and widening in credit spreads, leaving the 1y1y/1y4y SOFR/TONA basis broadly rangebound. Going forward, we expect the medium-term sector to outperform on a relative basis, supported by gradual widening in US credit spreads and US-bound investments and loans, and we think the 1y1y/1y4y SOFR/TONA basis flattener should work. The carry and roll on this position is currently +0.5bp, which is not attractive in terms of carry trade. However, we would approach the position as one in which paying in the front- end hedges the negative carry from receiving in the medium- to long-term sector. We see two risks to this strategy. First, if the global economy falls into recession and USD demand rises, the short-term sector could lead a widening move. Second, if US credit spreads tighten sharply, the SOFR/TONA basis in the medium-term sector could tighten by more than the front end. Exhibit 317:1y1y/1y4y SOF

records.text: US Economic Weekly | 15 May 2026 9 Core views Growth: to remain trendlike • The Iran conflict poses stagflationary risks as the oil shock is likely to weigh on consumer spending and business investment. But we still see several tailwinds supporting growth this year, including lagged benefits from Fed rate cuts, more supportive trade policy, ongoing AI-related investment, and favorable shutdown- related base effects. Taking these factors into consideration, we marked down our 2026 GDP forecasts. We now look for growth to come in at 2.1% on a 4Q/4Q basis and 2.3% on the annual average. Inflation: to remain stuck above the Fed’s target through 2027 • We now forecast headline PCE inflation to peak in 2Q 2026 at 4.1% and to remain above our prior forecast for the rest of this year due to higher oil prices. We expect headline inflation falls quickly next year, as oil retraces. But we project price levels at the end of next year to be above our prior forecast, capturing higher food inflation and some lasting impact on global supply chains. The surge in energy prices is likely to pass through to core inflation as well, with a lag. We now expect 4Q/4Q 2026 core PCE to come in at 3.3%, vs. 2.8% previously. GBP faces the greatest risk of a dovish surprise when we compare our forecasts to market pricing, which could further weigh on the currency. Finally, we think investors remain generally cautious on the currency given concerns that political and/or fiscal risk premia in UK assets could increase. The result is that, while we think GBP could outperform the USD in the near term, its gains in GBP/USD terms are limited, and we think GBP will lag its risk-sensitive peers such as in the Nordics, the Antipodeans, and higher-quality EMs. Key risks to the view: We think investors are generally more concerned with GBP downside risks than upside risks. The result is that GBP/USD rising above 1.40 is a likely underdiscussed – and underpriced – risk. A hawkish BoE pivot, leading GBP to 'outcompete' its G10 peers on carry, could be supportive here. We are also watching AI adoption in the UK closely; an increase in potential growth and neutral rates could offer a sustainable boost to the currency. Conversely, a meaningful increase in fiscal and/or political risk premium could prove a key headwind to the currency, particularly if investors become increasingly concerned about the UK's balance of payments.

records.text: 2 Source: Oddschecker Timing interacts with BoE At the time of writing, it is being briefed that the by-election will be conducted at this earliest opportunity. That date also coincides with the next BoE decision, which could complicate communications as the BoE's standard practice is to observe political quiet periods and avoid making significant public statements in the run up to elections. We think that on balance this further reduces the likelihood of a Bank Rate hike in June (see below for our broader arguments as to why we expect a hold), as we think the MPC has shown itself to prefer to retain optionality and defer big turning points until known moments of potential volatility have passed. Expect to hear more on policy in the coming weeks This week, policy platform papers have been released from different constituencies within the Labour Party, with the more right/centrist vision of shifting the tax burden from labour income to capital income being outlined by Labour Growth and a "soft left" agenda to reform fiscal rules and focus on longer-term investment outlined by the Tribune Group. However, with the increased likelihood now that Andy Burnham will be the most significant challenger, focus will be on his "Manchesterism" policy platform. We await a formal publication in the coming days and weeks, but from what is already known, its key tenets are bringing key sectors and services into public ownership, a more pro-European approach and devolution of powers to regions.

Export growth is likely to be modestly dented by logistical disruption linked to the Middle East conflict and by China’s export bans on products such as fertilisers and fuel, we think. That said, unless a prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz significantly hampers global growth, we do not expect a severe hit to China’s exports – especially given an ongoing auto-export boom and strong AI-induced semiconductor tailwinds (see Global Outlook Spring 2026: Looking beyond the war, dated 24 April). We no longer expect the PBoC to cut the policy rate this year. China’s Politburo meeting at end-April signalled a degree of confidence about the growth outlook that likely rules out any near-term monetary easing (see China: Politburo offers no hint of additional easing, dated 29 April). Moreover, banks’ net interest margin remains a major constraint. We do, however, see a risk of a rate cut in H2 2026 if growth drops below 4.5% due to greater repercussions from the energy shock. records.text: before the conflict escalation, and suggest entering a 10s20s SONIA steepener. We also have sympathy with paying the 10s20s30s SONIA fly, given the high correlation between the two structures. However, 10s20s offers slightly better carry and roll — around 1bp over three months versus roughly 0.5bp for 10s20s30s (despite having a similar carry-to-roll ratio) — making the simpler curve expression our preferred implementation. The key risk to the trade is a bear flattener, most likely driven by a more hawkish BoE repricing. In Exhibit 127 , we report UK gilt cross-market flies versus USTs and Bund/Buxl for both the 10y and 30y sectors, alongside the 1y1y swap fly as a proxy for the repricing in relative central-bank expectations. The underperformance in the 10y and 30y sectors has been mostly driven by front-end repricing. Since 27 February 2026, December 2026 meeting fixings have repriced by around 80bp, 115bp and 60bp for the ECB, BoE and Fed, respectively (see Exhibit 128 ). On this basis, the main driver of UK duration underperformance appears to be the relative repricing of BoE policy expectations, rather than a pure long-end term-premium shock.

Two shocks are currently converging – the minimum-wage increase announced in late 2025 and the rise in global energy prices – and a third may arise from the increasing likelihood of a strong El Niño event by the end of 2026. We expect these factors to keep inflation expectations under pressure this year and next. Consequently, even if an opposition candidate (Paloma Valencia or Abelardo de la Espriella) wins and domestic asset prices react positively, BanRep will likely need to restart the hiking cycle that it paused in April (see Colombia: Implications of BanRep’s surprise hold, dated 5 May). If the government-backed Ivan Cepeda wins, inflation will probably face an additional shock from a sharp depreciation of the exchange rate. BanRep’s response in the June and July meetings is still uncertain to us. Two factors make it unclear whether BanRep will resume hikes. ▪ In the event of an opposition victory, we cannot rule out that President Gustavo Petro will attempt another minimum-wage increase. Even a fraction of the c.70GW European DC pipeline we have identified could tighten power balances and support a broader inflection in electricity demand. What is increasingly clear, however, is that the data-centercenter opportunity is not just about incremental power demand, but also about how that demand is served. As AI workloads raise rack power densities, cooling is becoming a more strategic constraint alongside grid access. Generally, ser- vicers prefer to keep loans in pools if the buyout financing is more expensive than the MBS coupon payment. But there’s also Ginnie’s serious delinquency thresholds to contend with—no more than 5% of a servicer’s Ginnie book can be 90+. Ginnie recently relaxed that rule by allowing servicers to exclude loans currently in trial periods. That’ll help blunt some of the recent run up in delinquencies (Figure 34S e r i o u s d e l i n q u e n c y r a t i o s c o n t i n u e t o s h i f t u p w a r d s , t h o u g h l o a n s i n t r i a l s w i l l n o w b e e x c l u d e d f r o m G i n n i e ’ s 5 % c a p ). However, since many of these borrowers will fail their trials (they get two trial attempts, to be fair), there could be a moderate build in delinquencies until foreclosures can be processed. It’s going to be a bit difficult for us to see which servicers have actually breached the newly defined serious delinquency thresholds because the MBS data will still report loans in trials as being delinquent. There’s also no MBS disclosure that identifies whether a loan is in a trial. As a result, it’s going to be hard for us to have a firm sense of whether a servicer might be prepping for a wave of buyouts based on this data; merely observing the MBS delinquen- cy ratios won’t give us quite enough information to tell whether a servicer is actually in breach of their delinquency limits.

records.text: Air-cooled CRAC Air-cooled Compute Room Air Conditioner (CRAC) units operate similar to commercial split- system air conditioners. It provides very low energy efficiency (~1.5-1.8 PUE) compared to modern centralized or liquid-cooled systems since each CRAC unit has its own compressor, leading to less efficient part-load performance. Its closed-loop refrigeration system does not consume water. Where it is commonly used: These systems are typically found in small or edge data centers due to their simple, modular design; relatively low upfront cost; and minimal infrastructure requirements. They are generally not used in modern large-scale data centers because of their lower energy efficiency, limited cooling capacity, and lack of scalability since they don't rely on a centralized cooling architecture. How it works: An indoor Direct Expansion (DX) CRAC unit contains a refrigerant compressor, evaporator coil, and fan. It draws warm air from the server room and passes it over the evaporator coil, where heat is absorbed into a circulating refrigerant. The heated refrigerant is then pumped to a separate outdoor air-cooled condenser—often located on the roof or exterior of the building—where fans blow ambient air across finned coils to dissipate the heat into the atmosphere. Our commodity strategists expect that the accelerating pace of inventory depletion will ulti- mately force the reopening of the Strait in June and a market that stays tight even after flows resume. Consequently, JPMorgan now expects Brent Oil prices to remain in the low $100s through most of 2026 (avg ~$97) (link). Meanwhile, inflation continues to climb in response to the energy shock as evidenced by this week’s firm core CPI and PPI readings. And notably, OIS forwards now price in 60% odds the Fed could deliver a hike (not cut) by the December meeting. Encouragingly, however, the economy continues to exhibit resilience with this week’s retail sales topping consensus and continuing claims suggesting a possible decline in the unemployment rate at the next release. This follows a partial 0.5% increase in fuel taxes at the beginning of the month, with further adjustments postponed until June. The govern- ment has passed through approximately 23% of the global oil price rise into local prices, with the current local price sitting around 15% below import parity. Notably, the local price was about 20% above import parity before the conflict, providing some cushion to smooth the adjustment. Looking ahead, with Brent oil prices projected to remain in the low 100s for the remainder of the year, we now assume full convergence to import parity within a 4-6 month period and a partial fuel tax adjustment. This is expected to add 1.2%-pt to headline inflation from the oil shock through the remainder of the year, accounting for both direct and certain second-round effects. As a result, operators increasingly view cooling not as a single technology choice, but as a portfolio decision optimized at the regional and site-level. When retrofitting existing data centers, cooling technology choices are often constrained by legacy infrastructure. These constraints can include limited electrical distribution capacity, fixed chilled-water loop temperatures, insufficient floor loading capacity, restricted mechanical space for new equipment, or air-handling layouts designed for lower rack densities. In many cases, operators are also be motivated to reuse existing cooling assets, such as cooling towers, chillers, or piping networks, to reduce capital costs and downtime. This can favor incremental upgrades—such as efficiency enhancements, controls optimization, or hybrid cooling configurations—over full system replacement. By contrast, new-build facilities offer greater flexibility, allowing operators to tailor cooling systems to local climate, water availability, and long-term sustainability goals from the outset. 13 May 2026 31 Barclays | Thematic Investing

records.text: Asia Economic Weekly | 15 May 2026 5 RBNZ: pre-emptive tighten or look through In our view, there is a strong case for the RBNZ to look through the current energy spike, given inflation pressures are predominantly supply driven and that effective monetary conditions have already tightened materially. Core inflation measures are easing, demand is soft, spare capacity is building, and wage growth remains consistent with the inflation midpoint. That said, the case for front loading policy tightening is that headline inflation is set to rise further in the near term and risks entrenching inflation expectations, even if driven by supply shocks. A pre-emptive tightening could be viewed as insurance against second round effects, ensuring expectations remain anchored before supply side pressures spill over into non tradables and wages. Our base case is still that the RBNZ remain on hold in 2026, but we note a material risk of pre-emptive hikes. If the RBNZ do hike in 2026, this would likely mean cuts in 2027 as the effects of demand destruction become more evident.

One key point of our outlook is that the situation today is quite different from 2022. Europe appears more fundamentally vulnerable: fiscal space is much more limited, pent-up demand and savings will not help as much as they did just after Covid, and interest rates are higher. But, as of today, the energy crisis is also much less severe. Europe is less energy dependant than it was in 2022, and, even more importantly, natural gas prices are still very far from the high levels seen during 2022. As a result, absorption cooling remains niche and is rarely competitive with conventional data center cooling approaches. As AI-driven data centers expand, siting decisions are increasingly driven by power availability, permitting speed, land access, and geopolitics, rather than proximity to heat demand. As a result, heat reuse is pursued opportunistically, not as a primary factor in cooling architecture or site selection. Data Center Cooling Technology Overview There is no one-size-fits-all solution. Data center cooling system design can be highly site-specific and depend on a combination of technical, geographic, regulatory, and sustainability considerations. Key variables include regional climate conditions (e.g., ambient temperatures, humidity levels, and seasonal variability), availability and cost of water and electricity, sustainability objectives (including emissions and water-use targets), and data center characteristics such as facility size, workload profile, and server power density. Higher-density and AI-oriented workloads, in particular, are pushing cooling systems toward more advanced architectures—such as direct-to-chip liquid cooling or hybrid solutions—while traditional enterprise or cloud workloads may continue to rely on air-based or evaporative systems where conditions allow. The increase in the overall core reflected an increase in goods prices, along with a record rise (since data began in 2010) in wholesale/retail margins and transportation, with the latter two categories exhibiting some spillover from higher energy prices. Nonfuel import prices also rose 0.8% as demand from data centers yielded a record increase in computer prices. records.text: 4 Europe Economic Weekly | 15 May 2026 Europe China-EU trade: imbalance over tariff effects Chiara Angeloni BofA Europe (Milan) chiara.angeloni@bofa.com Ruben Segura -Cayuela BofA Europe (Madrid) ruben.segura-cayuela@bofa.com Please see the full report: Euro Area Viewpoint: China-EU trade: the story is macro imbalance, not tariff diversion Europe’s mopping up of China exports precedes US tariffs China’s trade surplus with the EU overtook that with the US in 1Q26, exceeding USD300bn for the first time. While the 2025 US tariff wave triggered a sharp and broad-based slowdown in Chinese exports to the US, EU imports from China rose 11.6% yoy last year. But this trend did not start in April 2025: EU imports from China were well above pre-pandemic levels even before last year’s tariffs hit. Tariff-induced rerouting: a second-order story US tariffs worked as intended against Chinese exports: we estimate that post April 2025, they slowed by ca20-26% across HS2 manufacturing sectors. Yet there has been no statistically robust increase in China’s export growth to the EU due to 2025 US tariff- induced trade rerouting. When controlling for tariff type, we find that reciprocal tariffs did have a major impact on diverting Chinese exports away from the US. But tariff specificities again fail to explain the aggregate surge in EU imports from China. In sum, tariffs reduced US imports but fail to explain any meaningful rerouting toward Europe. ‘Vent-for-surplus’ theory explains rising EU expo

While part of the strength reflects temporary factors such as energy price gains, underlying momentum is also gradually improving, as evidenced by firmer services inflation and strength in PPI segments tied to AI and electrification. That said, still-soft domestic demand is likely to cap the upside in inflation, while resilient external trade reduces the urgency for additional domestic stimulus. records.text: Immersion Cooling The immersion cooling market is fragmented, spanning specialist start-ups, system integrators, and a limited number of large industrial and IT vendors. Purpose-built immersion specialists dominate commercial deployments today, typically offering integrated tanks, heat-exchange systems, and control software, paired with third-party dielectric fluids. Large strategic entrants are increasingly shaping the ecosystem. Trane Technologies (via its LiquidStack acquisition), Schneider Electric (via the Motivair acquisition and ecosystem partnerships), Vertiv (through organic product development and partnerships), and Fujitsu now offer immersion cooling as part of broader data center infrastructure portfolios, generally positioning it alongside direct-to-chip liquid cooling rather than as a wholesale replacement. Private players include Asperitas, GigaIO, Green Revolution Cooling (GRC), Iceotope, LiquidCool Solutions and Submer, all of which focus on modular immersion platforms designed for hyperscale and enterprise AI environments. These companies typically partner closely with server OEMs and chip designers to certify hardware compatibility and streamline maintenance workflows. Fluid Handling & Treatment Equipment The market for data center liquid cooling fluid-handling components—including manifolds, hoses, fittings, pumps, valves, and water treatment equipment—is served by a mix of specialist suppliers and diversified industrial firms. Short JPYKRW. We maintain a constructive view on tech exposure, expecting stronger spillovers from equities into FX as foreign inflows accelerate. Since the onset of the conflict, EM equity earnings revisions surprised to the upside, with 2026 consensus EPS growth rising t o 45.3% (+11.5% since late February). The upgrade has been concentrated in commodity exporters (South Africa, Brazil) and notably Korea, where earnings expectations surged to ~200% (Figure 4). KRW stands out on valuation and flows. It remains the cheapest EM FX on a REER basis versus long-term averages (Figure 5), while real money investors have increasingly rotated into undervalued FX, supporting demand for KRW. In addition, the Bok’s commitment to limit excessive currency volatility provides an implicit downside buffer if risk sentiment deteriorates. On the funding side, we prefer to avoid adding outright USD shorts given existing carry exposures (TRY, BRL). Instead, JPY offers cleaner funding while we do not anticipate near-term BoJ intervention. Stronger Korean equity earnings and supportive flow dynamics contrast with a cyclically weak JPY in a risk-on environment, supporting our tactical short JPYKRW trade. Our adjustment shows spending grew from 2.7% of GDP in January to 2.9% in February and then 3% in March. Spending remained roughly 0.3% of GDP below the execu- tion in 2025. However, this happened in the context of capex at a comparable level as in 2025 (about 1% of GDP in 1Q26) and spending on goods and services sharply accelerating to levels exceeding 2025 - March was 0.5% of GDP, higher than February 2026 or March 2025 (each at 0.4% of GDP). The variable that has been the main driver of the spending decline is the wage bill (Figure 3). The Bolojan government lowered the wage bill in 2025, down to 0.7% of GDP per month in December. This level has been sustained in 1Q26 and, in our view, is unlikely to change. Hence, the decline in spending in 2026 versus 2025 appears to be sustainable and raises the chance of a budget deficit close to 5% of GDP for 2006 as a whole. records.text: odity categories BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH Against this backdrop, China-EU trade dynamics stand out. China’s trade surplus with the EU surpassed that with the US in 1Q26, exceeding USD300bn. This raises key questions about the structural versus cyclical forces driving Chinese exports to Europe: What is the extent of tariff-related trade rerouting? How much depends on genuine comparative advantage (e.g. productivity gains and technological advancements)? Are Chinese domestic subsidies playing any meaningful role? More structurally, are there signs of vent-for-surplus behaviour amid longer-term changes in Chinese domestic demand? Conversely, is there a structural shift in EU demand with respect to specific trade goods/sectors? There are definitely several factors at play. Focusing on China-EU trade flows, we examine: (1) evidence of 2025 US tariff‑induced trade re‑routing; and (2) the role of the vent-for-surplus hypothesis, before and after the 2025 US tariff wave. 1 The empirical literature on the 2018-19 US-China trade war consistently documents a large and causal decline in Chinese exports to the US, driven by tariff increases and concentrated in directly targeted sectors. Product‑level and customs‑data analyses show a sharp contraction in bilateral trade flows, accompanied by significant reallocation of sourcing away from China. We rebuild the liquid forwards from above buckets in log-forward space. This ensures that multi-year forwards are constructed as weighted averages of the exact inflation periods they cover. For example, 5y5y is built from 5y1y through 9y1y, while 10y10y is built from 10y2y, 12y3y and 15y5y. The final rich/cheap signal for each liquid forward is then the difference between the actual market quote and the PCA-implied fair value constructed from the underlying bucket curve ( Exhibit 238 ). Exhibit 239 shows YTD evolution of 5y5y versus its 1m rich/ cheap score. One can also look at 3m z-score to consider a longer trade time horizon. This is broadly consistent with an A/B-type energy outcome in the BoE’s April MPR framework, rather than a persistent Scenario C shock. For the UK, this still implies a difficult policy mix: weak real disposable income growth weighing on consumption, GDP growth remaining below potential, and headline inflation peaking at around 3.4% in 2Q26. Against this backdrop, we expect the BoE to remain on a prolonged hold, albeit with a tightening bias over the next couple of meetings, as policymakers assess the impact of oil supply disruptions and the timing of any reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. We pencil in one provisional cut next year, as inflation data should eventually give the BoE enough confidence to reduce restrictiveness modestly. This leaves us materially more dovish than current market pricing, which discounts around 70bp of hikes through 2027 at the time of writing. While the broad Dollar is close to flat over n the last few months, that obscures larger shifts under the surface and quietly building Dollar appreciation pressure. We have been emphasizing that terms of trade have been a key differentiator for FX returns in this more divided Dollar environment, and it is increasingly clear that two major forces—the energy shock and AI-driven demand—are responsible for the shortages causing that move (more in the ToT bullet below). Our economists have laid out how these factors have opposing effects on growth—we think the AI boom is one reason why global growth has slowed only moderately so far despite a longer disruption to global energy flows—but reinforce each other on the inflation side, at least in the near term. This is consistent with the direction of our macro forecasts: our global growth expectations have been roughly stable since the middle of March (Exhibit 1), despite a longer conflict, while inflation projections have continued to drift higher (Exhibit 2). We think this helps explain the Dollar’s strength over the last week following upside US inflation surprises that helped push global bond yields higher. Disinflation was gaining traction in 2H25 and the domestic activity mix point- ed to a gradual deceleration as tight financial conditions were transmitted through the economy. In this configuration, we viewed the near‑term inflation risks as manageable and the case for larger rate cuts as credible even in the presence of a pronounced acceleration of fiscal outlays in 1H26. This outlook faced a double whammy, particularly following the beginning of the conflict. Even with policy‑induced mechanisms limiting the direct pass‑through of the oil shock to pump prices so far, upward price pressures are now mani- festing elsewhere. Food and non‑food goods inflation have moved higher, reflecting more expensive commodities abroad and rising costs of freight, fertilizers and imported inputs. With services inflation still elevated amid a tight labor mar- ket, and with indexation channels likely to propagate non‑ser- vices pressures into services over time, we now see higher inflation inertia than in our pre‑war baseline. The strong momentum of activity at the beginning of the year reinforced the challenges to our more benign and disinflation- ary view. records.text: European Rates Weekly 14 May 2026 Citi Research 5 Why is the UK curve not steeper? The reaction of the gilt curve to political uncertainty has been limited so far, but there is likely asymmetric steepening risk brewing, in our view, especially now that Andy Burnham may have found a route back to Westminster. T o hedge, earlier this week we entered a £ 3m10s30s conditional bear steepener. Outright volatile with the curve stable: The outbreak of domestic political uncertainty has encouraged 10yr and 30yr gilt yields to historic highs this week, but the curve has been relatively stable so far. Below we put forward some reasons as to why the curve has been unreactive and suggest asymmetric risk for steepening ahead, especially with Andy Burnham on the move. There are probably a few reasons why the curve is not steeper: n(1) Awaiting a contest: While a leadership contest seems increasingly likely, it has still not been triggered at the time of writing. The health secretary Wes Streeting—widely seen as one of those most likely to challenge—resigned on Thursday but did not trigger a contest. That seemed to reduce the chance of an imminent leadership race, but then the news came after the gilt market close on Thursday (see BBC, 14May26) that MP for Makerfield Josh Simons will stand down to allow Andy Burnham to run in a by-election (note, the recent Gorton & Denton by-election was 31 days from announcement to vote). The size of new issue can thus not only affect its concession, but the issuer's outstanding bond spreads as well; for example, through higher firm leverage or temporary supply-demand imbalance. In our white paper Predicting Trading Volume of Corporate Bonds (27 April 2023), we found a spike in trading volume of all outstanding bonds of the issuer when the new issue is priced. The elevated volume lasted for two to four weeks before returning to its long-term trend. To analyse the spread effect, we conduct an event study of the issuer's outstanding bonds' spreads around the new issuance. For each outstanding bond of the issuer in the index, we calculate a relative spread by comparing its spread to peer bonds having the same credit rating and maturity horizon and in the same sector. We then aggregate these relative spreads to the issuer level by market value. We plot the median relative spread across issuers, grouped by the size of their new issues, in Figure 17 (US update). 14 May 2026 16 Barclays | Primary Market

records.text: How retail trading interacts with markets Stocks with above-average retail trading activity generally have above-average valuations, controlling for fundamental factors. A cross-sectional regression of EV/sales multiples across Russell 3000 stocks indicates that fundamental variables such as sales growth and profitability are the primary drivers of stock valuations today. Nevertheless, even after controlling for these characteristics, a one standard deviation increase in retail trading activity corresponds with a 0.16 standard deviation increase in a stock’s forward EV/sales multiple (roughly half a turn). Causality is difficult to prove through this analytical framework, however. Retail investors are generally more active in high valuation stocks (Exhibit 16), and the relationship between retail trading and valuation multiples may reflect a preference for stocks with valuations that are driven by a variable absent from our model. The beta of breakevens to oil has been declining over the past 6 months. As noted here, forwards have not risen as much due to the backwardation of the oil curve. This energy disruption affected the front end more. We published our z-score based model here. In contrast to the regression approach, which is based on estimating "fair value" and assuming market efficiency will result in the actual price converging with this value, the z-score model does a good job in predicting the near-term direction of the next move in breakevens. A high z-score of a variable can mean either of two things: 1) the variable is close to mean- reversion levels and will cause a reversal in breakevens, or 2) the variable will act as a leading indicator for breakevens and cause them to move in its direction. We find in our analysis that the behavior of some of these variables is not constant throughout history, as they sometimes act as leading indicators and sometimes mean- revert depending on the conditions. Beta-weighted breakevens are one example. Beta- weighted breakevens, which adjust breakevens for the move in Treasuries, have been trading range-bound over the past few years. They either act as leading indicators for 10- year breakevens or mean-revert, depending on the level of volatility.

Air-Side Economization Air-side economization uses filtered outside air to directly cool the data center when ambient conditions are favorable, bypassing mechanical cooling systems. This reduces energy consumption and wear on mechanical cooling systems and is common in CRAH + air-cooled chiller systems in cool and temperate climates. How it works: When outdoor air temperature and humidity fall within acceptable thresholds, dampers open to allow filtered outside air to flow into the data halls, displacing or mixing with warm return air. Exhaust fans remove the heated air from the space. This process bypasses traditional mechanical cooling systems, such as chillers or CRACs, significantly reducing energy use. The current YTD U.S. consumer backdrop risks becoming a classic rear-view mirror setup: reported demand still reflects a period of tax-refund-driven demand and benign energy costs offset by tariff pressure, while the forward demand pressure from higher oil prices is only beginning to work through wallets, and is thus far unnoticeable to most of our coverage universe. History is clear—when fuel prices spike, they act like a tax on consumers, compressing discretionary spend with a lag. YTD, the U.S. consumer remains surprisingly resilient; early signs suggest weakening demand risk is on the horizon. Our checks YTD have remained strong with a resilient consumer still spending broadly across discretionary categories. Inventory levels entering the year were quite clean, promotions are notably controlled across all of U.S. Retail, inflation is modest to immaterial across apparel, tariff pressure is subsiding, tax refunds are fueling demand, and high-end HH income cohorts are the driving force in spending. Retailers generally have their inventory purchases covered for the next six to nine months. Although the risk of oil shock on consumption is rising, we have yet to see any impact to date on retail company margins or demand. In this case, a straddle costing 3.5% means either a 50% chance of USDCOP moving 3.5% higher or lower, or a small chance of a large shift in one direction. We think of the presidential election as the latter case: the 3.5% is a probability-weighted average move of a small sell-off or a large rally. This is corroborated by the vol smile, which prices strongly positive spot-vol correlation in a USDCOP higher outcome and discounts lower USDCOP vol in the alternative case (Figure 7). With the risk reversal at its highest level since late 2022 (when USDCOP spot rallied through 4500 and implied vol traded above 20%), the shape of the surface suggests the risk of a repeat is in the price: in the same way that implied vol over the election prices a probability- weighted average spot performance, we think the shape of the smile reflects the mean of a higher-vol and lower- vol outcome. Still, with USDCOP already scaling the 20% level for spot near 4500, there is not-insignificant downside risk from these levels. India: Headline CPI inflation inched up; core inflation remained sticky In India, April headline CPI inflation edged up to 3.48% yoy (vs 3.4% in March). The marginal uptick was mainly on slightly higher food inflation and pick-up in restaurant and accommodation prices owing to upside pressure due to the West Asia conflict. Meanwhile, core inflation remained unchanged at 3.7% yoy for the fourth consecutive month, as sequential increase in services inflation was partially offset by lower gold prices. With the tactical hedge ratio around 2% in December 2025, and with some strategic hedging likely having occurred in recent years when the won traded weak, we view there may be room to expand the hedge ratio by 5- 10% from current levels, equivalent to USD30–60bn. records.text: 15 May 2026 Euro Weekly Digest Deutsche Bank AG Page 5 a reminder, the headline flash print was 3.04% YoY (up from 2.55% in March) while core HICP was 2.19% YoY (down from 2.29% in March). Based on the available final country prints (see Week in review section), no major revisions to these figures are likely (although the second decimal could be revised slightly lower). May flash PMIs (Thu) We have the flash May PMIs on Thursday. Recall the final April PMI prints reinforced concerns about potential stagflation. The Composite PMI in April was revised up slightly to 48.8 from the flash estimate of 48.6, driven primarily by an upward revision in services, notably Italy's stronger performance offsetting a weaker Spanish print. German and French services remained unchanged. The current level of euro area composite PMI marked the lowest since November 2024 and is consistent with a GDP contraction of -0.13% q/q, a downside to mkt. expectation of +0.2% and the ECB's projection of +0.1% for Q2. records.text: US Economic Weekly | 15 May 2026 9 Core views Growth: to remain trendlike • The Iran conflict poses stagflationary risks as the oil shock is likely to weigh on consumer spending and business investment. But we still see several tailwinds supporting growth this year, including lagged benefits from Fed rate cuts, more supportive trade policy, ongoing AI-related investment, and favorable shutdown- related base effects. Taking these factors into consideration, we marked down our 2026 GDP forecasts. We now look for growth to come in at 2.1% on a 4Q/4Q basis and 2.3% on the annual average. Inflation: to remain stuck above the Fed’s target through 2027 • We now forecast headline PCE inflation to peak in 2Q 2026 at 4.1% and to remain above our prior forecast for the rest of this year due to higher oil prices. We expect headline inflation falls quickly next year, as oil retraces. But we project price levels at the end of next year to be above our prior forecast, capturing higher food inflation and some lasting impact on global supply chains. The surge in energy prices is likely to pass through to core inflation as well, with a lag. We now expect 4Q/4Q 2026 core PCE to come in at 3.3%, vs. 2.8% previously. Core inflation could reach 2.3% by end 2027 Labor market: stabilizing around full employment • The labor market has been buffeted by shocks to supply (immigration restrictions) and demand (tariff uncertainty, AI, DOGE).
