Chinese exports surge: Despite a slowdown in China’s domestic market, reflecting tougher base effects and fading subsidies, its EV exports have accelerated in 2026. Exports rose by 12% q/q in Q1 and 32% m/m in March, the strongest monthly growth in three years. Export momentum to EM markets remains particularly strong, supported by favourable local policies. In addition, we see a potential tailwind from higher-for-longer fuel prices. Takeaways from Beijing Autoshow: We see clear read-throughs for the evolution of EV competition from the recent Beijing Autoshow (24 April to 3 May). With anti-involution measures now in place (see page 4), Chinese EV players can no longer rely on minor incremental improvements or aggressive pricing alone. records.text: With renewed focus on the Gilt market given ongoing policy uncertainty, the key question is whether these levels of yields and risk premium are justified. The first place to look for an explanation is the macro performance of the UK economy. Over recent years, UK growth has been weak relative to other economies, but inflation has been the highest. This combination of low growth and high inflation justifies an elevated risk premium as this attenuates the correlation of bonds with growth and weakens their hedge value for risk asset portfolios. In addition, Exhibit 3 and Exhibit 4 show that while macro uncertainty is well off its peak, the UK still exhibits the highest surveyed macro uncertainty among major economies. This has deeper roots in the structure of the UK economy and the nature of recent shocks — for example, a high dependence on gas in the UK energy mix, coupled with a relatively high level of inflation indexation across wages and prices. Risk premium is related to this macro uncertainty and volatility. Realised volatility in UK rates has also been much higher than other economies, and although GBP implied rates vol had fallen ahead of the war in Iran, it is now back to being the highest in major markets. records.text: Strategy: Opportunities in the front end and small caps Dominique Toublan BCI, US | Jack Sweeney BCI, US The front end has noticeably lagged, creating some opportunity. In Are we there yet? Recalibrating after the round-trip, we recently highlighted that performance has favored duration, with curves flattening across the board. More than 90% of 30y bonds trade tighter than they did at the end of February, while only about half of 1-4y bonds can say the same. Since we last published on this, the front end has noticeably played catch-up, with the percentage of bonds tighter growing from 54% to 68%, while the opportunity set had already become too limited in the long end (93% to 94% over the same period). Although high long-end Treasury yields will likely continue to drive interest in corporates with duration, given the drastic difference in moves, we believe the 1-4y sector offers more relative value spread opportunities. Additionally, seasonal factors historically suggest that duration underperforms in May/June (see Seasonality in index and credit risk factor returns), and we recently downgraded IG spread duration from positive to neutral (see Barclays Credit Factor Insights: Staying Tight). A microfluidics breakthrough goes straight to the silicon to cool up to three times betterMicrosoft - Microfluid cooling: Cooling at the micro level for Microsoft’s datacenters remaining largely compatible with conventional server form factors and operating models. D2C systems are typically deployed in two forms: • Single-phase D2C, where liquid (usually water with corrosion inhibitors or glycol) remains in liquid form throughout the loop and removes heat via sensible heat transfer. • Two-phase D2C, which uses a low-boiling-point dielectric fluid (i.e., a refrigerant) that vaporizes at the chip surface and condenses elsewhere in the loop, absorbing heat via latent heat. Today, single-phase D2C dominates hyperscale deployments due to lower cost, simpler fluid management, and greater operational maturity. However, as chip-level power densities rise, scaling single-phase systems requires higher flow rates, increased pumping power, and more complex manifolding—adding mechanical complexity and reliability risk. As a result, the industry increasingly expects broader adoption of two-phase D2C later this decade, subject to advances in cold-plate design, coolant distribution units, containment, and service models. Notably, the industry is also exploring microfluidic approaches that route coolant through channels etched directly into the silicon chips, bypassing traditional cold plates. The absorbed heat is then transferred to outdoor air-cooled chillers, which reject the heat to the atmosphere. CRAH + air-cooled chiller systems provide moderate energy efficiency (~1.3-1.6 PUE) with greater efficiency than CRAC units, but is less efficient for hot ambient temperatures relative to systems with evaporative cooling with wet cooling towers. There is no evaporative water loss with this closed-loop water system. Where it is commonly used: Common in large enterprise, colocation, and hyperscale data centers that do not require high-density liquid cooling. Due to the scale and capital investment required, it is generally not suitable for smaller sites. Best in temperate climates since higher ambient temperatures will reduce energy efficiency and require greater chiller capacity. records.text: M Global Insight 14 The bull case: global oil-led recession The old mild US recession case is now better framed as a global oil-led recession. The trigger is not a standard domestic demand rollover. It is a prolonged disruption to oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz, with crude above $150/bbl for several months, supply-chain stress, and gasoline balances clearing through demand destruction. US growth turns negative sequentially in 3Q26 and 4Q26, with real GDP at -0.9% and - 1.2% annualized. Headline CPI spikes first, reaching 5.1% in 3Q26, but recession risk then dominates inflation risk. The Fed cuts from 3.625% to 3.125% in 2Q26, 2.125% in 3Q26, and 1.625% in 4Q26, holding there through mid-2027 before normalizing as recovery begins. This is the Treasury bull case. The 2y falls to 1.65% in 4Q26, the 10y to 3.30%, and the 30y to 4.15%. The curve bull steepens sharply, with 2s10s near 165bp to 170bp. By 2Q27, the 2y retraces to 2.20%, the 10y to 3.55%, and the 30y to 4.30%, leaving the curve still steep but past the most powerful rally phase. Using a unique dataset of concessions from the Barclays US IG syndicate, we found that variations in concessions were well-explained by key market- and issue-/issuer-level supply and demand factors. Examining post-offering dynamics, we found that the median concession was eliminated in five trading days. In this study, we update our original research using new datasets from the Barclays US IG syndicate desk covering Jan 2014 to Sep 2025 and Barclays European syndicate covering Jan 2019 to Sep 2025 . We investigate and compare magnitudes, determinants and post-issuance dynamics to our original study to understand how concessions have evolved over time and between regions. Overall, we find that in US markets, average concessions have fallen significantly from an average of 13.3bp in the original period to 4.7bp recently; in the Euro market, they averaged 7.3bp recently. Furthermore, the average concession is now eliminated within one trading day post-offering (though larger concessions took longer than a week to be fully repriced). Despite these changing trends, we continue to find that concessions contribute a meaningful portion (11%) of the alpha earned by the average active US IG credit manager. Once the downside economic risk that Greenspan feared proved illusory, a large and concentrated hiking cycle followed, which some believed had been made necessary by the insurance cuts and the long delay after them before the FOMC began to tighten. However, if software enters a default cycle in the next few years, outcomes will be very different from either of those cycles, in our view. In the dot-com bubble, larger fallen angels (eg, Worldcom, Qwest) were a more influential component of default rates, and some of the larger default events were the result of fraud (eg, Global Crossing, Worldcom, Adelphia). Fiber overbuilding was also responsible for many of the telecom defaults, and when we think about the effect that all of this had on recoveries, the fact that most companies still had hard assets with salvageable value was likely what supported overall recovery rates. Fraud events will necessarily skew the aggregate values, but as a whole, recoveries did not crater even though there was a high degree of sector concentration within the defaulted universe. Virtually all new U.S. power plants employ closed-cycle or dry cooling.9 Conventional steam coal plants are among the most water-withdrawal-intensive: a typical U.S. coal plant in 2021 withdrew on the order of ~70 L/kWh.10 Nuclear plants also require very large cooling flows—often comparable to, and in some configurations higher than, coal—reflecting lower thermal efficiency and the need to reject nearly all waste heat via cooling systems. Older nuclear stations using once-through cooling can withdraw well over 100 L/kWh, while many U.S. nuclear units now rely on recirculating cooling, reducing withdrawal intensity by roughly an order of magnitude. Many advanced nuclear small modular reactor (SMR) technologies can significantly reduce, or even eliminate, cooling water use. For example, helium-cooled SMRs operating on a closed Brayton cycle can have virtually zero cooling-water withdrawals and consumption. Molten-salt and liquid-metal-cooled SMRs similarly avoid water in the reactor core, though most designs still generate electricity via a secondary steam Rankine cycle (or, in some cases, a supercritical CO₂ cycle). Even water-cooled SMRs can more readily integrate air-cooled or hybrid systems due to their modular size and passive safety characteristics, which reduce post-shutdown heat loads and simplify heat rejection. This provides high energy efficiency (~1.2-1.4 PUE), particularly in cooler climates, but is lower efficiency than wet towers systems in high ambient temperatures. There is no water loss given it employs closed-loop water systems, though dry coolers can require extensive rooftop or external area for installation. Where it is commonly used: This is an emerging approach in large enterprise, colocation, and hyperscale data centers that aim to minimize or eliminate water usage while maintaining the benefits of chilled water cooling. It is best suited for moderate or cool climates, as dry coolers may struggle to meet peak cooling demands efficiently in hot or tropical environments. records.text: keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear CREDIT, COMMODITIES AND SUSTAINABILITY | CORPORATE MARKETS MONTHLY OIL VIEW ▲ The protagonists in the Middle East conflict appear deadlocked – neither at war nor peace – and crucially, the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed to energy flows. Oil prices have therefore remained strong (mostly over USD100/bbl). We see few signs that hostilities in the Gulf will end imminently, despite recurring headlines of talks and unilateral agreements. With most of the circuit-breakers having been used, the supply shortfall is starting to manifest itself through reduced stocks (crude and products) in the Atlantic Basin. We see jet fuel stocks as especially vulnerable. However, when combined with higher jet fuel yields and proactive demand management, we think there is enough supply to get through the summer without shortfalls in Europe. GAS VIEW ▲ LNG markets are also short while Hormuz remains closed. Until now, the gas price impact has been moderated by seasonality. Without a strong drive for heating or cooling demand, consumers are able to postpone some of their demand in the hope of lower prices later. We expect this to change, though, when Europe needs to replenish storage tanks before the winter and when warmer weather hits Asia. Inflation driven by supply-side forces Demand-driven inflation continues to ease alongside labour market slack and subdued wage pressures. We analyse price dynamics across the CPI groups and find that rising inflation since mid-2024 reflects supply-driven and acyclical forces (52% of the CPI by weight), where price changes reflect category-specific developments that are relatively insensitive to domestic demand (e.g. electricity prices, property rates). We expect these trends to continue in 2026. However, there is little evidence of domestic overheating, with consumption, housing activity and business investment all soft. Wage growth remains contained and consistent with ~2% headline inflation over the medium-term, in our view.

New income tax cuts caused an abrupt jump in disposable income in January and a temporary jump in the saving rate, as spending gradually adjusts toward the new level of income. Given that tax cuts are reflected as a level-adjustment in the BEA income estimates, the subsequent months are likely to show lower income growth, and would have the effect of lowering the saving rate, as was the case in March. Altogether, the tax cuts have placed nominal personal income on a better footing. Incoming estimates suggest that labor income growth is on a softer trajectory. The April employment situation report showed average hourly earnings slowed to a pace of about 0.2% m/m (3.6% y/y). While private payroll income rose a solid 0.6% m/m in April, stronger than the 0.1% and 0.2% gains in March and February, respectively, on a 3m change basis, private payroll income rose just 3.3% annualized, barely enough to offset higher inflation, especially against the backdrop of higher gas prices. The income gains that we do see derive mostly from wage growth and favorable changes in the composition of labor market income. According to our state-space model, which estimates the underlying pace of monthly wage gains using signals from AHE, the Atlanta Fed Wage Growth Tracker, and the Employment Cost Index, underlying wage gains amount to 0.24% m/m (2.9% saar), unchanged from our last estimate. Swap spreads have remained particularly resilient since commencement of the Iran/US conflict, further supporting our view that only limited fiscal-risk repricing has occurred in the gilt market. We also believe that historically elevated outright yield levels have encouraged demand for gilts on asset swap, especially at the front-end, and have limited selling pressure at the back end. Anecdotal evidence suggests that the market remains long. We do not find valuations compelling and remain agnostic on swap spreads, although lingering domestic uncertainty leaves spreads exposed to downside risk. • Repo. We introduce a GBP repo-spread model to explain and forecast the GBP three-month repo spread versus SONIA. The framework focuses on the main balance-sheet and collateral channels driving repo richness and cheapness: 1) the quantity of reserves, 2) gilt collateral scarcity, 3) the composition of BoE liquidity provision, and 4) the supply of near-cash collateral, such as T-bills. Overall, the model suggests repo spreads should remain broadly stable in the near term, extending the recent stabilization, with only limited cheapening further out. Once-through cooling withdraws very large volumes of water but consumes little, returning warmer water to the source and creating thermal-pollution risks. Closed-loop (recirculating) cooling withdraws far less water but consumes more through evaporation in cooling towers or ponds. Dry cooling uses little or no water but is more capital-intensive and can reduce plant efficiency, especially in hot conditions. By 2020, roughly two-thirds of U.S. thermoelectric generation used closed-loop cooling, about one-quarter used once-through cooling, and less than 10% used dry or hybrid systems. This leaves a June hike as occurring only in a "middle of the road" scenario: there is some sort of solution to the Strait of Hormuz closure, but oil prices remain elevated. We note that this is exactly the scenario our commodity strategists expect to play out: the Strait reopens gradually starting in June, but oil and natural gas prices remain high for some time (see here). The ECB would then likely hike because inflation would be projected above target in 2027 and this would call for some insurance against the risk that inflation expectations increase by too much. As a result, banks hold fixed reserve buffers to insure against intraday liquidity needs. After all, reserves are immediately monetizable for payments and settlement purposes. They are also stable in value, carry no operational risk if offsetting trades fail, have no interest rate risk, and require no selling of securities to monetize. Moreover, there are frictions and stigma in the repo markets and Fed liquidity tools, respectively, that make contingent liquidity sources less usable. Even as banks have grown increasingly sensitive to intraday liquidity needs, they have simultaneously shifted toward secured funding as the preferred mechanism for covering cash shortfalls, while moving away from unsecured alternatives such as fed funds and short-dated commercial paper. If a reliable, rapid market mechanism were available to raise cash intraday against HQLA, this could make the payments system more efficient; in turn, banks can run smaller static reserve buffers and still meet payment peaks. Central to this is the “power unlock” narrative: management has indicated the potential to significantly reduce cooling-related power consumption (e.g., from ~40% toward ~10% in certain configurations), effectively reallocating ~30% of capacity back to compute. In this framing, ECL shifts from a marginal cost line to a throughput enabler—directly tied to hyperscalers’ ability to scale AI workloads under constrained power availability. • CoolIT enables a durable “razor / razor-blade” flywheel: CoolIT fundamentally enhances ECL’s business model by introducing an embedded hardware anchor that drives recurring monetization. The CDU acts as the “razor”—a core, installed component within direct-to-chip cooling architectures that is deeply integrated and therefore difficult to displace, reinforcing high switching costs. Around this, ECL layers the “blade”: ongoing pull-through across coolants/specialty fluids, water treatment chemistry, and monitoring, analytics, and service. This creates multi-year, annuity-like revenue streams tied to each deployed unit, with recurring revenues compounding on top of the initial hardware sale. We’re keeping an eye on increased UK political uncertainty following recent local n elections, which has helped push Gilt yields to their highest levels in decades, though we find that the bulk of the Gilt selloff since the start of the year instead reflects a sharp repricing in BoE expectations. That said, prediction markets are currently pricing a high chance of a Labor leadership change this year, which could result in a shift in the fiscal rules and upward pressure on yields. We also think increased political uncertainty presents asymmetric downside risks for Sterling over the near term, though bouts of currency weakness look more likely than a sustained depreciation trend. We’re also focused on US tariff policy. While the Court of International Trade recently n ruled against the 10% tariff that the Trump Administration imposed under Section 122, a higher court has since granted a stay and left the tariffs in place pending a full judicial review, which we believe will likely take long enough to allow the tariffs to remain in effect until the Administration replaces them with new tariffs under a different authority (Section 301 on unfair trade practices or Section 232 on national security). Finally, we’re keeping an eye on the potential for more frequent cyberattacks as AI n models become increasingly capable. records.text: US Economic Weekly | 15 May 2026 3 Inflation is inexcusable It has become increasingly clear in the last few months that inflation is a problem (Exhibit 1). Last year there was a view that inflation would be close to target once tariffs have rolled off the y/y rate. Some of this optimism was due to continued housing disinflation. Some analysts also argued that financial services inflation (due to the portfolio management component, which moves with stocks with a 1-2m lag) would normalize after a couple of outsized gains last year. These arguments feel a lot more tenuous now. After yesterday’s import price data, we estimate that core PCE will come in at 3.3% y/y (0.28% m/m) in April. Tariffs are still likely to start rolling off y/y core PCE in 2H ’26, but that effect should be at least partially offset by pass-through of the oil shock. Further, some of the increase in goods prices that was being attributed to tariffs now appears to be due to demand for AI inputs. So this inflation is likely to be stickier, and it’s having a much bigger effect on PCE inflation (the Fed’s target) than CPI (Exhibit 2, see report: Not a good wedge for the Fed). Housing disinflation continues, but at a much slower pace. Per our estimates, housing is unlikely to take more than 10bp off the y/y core PCE over the next 12m. Financial services inflation is due for another big leg up due to the ongoing equity market surge. It seems entirely plausible that core PCE could breach 3.5% y/y in coming months.

US Rates Research Breaking the 5% ceiling: Not a fade 30y yields have breached 5% without much difficulty. Continued economic resilience, even if the Fed remains on hold, could push yields even higher. Fiscal concerns are likely to remain at the forefront, and we are skeptical that the Treasury or the Fed will step in any time soon. As we write, 30y US Treasury yields have sailed past the much-watched 5% threshold. USTs are not alone; the sell-off has been global, with 30y gilts now nearing 6% (Figures 1 and 2). We have been arguing against fading the long end sell-off, and we continue to do so. The US economy has been resilient, raising questions about consensus views of a low neutral rate, and fiscal improvements put in place last year are at risk of slipping. United Kingdom In the UK, the energy outlook and geopolitical backdrop remain key drivers of BoE expectations and UK rates valuations. Higher energy prices would not only reinforce inflation concerns, but also squeeze real incomes, weigh on growth, and complicate the fiscal outlook. UK rates should therefore remain sensitive to energy, growth and fiscal credibility. That said, we see scope for yields to move lower, with front-end rates embedding a substantial tightening premium. We expect the 10y gilt yield to decline towards around 4.5% by year-end as the market prices out what we view as excessive tightening expectations. We therefore recommend positioning for a lower trough rate via a long SFIM7 position. At the long end, we find only modest evidence of a term-premium increase, with cross-market analysis suggesting that only part of the move reflects UK-specific fiscal and political risk. Combined with our bullish front-end view and still- uncertain domestic backdrop, this supports initiating 10s20s SONIA steepeners. Swap spreads have remained resilient since the onset of the Iran/US conflict, suggesting limited fiscal-risk repricing in gilts. Elevated outright yields have likely supported ASW demand, particularly at the front end, while limiting back-end selling pressure. Markets are pricing in a risk premium for a scenario where left-leaning Roberto Sánchez advances to the run- off. Warming inflation and a wary Fed April CPI inflation data were close to expectations, but both PPI and import prices ran hotter. We estimate that the core PCE deflator rose 0.25%m/m, pushing the over-year-ago rate up from 3.2% to 3.3%. The PPI isn’t a good predictor of future consumer price inflation, but the accumulation of signals from the inflation reports, other business surveys, and hawkish (or at least more balanced) statements from Fed speakers were the catalyst for higher yields this week. Energy prices again drove inflation higher last month, albeit not as much as in March. Head- line CPI increased 0.64% (3.8%oya), while core rose 0.38%m/m (2.8%, Figure 2). The over-year-ago rate is now free of distortions from last fall’s government shutdown, as earlier missing rent data were captured in this update. That should have at least doubled monthly rent and OER price increase for April, but even excluding those two segments the core rose 0.26%m/m, or a 3.2% annualized pace. Core goods inflation was essentially flat on the month, although we think some used car price increases are still in the pipeline. Meanwhile, supercore—core services excluding rent and OER—rose 0.45%, well ahead of its average pace over the prior year.

Equity market drawdowns Retail trading activity in index-linked US equity ETFs has increased during each of the largest recent equity market selloffs. Retail trading volumes in the largest US equity ETFs (SPY, VOO, IVV) increased markedly during S&P 500 drawdowns in 2020, 2022, and 2025. While trading volumes across all investor types tend to rise during drawdowns, the retail share of trading in these ETFs also increased in 2020 and 2022. In contrast, during the 2025 selloff, retail trading volumes in the largest index ETFs increased sharply in absolute terms but declined as a share of total trading volumes. During the S&P 500 drawdown in March 2026, retail trading volumes in index ETFs rose only modestly in absolute terms and again declined as a share of total trading volumes. Within the market, retail trading activity has also tended to increase in stocks with sharp single-day declines. Stocks with larger declines have generally experienced larger increases in retail activity, and the elevated activity has generally persisted during the few days subsequent to the selloff. The good news? Price momentum, we think, will drop from March as negative base effects drag on the annual price calculation. Put simply, annual price resets won't be as large this year as they were last year - especially in the services basket. The bad news? Prices will remain well above the Bank of England's 2% target. Indeed, only three months ago, forecasters, including us, were expecting CPI to drop to around 2% y-o-y in April. Where do we see inflation instead? For CPI, we expect headline inflation to slow to 2.98% y-o-y, with core CPI dropping to 2.61% y-o-y. Services CPI, we think, will drop to 3.41% y-o-y. And RPI, we estimate, will have slowed to 3.23% y-o-y. Looking ahead, we expect price momentum to pick back up as the Iran shock catches up with the inflation data. Indeed, dual fuel bills won't rise until the summer. Rising food and core goods inflation, we expect, will also push momentum a tad higher. Risks to our projections remain skewed to the upside. We start by assessing the impact of the 2025 US tariff wave on China’s exports to the EU (cross-checking against China’s exports to the US as a control) and any tariff-specificity attached to Chinese product baskets more heavily tariffed than EU goods. Our sample ranges from 2021 to January 2026. We classify HS2 sectors into three categories: product‑specific tariffs (Section 232), country‑specific tariffs (reciprocal), and a tariff- excluded group. We define the tariff implementation period as post April 2025. We first identify the tariff shock within each destination by running separate HS2 fixed‑effects regressions for the US and the EU, using a post‑April 2025 dummy to capture the introduction of the new tariffs. Across all HS2 sectors, the 2025 tariff episode is associated with a large and robust slowdown in Chinese export growth to the US. In our specifications, we find a statistically significant decline in Chinese export growth to the US of ca20-22% post April. The results also hold once year fixed effects are included. By contrast, Chinese export growth to the EU displays a mild – but not statistically significant – increase. records.text: id is routed to a heat exchanger or a Coolant Distribution Unit (CDU), which transfers the heat to a separate facility water loop. CDUs—which comprise a network of pumps, heat exchanges, and control systems—isolate the server liquid loop from the facility loop and can control liquid pressure, temperature, and flow rates for the liquid cooling system. The warmed facility water is then pumped to outdoor air-cooled chillers. These chillers use a refrigeration cycle to remove heat from the water and reject it to the atmosphere via integrated air-cooled condensers, where fans blow ambient air across finned coils carrying the hot refrigerant. The cooled refrigerant is recirculated within the chiller, and the chilled water is returned to the CDU or heat exchanger. records.text: Although retail trading assets represent roughly 10% of US corporate equity assets, retail trading activity has recently accounted for roughly 20% of total US equity trading volumes. According to Bloomberg estimates, retail traders accounted for 19% of US equity trading volumes on average over the last 4 quarters, below a peak of 24% in 2021 and up from 15% a decade ago. As of Q1 2026 retail traders accounted for 17% of US equity trading volumes. Nevertheless, retail’s 17% share of trading volume is smaller than the 34% attributable to institutional investors in aggregate. FINRA estimates show that retail accounts for a smaller 11% of trading volumes. However, institutional investors typically interact directly with only a small portion of retail order flow. Retail brokers route over 87% of order flow to specialized market makers known as wholesalers. A recent analysis from Schwarz et al. (2025) suggests that wholesalers execute 84% of retail orders against their own inventories, a practice known as internalization. Retail orders that are not internalized are routed to another market maker, to dark pools, or to traditional exchanges. As a result, investors are able to access directly only a small share of retail trading activity. Retail trading volumes are more likely to reach exchanges in volatile markets or when retail order flow becomes large and correlated, however. records.text: AI, Momentum, and the One Big Trade Friday’s volatility notwithstanding, the US equity market has continued to reach new highs on the strength of the AI trade. Through Thursday, the S&P 500 had returned 10% YTD in 2026, with TMT (the Information Technology and Communication Services sectors plus AMZN and TSLA) accounting for 85% of the return. The S&P 500 excluding TMT has returned just 3% YTD. NVDA, which accounts for 9% of S&P 500 market cap weight, has contributed 20% of the aggregate S&P 500 YTD return. The narrow rally has compressed US equity market breadth to one of its tightest levels in recent decades. During the past month, as the S&P 500 has climbed to register 14 new record highs, the share of index constituents trading above their respective 200-day averages has declined. The median S&P 500 stock now trades 13% below its 52-week high. In the past, sharp declines in equity market breadth have signaled larger than average market drawdowns and increased Momentum factor volatility. However, today’s narrow breadth is not necessarily a bearish directional indicator for the equity market. Comparably narrow breadth in May 2023 preceded a period of S&P 500 volatility during the following few months but not the end of the bull market, and breadth today is far less narrow than the market in 1999-2000. The broad direction suggests a shift towards giving more space to market forces, with a policy focus on quality and industry discipline. Stringent new battery safety and design standards are set to be implemented in July 2026. Pricing discipline is also being enforced, with new guidelines prohibiting the sale of vehicles below cost. As of May, Milliman reported funded ratios reached the post- GFC high of 107.8%. STRIPS investors tend to be important participants of 30y bond demand, as they consistently STRIP the last few on-the-run bonds while reconstituting as the STRIPS rolldown into the 23yr to 27y sectors (Figure 11). Milliman recently reported that the equity allocation of their universe of corporate plans fell to 24.1%, as of FY25, down from 24.7% (32% at the end of 2020). As a reminder, corporate defined benefit plans tend to follow a ‘glide path’ which shifts equity investment into fixed income as funded ratios rise. Their funded ratios move higher when equities appreciate or when yields move higher, which reduces the present value of their discounted liabilities. We think many of those plans target a terminal level of around 20% in equities, and perhaps that is an underestimate. This implies there is very little room for further reallocation from here. Conversely, during yen-buying interven- tion (selling dollars, buying yen), the yen acquired from selling dollars is used to redeem FBs, thereby reducing the outstanding balance of Foreign Exchange Fund Bills. As of the end of December 2025, the outstanding amount of Foreign Exchange Fund Bills stood at JPY 95.2 trillion. Following the recent yen-buying, dollar-selling interventions, it is expected that over the next 3–6 months, the FB balance will be reduced by an amount equivalent to the total intervention (currently just under JPY 10 trillion). In fact, after the yen-buying, dollar-selling interventions in September–October 2022 and April–May 2024, the outstanding balance of Foreign Exchange Fund Bills declined. records.text: Canada Economics Weekly 15 May 2026 Citi Research 5 Thursday, May 21, 7:00am CFIB Business Barometer (May) The monthly CFIB survey remains our preferred monthly survey indicator for signals on both inflationary pressures and demand trends. CFIB price plans jumped in April to 3.2% over the next year, keeping us cautious around the potential for some near-term stickiness to core inflation. Price plans were elevated for a few months in early 2025 following various tariff announcements, and did reliably signal some pickup in annual core inflation. But as demand remained soft, both price plans and core inflation eased. In the current episode, it is less clear to us if the jump in price plans reflecting rising energy prices (which may even rise again in May data) will result in higher consumer prices. Unemployment is a bit higher compared to a year ago; population growth has slowed and will limit aggregate consumption; and households are facing higher interest rates as mortgages reset. Demand details remaining weak in the CFIB survey would be an indication that more medium-term signals for core inflation— like the share of firms indicating significant difficulty meeting demand in the BoC’s quarterly Business Outlook Survey—could remain soft. United States | Inflation forwards relative value We expand on our framework previously published here. We calculate fair value of inflation forwards using Principal Component Analysis (PCA). It is a statistical procedure that allows us to summarize the information in a data set by transforming the input variables into different sets of fewer variables called principal components. The goal is to separate broad curve moves from idiosyncratic richness or cheapness in individual forwards. We compare each forward against a PCA-implied fair value that reflects the level and slope factors of the curve. The PCA is run on a clean set of underlying forward buckets rather than directly on overlapping market forwards. The key point is that each inflation forward represents inflation over a period of time, not a single point on the curve. For example, 1y1y covers inflation from year 1 to year 2, while 5y5y covers inflation from year 5 to year 10. While more member states are likely to prolong their support packages as geopolitical tensions persist, the overall fiscal impulse is currently modest. Spain could be an exception to this, as some of the measures approved in March may expire sooner than initially expected. In particular, the VAT on electricity and gas is likely to return to 21% (from 10%) on June 1 instead of July 1 . This is triggered by a clause in the emergency decree that allows the reduced rate to be withdrawn earlier if YoY inflation for those components didn't exceed 15% in April. The reduced VAT rate on fuels is expected to remain in place until the end of June. The inflationary impact from these measures appears much more muted compared to previous interventions. The annualized cost of the support announced so far is approximately 0.3% of GDP, significantly less than the packages in 2022 which amounted to around 3% of GDP and contributed to higher inflation. As the current measures are largely being financed through budget savings or additional tax revenue, they do not involve significant deficit spending, thus limiting the near-term pressure on inflation from fiscal policy. We test the latter, whereby external markets absorb surplus domestic capacity. We find that sectors with underperforming Chinese domestic demand systematically show stronger export volumes and significantly weaker unit value growth than other sectors in 2021-26. This pattern holds when 2025 trade dynamics are excluded, consistent with a vent-for- surplus mechanism driven by excess capacity, not a tariff-induced diversion story. Import unit value compression is a key channel Our panel results indicate ca3–3.5pp additional annual price compression in sectors where Chinese domestic demand is underperforming. Notably, this pattern is stronger pre-2025, implying that excess supply pressures were already entrenched. Post 2025, pricing compression becomes more generalized across sectors, consistent with a broader demand shock triggered by US tariff hikes rather than targeted re-allocation. Brussels is ramping up its scrutiny of trade dynamics The EU is moving decisively from monitoring to enforcement. records.text: Latin America Outlook Slowing, but still flowing Tighter financial conditions across most of the region contributed to slowing down, but not killing, credit growth. Some deterioration in quality has been observed as the debt service burden increases. • In Brazil, credit concessions continued to grow despite the monetary tightening implemented by the BCB in 2024-25, albeit at a slower speed and amid some deterioration in quality. The government recently relaunched a debt renegotiation program to address a record-high commitment of household income to debt service. • In Mexico, the credit market is still expanding, but at a slower and more uneven pace than a year earlier, while non-performing loans increased slightly. • Lower interest rates in Argentina are unlikely to become a major engine of growth in the coming quarters as the country's credit channel is shallow, with limited power of monetary transmission. As well, there is limited room for credit to expand meaningfully from the supply side. • In Colombia, new credit disbursements have significantly decelerated in recent months, reflecting the transmission of monetary policy tightening. Conversely, Peru has seen credit acceleration, likely reflecting the easing of monetary policy last year, though its sustainability might be tested soon. • Ecuador's current account surplus allows robust credit growth in its dollarized economy. Macroeconomic fundamentals and monetary policy: The eurozone economy should prove resilient to the energy shock, delivering continued growth despite higher inflation. However, we no longer forecast significant GDP acceleration. High energy prices are likely to curb consumption, limit productivity growth and reduce the return on German public investment. We therefore lower our growth forecasts by 0.3pp (to 1.0%) for this year and by 0.2pp (to 1.3%) for 2027. Meanwhile, we see eurozone inflation averaging 3% this year and 3.3% in 2027. We expect the European Central Bank to respond to the size and persistence of the predicted inflation overshoot with 50bp of rate hikes, starting in June. Fair value: The EUR remains significantly cheap relative to its long-term fair value, with BNP Paribas’ long-term FEER model suggesting an equilibrium level of 1.39 against the USD. Balance of payments: Global investors remain overweight US assets and the USD, we think. Should they diversify these holdings (as we expect), EU assets and the EUR would likely benefit from inflows. The dotted line delineates the original study's and update's periods. Source: Bloomberg, Barclays Syndicate, Barclays Research Determinants of Concessions A concession is a price characteristic of a new issue. Price is the direct result of supply and demand for the bond. We examine here several factors that may affect concessions and discuss their rationale and definition. We broadly categorize them as supply-side, market-wide demand-side, and issuer-/issue-specific demand-side factors. Supply-Side Drivers We consider supply characteristics as those reflecting the amount of the issue and issuer the market has to absorb. If the demand curve is downward sloping in price (ie, lower price/wider spread → more demand) and supply curve is upward sloping in price (ie, higher price/tighter spread → more supply), a larger issue would suggest a larger concession. The most intuitive indicator of supply is the absolute size of the deal, which we measure as its dollar value in log terms. We also evaluate the deal's relative size to the issuer's outstanding debt. records.text: 2 US Economic Weekly | 15 May 2026 Stagflation or reflation? Aditya Bhave BofAS aditya.bhave@bofa.com • The economy is being buffeted by a plethora of supply and demand shocks. The tails of the economic and Fed policy distribution are fat. • Inflation is clearly a problem. But are we experiencing stagflation or reflation? Resilient spending and booming earnings point to reflation. • But we think the jury is still out. With the fiscal tailwind fading, the true test of consumer and labor resilience might still be ahead of us. The labor market would have to start tightening for reflation and rate hikes to become our base case. Crucible of confusion There probably isn’t any historical precedent for the plethora of shocks buffeting the US economy. On the supply side, we are facing three negative shocks – Iran, tariffs & immigration policy – and a positive one – AI. There is uncertainty about when and how much each shock will impact activity and inflation. The economy is also experiencing two positive demand shocks: fiscal stimulus from the OBBB and AI investment demand. Moreover, the World Cup is starting in a few weeks. Its effects on spending, inflation and employment should be mostly transitory. But the resulting distortions to the data could make it hard to get a clean read on the underlying state of the economy until late summer. To add another layer of uncertainty, incoming Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has a very (and at times unwarrantedly) hawkish past but a strong dovish leaning

records.text: US Economics Weekly 15 May 2026 Citi Research 8 Housing Starts – Citi: 1371k, median: 1418k, prior: 1502k Housing Starts MoM – Citi: -8.7%, median: -3.5%, prior: 10.8% Building Permits – Citi: 1376k, median: 1393k, prior: 1363k Building Permits MoM – Citi: 1.0%, median: NA, prior: -11.4% Housing starts jumped in March to levels near the recent highs of the last few years, but we expect a moderation in housing starts in April to 1371k. Building permits for housing units should rise modestly to 1376k. Recently, the trend of starts of multifamily units has been rising, but with permits for multifamily units remaining more stable. This should act as a ceiling on how on much further multifamily starts can rise. The project is contractually obliged to replenish any water consumed to achieve water positivity. • Amazon (Planned Mississippi Data Centers): AWS is expanding in Mississippi and in April 2026 announced a partnership with Veolia to deploy reclaimed-water cooling systems at its new campuses. We argued that the well‑understood effects of QT and expectations of fiscal easing may already be embedded in swap spread valuations, limiting the need for steady cash underperformance versus derivatives. This year’s surprise has instead been the muted response of swap spreads in risk‑off episodes, in contrast with past cycles. Indeed, the ECB’s measure of systemic stress has barely moved in the current conflict and remains near the bottom of its historical range ( Exhibit 95 ). Purchasing new issues and earning their concessions can therefore represent a valuable source of alpha for credit portfolio managers. Consider an investor who holds a portfolio mimicking the Corporate Index and replaces secondary bonds with new issues every month. We assume the manager receives allocations in proportion to portfolio (ie, market) weights. The outperformance ('alpha') of a single new issue i can be approximated as: Alpha from New Issue i ≈ Concessioni * Spread Durationi * MVi / MVindex The total alpha for the portfolio from new issues is Alphai summed across all i. Figure 18 plots the annual alpha from concessions in the US and Europe. In the US, the average alpha was 9.3bp/y through the entire period. This outperformance significantly varied over time: three years showed alphas ≥20bp (2008, 2009, and 2020), and two more years showed alphas ≥10bp (2013 and 2015). For context, in our white paper Systematic Investing as a Complement to Active Credit Management (19 October 2021), we found that the average active IG credit manager delivered 83bp/y of outperformance between 2011 and 2020. Potential alpha from concessions during this period (9.1bp) thus constituted a meaningful portion (11%) of the overall performance. records.text: PI weights in Europe far outpace the US Last but not least, the spending side of the equation delivers an even clearer picture, and higher taxes are likely partly to blame. Energy expenditures (including taxes) in the Euro area amount to over 12% of GDP and are more than double those in the US, which hover around 6% of GDP (Exhibit 3). This argues for a larger sensitivity of inflation and growth in the Euro area, as the cost push shock is twice as large. In addition, the composition of the Euro area HICP compared to the US PCE tells the same story (Exhibit 4). While the share of oil in the PCE basket is roughly 2%, this weight is close to 4% in the Euro area HICP basket. Furthermore, while the overall energy (oil, electricity, and gas) weights in US PCE are roughly 4%, they are close to 10% in Europe. Domestic energy policies appear as likely drivers. Relative monetary policy biases may still be unwarranted While the higher inflation sensitivity of the Euro area vs the US may argue for a more hawkish monetary policy stance, the hawkish bias from the ECB appears somewhat unwarranted given that inflation was already below target and the shock to economic activity is also larger in Europe. If anything, the hawkish bias should rest with the Fed. Trade-off between PUE and WUE. Cooling system design involves a fundamental trade-off between electricity efficiency (PUE) and water intensity (WUE). Data centers that avoid or materially limit evaporative cooling typically achieve very low on-site water use but may require higher electricity input for cooling, particularly in hot climates or during peak conditions. Conversely, facilities that employ evaporative cooling can achieve lower PUE, especially in warm environments, but at the cost of higher direct water use. “Direct-to-chip liquid cooling allows data centers to cool systems more effectively than traditional air conditioning, consuming less power and water.” — Nvidia: AI at COP29 - Balancing Innovation and Sustainability As a result, decisions around this trade-off are increasingly shaped by regional water and power dynamics. Implications for the Outlook We see two implications of this “rocket and feather” passthrough for the outlook. First, the asymmetric passthrough creates upside risks to the core inflation outlook. That is, declines in energy prices from here (following a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz) might provide little relief for the core inflation outlook, while further energy price increases could push up inflation sharply further. This can be seen by mapping symmetric energy price assumptions into core inflation using our cross-country panel regression results (Exhibit 5). The LIHTC program was created by the Tax Reform Act of 1986 and remains the federal government’s primary policy tool for the development of affordable rental housing. LIHTCs are awarded to developers to offset the cost of constructing rental housing, in exchange for agreeing to reserve a fraction of rent-restricted units for lower-income households. Developers may claim the tax credits in equal amounts over a ten-year period once a property is “placed in service,” meaning it has been completed and is available to be rented. Given the need for upfront financing to complete construction, developers typically sell the ten-year stream of tax credits to outside investors in exchange for equity financing. . How it works: CRAH units circulate warm server room air across chilled-water coils, transferring heat into a chilled water loop. This chilled water is cooled by remote water-cooled chillers, which extract heat from the water and transfer it to a separate condenser water loop. Instead of using wet cooling towers, the condenser water is routed to outdoor dry coolers—large air-to-water heat exchangers equipped with fans that blow ambient air across finned coils to dissipate heat into the atmosphere. Because dry coolers rely solely on sensible heat transfer (no evaporation), they consume no water under normal operation. Adiabatic cooling optional enhancement: The system is often paired with adiabatic cooling. The data center cooling system can operate in dry mode most of the year, with adiabatic assist activating during higher ambient temperatures to maintain cooling capacity while using only a fraction of the water required by traditional wet cooling towers. 13 May 2026 36 Barclays | Thematic Investing

The median survey-based BoJ path in the April QUICK Monthly Bond Survey (answered during 27th-30th April period) is also a less hawkish path than market pricing. We interpret the gap between market pricing and actual investor expectations as an inflation risk premium, reflecting market concern that the BoJ could fall behind the curve. As noted above, however, we think the environment, particularly in 2Q26, is one in which downside risks to growth are likely to come into focus. Once the market shifts its attention from inflation concerns to growth concerns, we think this inflation risk premium should fade. We expect the 10y JGB yield to decline to 2.1% by 4Q26.

We think the Bank of Japan will look past this week’s weak sentiment data and focus on signals of rapidly building price pressures. The April corporate goods price report highlighted a surge in a wide range of petro-product prices and an ongo- ing firming in AI-related tech prices, raising risks of faster passthrough into consumer prices. Increased fiscal spending due to a possible extension of household energy subsidies adds to the upward pressure on long-end JGB yields. We con- tinue to expect a June rate hike. EM’s hawkish pivot broadens EM Asia has been at the forefront of EM’s recent hawkish shift. Though the group of hikers remains small, next week we expect Indonesia to join the Philippines––along with Paki- stan and Georgia in the EM Edge—in hiking policy rates in response to the Middle East conflict. While Indonesia’s infla- tion has been contained by subsidies, a surge in diesel prices signals a pickup. Importantly, the rupiah remains under sig- nificant pressure, having weakened past the 17,000/USD threshold last seen during the Asian Financial Crisis and underperforming regional peers despite stabilization efforts. We expect Bank Indonesia to hike 25bp to 5% next week to stem further FX losses

records.text: Ben Luk 14 May 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Emerging Markets Weekly: Going Long CNH and KRW Investors continue to look through the ME tensions, with equities pushing to all-time highs despite higher oil prices. Risk assets were supported: EM FX benefited from broad USD weakness, EM bonds have largely shrugged off oil -driven inflation concerns, and EM equities continue to ride the global AI/tech narrative. However, real money activity has shown signs of fatigue, with recent outflows across both bonds and equities, while FX flows were broadly neutral. Despite this slowdown, we became more constructive towards Asia this week. Aggregate risk sentiment remains buoyant, and we see scope for the region to catch up, supported by a reduction in geopolitical risk premium following improved tone in US–China trade discussions, alongside positive spillovers from stronger global equity markets. We took profit on our long TWDINR and initiated long CNHINR and short JPYKRW, reflecting our preference for currencies leveraged to regional growth and improving China sentiment, while funding against laggards or low-beta expressions. We also have sympathy with paying the 10s20s30s SONIA fly, given the high correlation between the two structures. However, 10s20s offers slightly better carry and roll — around 1bp over three months versus roughly 0.5bp for 10s20s30s (despite having a similar carry-to-roll ratio) — making the simpler curve expression our preferred implementation. The key risk to the trade is a bear flattener, most likely driven by a more hawkish BoE repricing. In Exhibit 69 , we report UK gilt cross-market flies versus USTs and Bund/Buxl for both the 10y and 30y sectors, alongside the 1y1y swap fly as a proxy for the repricing in relative central-bank expectations. The underperformance in the 10y and 30y sectors has been mostly driven by front-end repricing. Since 27 February 2026, December 2026 meeting fixings have repriced by around 80bp, 115bp and 60bp for the ECB, BoE and Fed, respectively (see Exhibit 70 ). On this basis, the main driver of UK duration underperformance appears to be the relative repricing of BoE policy expectations, rather than a pure long-end term-premium shock.

records.text: M Global Insight 82 The Bear case : US Aggregate Demand Upside Our rates bear case is based on the demand-led upside scenario among our economists’ four alternative scenarios. In this scenario, strong US consumption, firmer corporate animal spirits, and robust non-AI capex led to a demand-driven reacceleration in inflation, prompting the Fed to resume rate hikes in 2H26. Under this scenario, our economists expect the BoJ to accelerate the pace of rate hikes from 2H26 and raise the policy rate to 2.0% by 4Q27. In this environment, We think rate expectations should rise sharply into 2H26 and expect the 10y JGB yield to reach 3.15% by 4Q26. Thereafter, as the market increasingly views the BoJ as having reached neutral, we expect the 10y yield to move broadly sideways through 2027. Meanwhile, the super-long sector should outperform the belly during the rate sell-off, supported by strong demand from overseas investors at higher yield levels given their attractive valuation. We expect the 10s30s curve to bear-flatten toward around 95bp. records.text: . Colombia: Inflation accelerates In Colombia, April’s inflation came in above expectations, with both headline and core measures continuing to acceler- ate. The upside surprise relative to our forecast was once again driven by stronger‑than‑anticipated food and regulated prices, while core inflation broadly tracked our projections. Although sequential momentum in both headline and core inflation eased modestly, it remains well above the central bank’s target range and last year’s pace. More importantly, emerging signs of persistence suggest not only further increases ahead but also greater stickiness in inflation dynam- ics. In response, we have revised our year‑end inflation fore- cast to 6.5%oya, primarily reflecting higher food prices. Core inflation is also projected to continue rising, reaching 6.4%oya by December. Forecast risks remain skewed to the upside. Key upside risks include higher food and energy inflation—amid higher oil and fertilizer prices and the possi- bility of a strong El Niño in 2H. At the same time, services inflation could accelerate further, driven by the unusually large minimum‑wage increase set to take effect around year‑end. April’s details underscore the trend. Headline inflation rose 0.78% m/m in April, around 10 bp above our forecast. Food and alcoholic beverages and housing were the main contribu- tors to the monthly print. US Economic Weekly | 15 May 2026 3 Inflation is inexcusable It has become increasingly clear in the last few months that inflation is a problem (Exhibit 1). Last year there was a view that inflation would be close to target once tariffs have rolled off the y/y rate. Some of this optimism was due to continued housing disinflation. Some analysts also argued that financial services inflation (due to the portfolio management component, which moves with stocks with a 1-2m lag) would normalize after a couple of outsized gains last year. These arguments feel a lot more tenuous now. After yesterday’s import price data, we estimate that core PCE will come in at 3.3% y/y (0.28% m/m) in April. Tariffs are still likely to start rolling off y/y core PCE in 2H ’26, but that effect should be at least partially offset by pass-through of the oil shock. Further, some of the increase in goods prices that was being attributed to tariffs now appears to be due to demand for AI inputs. So this inflation is likely to be stickier, and it’s having a much bigger effect on PCE inflation (the Fed’s target) than CPI (Exhibit 2, see report: Not a good wedge for the Fed). Housing disinflation continues, but at a much slower pace. Per our estimates, housing is unlikely to take more than 10bp off the y/y core PCE over the next 12m. Financial services inflation is due for another big leg up due to the ongoing equity market surge. It seems entirely plausible that core PCE could breach 3.5% y/y in coming months.

While notable, this backward-looking data is in line with our expectations for a gradual deterioration in the labour market. The increase is not a new story but a continuation of an upward trend seen for over a year. Part of this rise is technical, with about half of the increase over the last year attributable to a late-2023 labour market reform that reclassified some inactive individuals as unemployed. records.text: will buy the supply has little meaning in the absence of knowing the timing and price at which those purchases occur. • What determines timing and price at which investors make the decision whether to buy, hold, or sell? More often than not, the answer comes back to the macro environment and its impact on central bank decision making. In the absence of knowing who will buy, when, and at what price, how should investors think about supply and its impact on price? We discuss the impact of supply on price in Between a Rock and a Hard Place, April 17, 2020. In short, sovereign supply moves market prices the most when expectations form or change from previous expectations for sovereign supply. • In 2026, surprises to the outlook for fiscal policy seem most likely to change expectations for the sovereign supply outlook. • This means that bond yields can fall (rise) if investors come to expect less (more) supply than they thought before – even if that supply is more (less) than what they had to buy previously.

The PBoC’s recent USDCNY fixings, in our view, clearly reflect a stance to keep FX stable and curb expectations of excessive renminbi appreciation. We believe negative US–China rate differentials and the underlying macro conditions will also limit RMB appreciation. We think the depletion of excess FX holdings has reached a point where exporter concern about FX losses has likely eased (see China: Politburo offers no hint of additional easing, dated 29 April). So, while exporter settlements will still support USDRMB, we think the pace will not regain its previous high, reflecting the PBoC’s apparent fixing bias and a stable RMB. Instead, we think exporters may be drawn to actions that cap USDRMB upside if the dollar stages a pronounced rebound. Meanwhile, we are observing more FX buying demand when spot trades lower. As such, we expect USDRMB to trade in a tight range in the near term. The PBoC may be inclined to let the USDRMB trading range move slightly lower if DXY continues to trade lower or regional peers continue to strengthen. The RMB index might consolidate at around 99-100 accordingly, and we still like the CNH as a funder to express bullish views elsewhere (see FX: Tactical short CNHTWD, dated 20 April). The increase was far more pronounced for Chinese imports than for EU imports, underscoring the much heavier tariff shock faced by China at the peak of the trade escalation (Exhibit 1). Exhibit 2 illustrates the resulting tariff gap between China and the EU across major goods sectors. In early 2026, the tariff landscape shifted again. However, the path from here is not easy. We outline the path to the premiership and the challenges we see: nThe NEC still must approve his candidacy. Labour rules require its National Executive Committee to approve any candidate running for MP . At the time of writing, Mr Burnham has requested their permission.1 Whether or not it is allowed is up to the 9-person committee. Notably, they turned him down for the Gorton and Denton election in January (see: UK Economics - Prime Minister Burnham – How Likely Is It?). This time, we think it likely they approve him because he is seen by many as the most viable candidate to take Labour into the next General Election. One committee member has already spoken out suggesting it would pass, while his team has actively courted their support. 2 nMr Burnham’s victory in a by-election is not guaranteed. Makerfield has been held by Labour since its creation as a parliamentary seat in 1983. However, history has not proved the most useful guide for the current, fractious nature of UK politics. It is worth noting that in the 2024 UK General Election, Josh Simons—the Labour MP for that seat until this afternoon—won 45% of the vote share. Reform was second at 32%. Adams, CFA David.S.Adams@morganstanley.com +44 20 7425-3518 G10 Rates Outlook: Between A Rock and A Slick Place G10 rates investors rarely get an oil shock they can look through with confidence. Our baseline asks them to do just that, but only after paying respect to two tails: an oil-led recession, where demand destruction wins, and a permanent oil premium, where inflation risk keeps central banks tighter for longer. In the US, AI capex and fiscal support keep the expansion alive through mid-2026. Oil stabilizes near $90/bbl this year and falls toward $80/bbl in 2027, but the path matters more than the destination. One quarter looks like a relative-price shock. A second quarter forces gasoline balances to clear through prices and demand. Our UST path is not a literal translation of the economists' baseline. It starts with 40% on baseline, 15% on US aggregate demand, 10% on AI productivity, 15% on global oil-led recession, and 20% on permanent oil premium. By 4Q27, the weight sits fully on baseline. Election premium: We expect EUR/CHF to decline into the April 2027 French presidential election (which will be followed by an Assembly election in June 2027). EUR/CHF is a clean expression of European political risk: it fell roughly 4% around the dissolution of the National Assembly in June 2024. EUR/CHF also declined into the first round of the 2017 French elections and during the 2011-12 sovereign crisis. We expect CHF political risk premium to rebuild from late 2026 and reach its peak in 1Q 2027. Yield differentials: We think yield differentials will move in a EUR/CHF negative direction; markets have priced 80bp of the 50bp of ECB hiking we expect and only 15bp of the 50bp of ECB cutting we expect. A shift lower in European yields relative to Swiss yields would likely put further downward pressure on the pair. Risks to our view: The principal risk is that SNB sight deposits start rising sharply as EUR/ CHF approaches 0.90 or 0.88, signalling that the SNB does not in fact tolerate the strength we have built into the forecast.

Large US banks and foreign banks are also deploying more cash in front-end markets, with total fed funds sold and reverse repo at three-year highs (see Exhibit 266 ). • Uncertainty about the next rate action by the Federal Reserve has led banks to slow purchases of Treasuries and opt for more activity in front-end markets. Current Fed balance sheet guidance also calls for reserve management purchases (RMPs), mostly in T-bills, as needed to maintain an ample supply of reserves. • These RMPs greatly reduce the likelihood of tighter funding conditions and are a strong guardrail against repo cheapening (see Crisis of Confidence in the SRF). Air-side economization requires careful filtration and humidity control to protect IT equipment from contaminants and moisture fluctuations. Water-Side Economization Water-side economization uses cool ambient air to reject heat from the chilled water loop, bypassing mechanical water-cooled chillers. This reduces energy consumption and wear on mechanical cooling systems and is common for water-cooled chiller + wet cooling tower systems in cool and temperate climates. How it works: The data centers chilled water loop is connected to a heat exchanger that interfaces with a separate condenser water loop. When outdoor temperatures are low enough, the condenser water is cooled directly by dry coolers or cooling towers without engaging the chillers. The economizer transfers heat from the chilled water loop to the cooled condenser water, effectively bypassing the chiller. This reduces energy use during favorable weather conditions. When ambient temperatures rise, the system switches back to chiller operation. Adiabatic Cooling Adiabatic cooling enhances air-based heat rejection by using evaporative cooling to pre-cool ambient. The precedent exists: some countries, such as Croatia and Malta, achieved fast-paced adoption despite starting with high debt stocks above the 60% threshold, but they accepted the politi- cal cost of fixing the budget and put debt on a credible descending path. The legal bit Fulfilling the Maastricht criteria, although most widely dis- cussed, is not the only criteria for Euro adoption. A country must also achieve legal convergence, and its national legisla- tion (including central bank statutes) must be compatible with the ECB. The latest Convergence Report published by the Commission in 2024 states that the NBH Law remains incompatible in several areas, notably (1) the independence of the NBH, (2) the prohibition of monetary financing (i.e. the central bank cannot fund the government directly), and (3) the NBH’s inte- gration into the ESCB at the time of Euro adoption. It calls for the authorities to take remedial action to correct these incompatibilities. However, having fully compatible legisla- tion is quite exceptional, and the needed legal adjustments appear achievable in the current political context. A final point to note is that although not formally required by the Treaties, prior policy commitments have increasingly become part of the practical pathway into joining the Euro Area. This means receiving the coupon payment by holding the bond and subtracting the cost to finance the bond. Another way to think about carry is to compare the bond’s forward yield with its current yield. If the forward yield is higher than the spot yield, it means that the market expects the bond's price to decline. In this case, the bondholder is being compensated for holding the security. The gap between the forward yield and the spot yield therefore captures the carry embedded in the bond over that horizon. We compute the bonds forward pricing using the Proceeds Method. In this method, the bonds forward price is obtained by growing the price at the repo rate over the holding horizon, while subtracting the coupons received, adjusted for reinvestment, as well as the accrued interest at the forward date. At its peak, the communications sector (which captures cable satellite, media, and wirelines/wireless) grew to over 40% of the (albeit small) high yield index (Figure 1). Following the dot-com crash of 2000, the communications sector's attribution to the overall index OAS1 peaked at 23.5% in May 2002 (Figure 3). The sector's effect on OAS returned close to neutral by late 2003. A similar phenomenon played out in energy during the 2014-16 oil downturn. After the sharp decline in oil prices that began in the second half of 2014 intensified through 2015, spreads widened and energy's percentage contribution to overall index OAS rose to 11.9% by March 2016 (Figure 4). records.text: 5 North America Economic Research 15 May 2026 J P M O R G A N Global Data Watch: The price of war, and resilience • Energy prices and cyclical strength signal sustained sticky core inflation • Consumer spending softer in Europe and Japan, but holding up in the US • Absent weakening growth, central banks to turn more hawkish • Next week: DM flash PMIs (May); UK/Jpn CPI; BI hike For more than three years we have pushed back against the prevailing Goldilocks view incorporated in central bank forecasts and market pricing that US and global inflation would return towards 2% target levels alongside still-solid growth. In the event, global core consumer price increases outside China have remained elevated around 3%ar since 2H23. This has come alongside sustained above-potential growth and tight labor markets that have fueled pressure on both goods and services prices. Two recent developments are upending the debate about inflation inertia and the monetary policy path. The energy price spike is now raising inflation and generating a sharp squeeze on household purchasing power that could intensify if the Middle East conflict keeps the Strait of Hormuz closed. The risk of a negative growth shock raising unemployment rates is thus high, an outcome that would ultimately prove disinflationary and warrant lower policy rates. records.text: M Global Insight Morgan Stanley Research 7 G10 FX Outlook: A Bit More Slack for the Greenback We expect modest USD weakness to continue in the coming months, with the DXY bottoming at 95 in 3Q26. However, this move is likely limited in size and duration, marking the final phase of the cyclical USD selloff that began in early 2025, with the DXY retracing its losses to end 2027 around 100. The macro backdrop supports a softer USD. Growth remains resilient, core inflation is easing toward trend, and supportive fiscal, monetary, and regulatory policies are sustaining strong risk appetite, particularly for US equities. US interest rates and rate differentials are expected to decline in the coming months, with the ECB and BoJ hiking rates closer to Fed funds continuing the medium-term trend of US-RoW rate convergence. In terms of our four-regime USD framework, we think markets may vacillate between the USD Bear and Carry Regimes, the common theme of which is risk currency outperformance versus the USD. We also expect the DXY’s discount to rate differentials to widen modestly. Continued investor debate over the USD’s long-run safe haven status suggests a higher equilibrium level of risk premium in the currency all else equal, which should be reflected in a greater discount to rates-implied 'fair value'. records.text: M Global Insight 114 CAD | Stuck in the middle with u(ncertainty) Pair CCY view 2Q26 3Q26 4Q26 1Q27 2Q27 3Q27 4Q27 USD/CAD Neutral 1.36 1.35 1.35 1.36 1.36 1.36 1.36 CAD remains increasingly driven by global growth and risk sentiment rather than oil alone. CAD's beta to risk and global growth should keep the currency supported through 2026, but stronger US growth and persistent trade uncertainty likely keep USD/CAD near the upper end of its range through much of 2027. What to watch: USMCA negotiations and Section 232 tariff treatment, Canadian business investment and FDI flows, infrastructure and energy investment, and whether Canada can participate more meaningfully in AI- and manufacturing-linked demand. USD/CAD's beta to risk and global growth should provide some benefit to CAD through 2026, though uncertainty around trade policy and a weak domestic backdrop keeps the benefit capped. Indirect effects from uncertainty and weak investment matter more for CAD than the direct effects of tariffs themselves. Concurrently, the domestic backdrop likely keeps the BoC cautious through 2026 as restrictive financial conditions, housing sensitivity, and weak productivity continue to weigh on activity. CAD has recently traded closely with US equities and growth indicators than with commodity prices alone. While higher energy prices and commodity investment provide some support to the economy, they have not materially changed the broader structural backdrop due to export capacity limits.

Brent crude oil averaged $102/bbl in April, up from nearly $100 in March and $69 in February. Western Canadian Select edged up to an average of $82 per barrel in April, from $80 in March and $49 in Febru- ary. Prices for gasoline at the pump shot up 9.1% in April after surging 21.2% in March. Year-ago growth in food prices should remain elevated in April as energy is a key input cost for food in Canada, much of which is imported. Meanwhile, core prices will likely continue to run around 2%. We expect a 0.2% rise in the seasonally-adjusted exclusionary core CPI (excluding food and energy), with the year-ago pace staying at 1.9%. The BoC’s preferred core measures are likely to remain near the middle of its target band in April, with the annualized three-month run rate for core inflation settling around 2% after four straight months of softer readings. The equivalent measure for the exclusionary core should remain below 2%. Our model has a good fit by design, due in part to the inclusion of the (orthogonalised) global term premium. Our European economics team showed that, based on fiscal fundamentals, UK risk premium was high vs peers, but in this exercise we use this good fit to quantify the drivers of Gilt term premium rather than longer-run macro valuation2. We find that supply factors, including from BoE QT, as well as the broader increase in bond supply alongside the repricing in G3 term premium, explain the bulk of the repricing. We do find a modest role for policy uncertainty in boosting the UK term premium in previous years, but by nature of the index used (which remains low at the current period) it has had little impact recently. This analysis helps show why Gilt yields and the Gilt term premium are at historical highs. First, all major bond markets have seen significant weakness in long-end bonds among a generalised repricing of growth and inflation risk. Second, the UK has experienced the highest levels of inflation, the greatest macro and policy uncertainty (by a range of measures). And finally, the model above shows the largest duration-adjusted increase in supply amid a shifting composition of demand. records.text: M Global Insight Morgan Stanley Research 13 By 2Q27, our targets are 3.60% for 2y, 3.85% for 5y, 4.20% for 10y, and 4.75% for 30y. By 4Q27, the 2y and 10y sit around 3.45% and 4.15%, 48bp and 33bp below forwards. The curve matters more than outright duration: 2s10s flattens to 40bp in 2Q26, then steepens to 60bp by 2Q27 and 70bp by end-2027. The inflation mix limits the long-end rally. We expect 5y and 10y breakevens at 2.60% and 2.40% by end-2026, then 2.35% and 2.25% by mid-2027 as energy settles. We see 10y real yields at 1.85% in 4Q26 and 1.95% by mid-2027, supported by restrictive policy, AI productivity hopes, and Treasury supply. Bills, buybacks, Fed RMPs, and bank-regulation changes should also support USTs versus SOFR swaps. The bear case: US aggregate demand upside The demand upside case becomes the UST bear case. Strong wealth effects support consumption, while animal spirits keep business spending elevated. US growth rises above baseline, global exporters benefit, labor demand strengthens, and unemployment declines in 2H26. The inflation trade-off arrives later: demand runs ahead of supply and price pressure re-emerges into 2027. In this scenario, US real GDP growth reaches 2.9% 4Q/4Q in 2026 and 3.1% in 2027, versus 2.3% and 2.6% in the baseline. Headline CPI runs at 3.7% 4Q/4Q in 2026 and 2.3% in 2027. records.text: ...while bonds started to shriek Inflation concerns pressure long-end yields As the Trump-Xi meeting this week did little to raise hopes for a coordinated US-China effort to pressure Iran into reopening the Strait of Hormuz, the combination of a persistent oil supply shock, increasing inflation rates and still-resilient demand became a recipe for higher interest rates. Yields of longer-dated government bonds surged across regions. 30-year bonds in the US, UK, France, Japan and Germany rose to 5.1%, 5.8%, 4.6%, 4.0% and 3.7%, respectively. Policy rate paths reprice, including for the Fed Along with the pressures on yields at the long end, markets also added to their expectations for central bank policy rate hikes. For end-2026, markets now price a full three hikes for the ECB, between two and three hikes for the BoE, and a full two hikes for the BoJ. For the Fed, the implicit cumulative probability for a hike by year end is just over 60%, but the turnaround from pricing rate cuts until just a few weeks ago is remarkable. There is no longer an expectation of any cut and by Q1 27 the market now prices one hike. Politics don't help in Japan and UK In some cases, political developments further add to the macroeconomic complications. Based on his prior public comments as a Fed governor in 2006-11 and thereafter, we view Warsh as an inflation hawk and doubt that he would push for lower rates as long as they endanger price stability over the longer run. Warsh has been open to lowering rates, but has conditioned such cuts on reducing the size of the Fed's balance sheet or AI-related disinflationary forces. In the current situation, even if Warsh were inclined to cut the policy rate, communications by FOMC participants indicate that a consensus of FOMC voters sees two-sided risks to the funds rate and that the committee is firmly on hold, given the recent elevated inflation prints, the resilient activity and labor market conditions and the uncertainty about the developments in the Middle East and their effects on energy prices and the economy. In response to a structural increase in demand for T-bills from money market funds (MMFs) – resulting from SEC regulatory reform – Treasury has been able to methodically increase the role T-bills play in its issuance portfolio. • Since making a low at 10% in October 2015, the bill share of outstanding marketable debt has been in an upward trend (see Exhibit 261 ).
