How far can 30y yields go? 5.5% does not seem far-fetched Figure 12 and 13 show a scenario analysis for the entire yield curve under different assumptions about the economy, inflation, Fed policy outlook, and term premium. The main thing that stands out is that even if the Fed does not hike, a prolonged period of Fed on hold but without signs of slowing growth would likely lead to a further increase in 30y yields as investors reassess the neutral rate and expectations component. The fiscal profile is unlikely to be much better against that backdrop, given the interest rate sensitivity of budget deficits and investors' likely demanding a high term premium to extend duration. We estimate that 30y yields can rise to about 5.4% in this scenario, and Fed hikes could push them a bit further if growth remains strong. Figure 13 also highlights what needs to happen for 30y yields to fall meaningfully. Were growth to moderate, neutral rate estimates would re-anchor lower and 30y yields cold return to the 4.5-5.0% area. If the US economy enters a recession, then 30y yields could fall to close to 4%, but would likely lag the front to intermediate sector significantly. 15 May 2026 5 Barclays | US Rates Research

This solution significantly improves cooling efficiency and enables more precise temperature control compared to traditional methods.” — Microsoft - Sustainable by design: Transforming datacenter water efficiency, July 2024 Liquid cooling also delivers mechanical and spatial advantages. Replacing bulky air-cooled heat sinks with compact cold plates can free up server volume, reduce congestion, and support higher compute density at both the server and rack level—an increasingly critical consideration as power availability and data center footprints become constrained. Liquid cooling itself is not new. It has been used for decades in high-performance computing (HPC) and supercomputing environments, and hyperscalers began deploying it selectively for AI workloads years ago. For example, Google introduced direct liquid cooling for its TPU v3 platform in 2018. What is new is the deployment of liquid cooling at hyperscale, driven by the mainstream adoption of GPU-dense AI systems, particularly NVIDIA’s Blackwell and subsequent architectures. Microsoft has explicitly indicated that chip-level liquid cooling is becoming a standard design assumption across its owned data centers, reinforcing that liquid cooling is no longer a niche solution. records.text: The strength of the AI trade has lifted the S&P 500 to 14 new highs during the n past month against a backdrop of narrowing breadth and surging Momentum. The S&P 500 has returned 10% YTD, with technology accounting for 85% of the index return and the S&P 500 excluding technology returning just 3%. The rally has also driven a 25% return in our Momentum factor during the past three months, one of its sharpest upswings on record. With AI and Momentum moving hand in hand and driving the direction of the S&P 500, many investors have expressed the view that the equity market today is “one big trade” rather than “a market of stocks.” Similar sharp Momentum rallies in the past have preceded near-term n Momentum strength but medium-term equity market weakness. Since 1980, following 11 other comparable rallies, Momentum usually extended for another month before peaking and turning lower. For the S&P 500, sharp Momentum rallies with the market near a high usually preceded soft returns during the following few months. These episodes included mid-1998, late 1999, mid-2015, and late 2021. Today, we expect the macroeconomic backdrop and the outlook for AI will determine the trajectories of both Momentum and the broad market. Much of the recent equity market momentum has corresponded with surging n near-term earnings estimates. Bottom-up consensus estimates for S&P 500 EPS in 2026 and 2027 have each risen by 8% YTD. Morgan Core CPI Core PCE Core PPI Nonfuel import prices While core goods inflation was cool in CPI, it was hot in the PPI and import price reports. The core PPI jumped 1.0%m/m, similar to some of the peak monthly readings from the 2021- 22 inflation surge, despite services less trade, transportation, and warehousing rising just 0.1%. The increase in the overall core reflected an increase in goods prices, along with a record rise (since data began in 2010) in wholesale/retail margins and transportation, with the latter two categories exhibiting some spillover from higher energy prices. Nonfuel import prices also rose 0.8% as demand from data centers yielded a record increase in computer prices. As the data came out during the week, a number of Fed Dis- trict Bank Presidents weighed in. Among others, Goolsbee worried about “overheating,” Collins said she was “particu- larly concerned about inflation,” Schmid said inflation remained the most pressing risk, and Williams said there was no reason to either raise or lower rates, although he still viewed policy as mildy restrictive. Only Williams is a voter this year. Still, their comments, along with the dissents over language from Hammack, Kashkari, and Logan at the last meeting, imply the policy language will get a serious vetting at the next meeting—especially as Warsh argued against any forward guidance in his Senate confirmation testimony. Tightening bias in EM Asia rising We now expect pre-emptive policy tightening by the Bank of Korea (BoK), with hikes starting from Q3 26, driven more by oil/inflation expectations and financial-conditions/ equity effects than clear demand-driven inflation. Our revision in the policy rate forecast is derived from our view that the tech supply chain's export boom in Korea is creating a tectonic shift in GDP: We nudge up our 2026 and 2027 GDP growth forecast to 2.6% and 2.0% from 2.4% and 1.5%, respectively. While it is difficult to gauge how much of the effect on GDP will be cyclical, structural, or a one-off boost, we believe the key features of this innovation shock are 1) the unevenness of growth between the different segments of the economy, and 2) that it is unlikely to last forever. We believe the BoK has room to wait-and-see with domestic demand gradually recovering from the weak momentum in 2025 and uncertainty around how structural and cyclical the tech upcycle could be. However, another layer of exogenous shock from oil prices and caution against another inflation expectation spiral as well as the policymakers' assessment on growth likely tilts the bias towards a modest monetary policy response, in our view. Due to their low duration (the longest maturity tenor is 12 months), adjusting bill issuance is the least disruptive and most cost-effective way to change borrowing quickly, especially when Treasury’s borrowing needs shift rapidly. As shown in Exhibit 261 , the bill share rises during periods of recession (marked in gold) as automatic stabilizers for transfer payments bring forth unexpected changes in borrowing needs, which are then met via sharp increases in T-bill issuance. • During the GFC, the T-bill share peaked at 34% of outstanding marketable debt. After the Covid-19 pandemic, the T-bill share peaked at 26% and has hovered just below pre-GFC averages over the last few years. Adjustments to T-bill issuance are also utilized during debt limit episodes, both from constraints on borrowing during the impasse, as well as the subsequent increase in borrowing needs necessitated to rebuild the cash balance.

records.text: Euro Area Viewpoint | 14 May 2026 3 Structural or cyclical beyond 2025 record year? China-EU trade dynamics were eye-catching in 2025, with the trade deficit widening by 16%. On average last year, the EU import value from China rose 11.6% yoy, the import volume was up 14.3%, while the aggregated EU import unit value from China declined by ca 2% (Exhibit 3). Looking at trends by sector, our China Economics team (see report: China Viewpoint: Will Europe remain a key destination for China’s exports amid US tariff shocks? 19 November 2025) noted that machinery and electronic equipment, small packages (de- minimis), and autos contributed most of the robust 2025 growth in EU imports from China, explained by sector-specific drivers. Machinery and electrical equipment imports were partly cyclical, in contrast with double-digit growth in Chinese auto exports as a result of a more structural trend driven by Chinese EV makers’ comparative advantage in tech-advancement and cost efficiency. They attributed tariff-induced trade diversion away from the US and into Europe to certain consumer goods exports such as de-minimis, toys, and textiles. Testing the vent-for-surplus hypothesis As noted before, Exhibit 3 suggests that Chinese exports started to deviate from their pre‑pandemic trend before 2025. We therefore extend the analysis by testing the vent‑for‑surplus hypothesis in EU‑China trade dynamics. Under this mechanism, a domestic demand-driven decline in sectoral turnover leads to excess capacity that firms are keen to reallocate to foreign markets. Ceteris paribus, clearing surplus production abroad would be associated with lower prices. In trade data, this would show up as stronger export volumes accompanied by weaker unit value growth. To test this hypothesis, we first attempt to identify Chinese manufacturing sectors that displayed domestic demand underperformance. We follow the methodology set out in the ECB Economic Bulletin 1 (July 2025). We proxy real domestic sales as nominal operating income minus exports, deflated by sector-specific producer price indices. Immersion Cooling: Max Performance, but Maximum Friction Immersion cooling submerges entire servers—compute, memory, and power components—in a dielectric fluid, eliminating server fans, heat sinks, and internal airflow. From a thermal standpoint, immersion offers some of the highest achievable heat-flux removal and can support extreme rack-level power densities. records.text: inforcing that liquid cooling is no longer a niche solution. Risk of Cooling Labor Constraints Advanced data center cooling systems are highly labor-intensive compared to other data center subsystems. These deployments require extensive on-site skilled trades (plumbers, pipefitters, HVAC technicians, welders, electricians, controls specialists, commissioning engineers). For example, installing a liquid cooling loop or chiller plant involves complex networks of pumps, valves, heat exchangers, and piping custom-fitted and tested on-site—far more fine-grained work than connecting prefabricated power distribution modules or server racks. As a result, cooling systems demand significantly more skilled-trade hours per megawatt of capacity and can comprise an outsized share of a project’s build cost. Chase Lochmiller, the CEO of Crusoe (private), which is the developer behind the Stargate campus in Abilene, Texas with up to 2.1 GW of power capacity for Oracle and Microsoft, recently quantified the labor costs for data center development at $4.7 million per a megawatt, equating to roughly 25% of the total cost of a facility with behind-the-meter power (likely even higher when excluding behind-the-meter power).18 13 May 2026 15 Barclays | Thematic Investing

The other group gives the impression of not being convinced yet that there is enough evidence of a broad inflation shock to support a hike in June. If this division on the Council holds, it creates numerous questions. Is the market overpricing a June hike? Would Lagarde be willing to hike in June with only a small majority? What compromises could be made to ensure a large majority for a June hike (e.g., on communications)? If there is no hike in June, would the hike merely be delayed to the next meeting in July? Or to the next forecast round in September? Or would remaining on hold in June significantly lower the probability of any hikes at all? Maybe the divisions should not be overstated, however. Maybe the doves are merely being cautious. The ECB is supposed to be data dependent. It has not pre- committed to a path for policy. Data (and events) over the next few weeks will determine what happens at the June meeting. Our view remains that a measured tightening, starting with a 25bp hike in June, is consistent with the data that has been emerging. Many of these companies explicitly target high-performance computing (HPC) and AI data centers with purpose-built offerings, particularly leak-free quick-connect couplings. Large industrial players have increasingly entered the space—often through acquisitions and new product lines announced since 2024— reflecting a broader wave of consolidation and growth driven by accelerating adoption of liquid cooling. Publicly listed companies active in this market include Belimo, Dover, Ecolab, Gates, Ingersoll Rand, Parker-Hannifin, Pentair, Sulzer and Xylem. Private companies include Danfoss (industrial group with a broad portfolio of liquid-cooling couplings, hoses, and fittings), DCX Liquid Cooling (a full-stack liquid-cooling system manufacturer producing cold plates, manifold assemblies, sealed coolant loop modules, and CDUs), Molex (a Koch Industries-owned business that has expanded into advanced connectivity and fluid-handling solutions), Stäubli (a major manufacturer of leak-free quick-disconnect couplings), and Victaulic (a large piping and connection-systems supplier serving liquid-cooling manifold and piping applications). 13 May 2026 44 Barclays | Thematic Investing

Catalyst.Metric: Tariffs, EU imports from China, export volumes, unit value compression

records.text: reciprocal tariffs did have a major impact on diverting Chinese exports away from the US. But tariff specificities again fail to explain the aggregate surge in EU imports from China. In sum, tariffs reduced US imports but fail to explain any meaningful rerouting toward Europe. ‘Vent-for-surplus’ theory explains rising EU exposure EU imports from China being well above pre-pandemic trends even before 2025 suggests other structural forces are at play, including genuine comparative advantage, targeted domestic subsidies and vent-for-surplus behaviour. We test the latter, whereby external markets absorb surplus domestic capacity. We find sectors with under- performing Chinese domestic demand systematically show stronger export volumes and significantly weaker unit value growth than other sectors in 2021-26. This pattern holds when 2025 trade dynamics are excluded, consistent with a vent-for-surplus mechanism driven by excess capacity, not a tariff-induced diversion story. Import unit value compression is a key channel Our panel results indicate ca3–3.5pp additional annual price compression in sectors where Chinese domestic demand is underperforming. Notably, this pattern is stronger pre-2025, implying that excess supply pressures were already entrenched. Post-2025, pricing compression becomes more generalized across sectors, consistent with a broader demand shock triggered by US tariff hikes rather than targeted re-allocation. Aware of the issue, the federal government recently relaunched a debt renegotiation program (Desenrola 2.0) for 90 days, aimed at reducing delinquency by allowing low- and middle-income borrowers to restructure or settle outstanding debts with discounts ranging from 30% to 90%, providing improved terms and up to 48 months for repayment. Borrowers negotiate directly with their creditors (mainly banks) and the government acts as a facilitator, but not as a counterparty to the debt. There is no public subsidy to the discount itself, to be determined by the banks, but the government provides a credit guarantee fund (mobilizing as much as BRL15bn in financial resources) that partially covers the risk on restructured loans. In Mexico, overall bank credit to the private sector posted an annual growth of 1.8% in April 2026 (in real terms), a sharp deceleration from the 9.0% pace observed in April 2025. Along with certain of the more popular iBoxx indices, the US Agg index family currently excludes 144A for Life securities. We believe this exclusion made a lot of sense in the 1970s when the index was rolled out and non-QIB individual investors were oftentimes direct buy- ers of corporate bonds. Fast forward to today and the vast majority of bond-buying is through QIB-eligible mutual funds and ETFs and thus this exclusion makes far less sense. There are of course other differences as it relates to 144A for life securities, such as a lack of public disclosure, but these, in our view, are not grounds for index exclusion relative to for example the $38bn of mostly EM bonds in the US Agg that are fully registered but in jurisdictions such as the Cayman Islands, Bermuda and the Virgin Islands. Bloomberg led an investor consultation to add 144A for Life to the US Agg in October 2023, but this propos- al never went forward (we discussed this here at the time). In contrast, the Bloomberg Uni- versal and Global Agg indices as well as the benchmark ICE indices do include 144A for Life securities, as does every major HY index to our knowledge. Water Tech: Complementing Cooling-System Design Water Tech is increasingly central to managing water-related execution risk, complementing cooling-system design choices. Cooling architectures determine baseline water intensity, but reuse and digital solutions can help reduce reliance on freshwater withdrawals, while water treatment remains critical for system reliability and uptime. This is becoming more important as water demand intensifies both on- site and upstream—across data center cooling, semiconductor manufacturing, and power generation—particularly in regions facing water stress, infrastructure constraints, or heightened regulatory and community scrutiny. More broadly, the data center build-out and hyperscaler water positive targets will support further investment in water infrastructure and local projects like irrigation upgrades. Water treatment technologies will be needed to meet varying quality requirements across the AI stack. In data centers, water used in cooling systems is subject to scaling, corrosion, and fouling, driving demand for treatment solutions and translating into a recurring revenue stream for companies providing consumables like chemicals. In addition, rising purity standards are increasing the water intensity of semiconductor manufacturing. Importantly, this dynamic reflects the importance of water quality in addition to supply. To reduce reliance on water withdrawals, reuse strategies are being explored for data center cooling. Reuse has gained traction in water-intensive industries, including semiconductors, where companies have actively integrated water recycling into operations. In data centers, however, water consumption is largely driven by evaporative cooling, where water is lost to the atmosphere. As a result, opportunities for reuse center less on recycling water back into operations and more on substituting freshwater withdrawals with alternative sources, such as treated municipal wastewater. Early data-center efforts to integrate on-site wastewater recycling include xAI's plans for its Colossus data centers and Amazon's partnership with Veolia (see Examples of Water Infrastructure Projects for Data Centers below).21 Looking ahead, we see potential for reuse to support siting flexibility, strengthen operational resilience, and help garner community support in some regions. records.text: US Focus When tides turn: Lessons from sector-driven default cycles The risk of a software-driven default cycle has risen amid the age of agentic AI. We study the TMT default cycle in 2000 and energy in 2015 and find that, while early, software defaults are progressing similarly. However, we expect a more prolonged default accumulation and weaker recovery outcomes. Software concerns persist. With equity multiples yet to recover in a meaningful way, software valuations remain under pressure. Software loans are lower by 6-7pts on the year, while the index as a whole is down only 1.25pts. Investors looking ahead to the $70bn+ of software BSLs maturing in 2028-29 are preparing for refinancing struggles and, in some cases, defaults. We study TMT and energy default cycles to better understand cumulative default rates. Sector-driven default cycles that are fresh in investors' minds include TMT after the bursting of the dot-com bubble and energy around the time of the commodity crisis in 2015. We analyze these cycles and find that cumulative par-weighted default rates within those sectors rose to 35-45% in the six-year period following the start of the default wave. records.text: he curve. The residual is simply the difference between the market forward and the PCA fair value. A positive residual means the forward is trading above fair value, or rich. A negative residual means the forward is trading below fair value, or cheap (Exhibit 234 ). We then convert the residual into a rolling z-score, so that the signal is scaled relative to the forward’s own recent history. We show PC1 against a representative forward such as 4y1y. When PC1 rises, the general inflation-forward curve level is usually moving higher; when PC1 falls, the curve is generally moving lower ( Exhibit 235 ). PC2 is the slope factor. It captures the main relative move between shorter-dated and longer-dated inflation forwards after removing the overall level move. We compare PC2 against long-versus-front inflation forward slope, such as 20y5y minus 2y1y (Exhibit 236 ). This gives us a statistical measure of whether the inflation-forward curve is unusually steep or flat versus its own history. PC3 is the curvature or butterfly factor of the inflation-forward curve. It shows when one part of the curve, such as the belly, moves differently from the front and long end. We compare PC3 with a butterfly-style expression like 1y1y+9y1y−2×4y1y to show that it is capturing curve curvature ( Exhibit 237 ).

We therefore tested reserves in both levels and changes, including log reserves and reserve-runoff variables. The expected signs are intuitive: higher reserves should be associated with lower repo spreads, while faster reserve runoff should push spreads wider. 2) APF gilt holdings. APF gilt holdings capture collateral scarcity. A higher APF holding ratio means a larger share of the gilt market is held inside the APF, reducing the free float available for repo transactions. We therefore use APF holdings as a percentage of total nominal gilts outstanding, rather than the APF stock alone. 3) Treasury bill supply. Treasury bill supply captures the short-collateral channel. More bills outstanding should increase the available stock of safe, short-dated collateral and should therefore be associated with wider repo spreads versus SONIA. We tested both the level of bills outstanding and bills outstanding relative to reserves, in levels and changes. 4) Composition of BoE liquidity provision. The UK is undergoing a regime shift in the way reserves are supplied. Since the GFC, and especially during QE and TFSME, reserves were largely provided through asset purchases and term funding schemes. HFA multifamily programs benefit from several structural credit strengths that have histori- cally supported strong ratings across the sector. Persistent demand and strong performance indicators : The persistent demand for affordable rental housing, particularly LIHTC-qualified units, tends to produce stronger performance indicators relative to conventional multifamily properties. Because LIHTC properties offer below-market rents and are often newly constructed or substantially reha- bilitated, they are frequently well-situated competitively within their submarkets. This combination of affordability and physical quality supports high and stable occupancy rates, which in turn translates into low delinquency and foreclosure experience across HFA loan portfolios (the national LIHTC portfolio maintained a median physical occu- pancy of 97% and a cumulative foreclosure rate of under 0.5% as of 2024, according to CohnReznick’ s 2025 Affordable Housing Credit Study). We start by assessing the impact of the 2025 US tariff wave on China’s exports to the EU (cross-checking against China’s exports to the US as a control), and any tariff- specificity attached to Chinese product baskets more heavily tariffed than EU goods. With capex, cumulative figures are normally reported. Burnham has, per Reuters, also advocated tax cuts for low income earners, tax hikes for high income earners, and taxes on expensive homes. Note, Chancellor Reeves introduced an annual levy on more expensive houses in the Budget last year. Elsewhere, Burnham has historically been pro-EU, and has advocated for devolution of power in order to improve regional growth. He is in favour of changing the UK's voting system, from first-past-the-post towards proportional representation. For the Fed, markets have aligned with our call for a Fed rate hike next year, and the latest developments raise risks of an earlier move. ECB & BoJ to hike in June; BoE less clear There are still four weeks until the ECB’s June policy meet- ing. Incoming commentary supports a hike but emphasizes data dependence. A deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz could alter the calculus, but our commodities analysts expect oil prices to stay high for a while, and natural gas prices to rise, regardless. We expect next week’s flash PMI to edge up after large falls in March-April, with output prices staying high. All of this points to a June rate hike and one more thereafter. The ECB will also view an initial 25bp hike as a relatively modest move that leaves its policy rate in its neutral range. The BoE has set a higher bar for rate hikes than the ECB, reflecting the UK’s weaker labor market. Despite this, growth indicators have surprised positively, with 1Q GDP up 2.5% annualized and April PMI showing resilience. Inflation indi- cators have risen sharply, demonstrating greater responsive- ness than in the Euro area. Still, the BoE is cautious about the scale of tightening priced in by markets, which is weighing on the housing market. We still expect a June hike, but risks are tilted towards a delay until 3Q. If the Option-Adjusted Basis Net of Carry (OABNOC) is lower for the front month than for the back month contract, the calendar spread is considered rich. 2) Changes in short-term funding rates. An increase in funding rates generally causes futures prices to rise relative to cash prices, since it decreases the carry basis. Thus the calendar spread reflects changes in the shape of the short end of the yield curve: for example, if four-month funding rates rise while one-month rates remain the same, the calendar spread would be expected to fall. Changes in funding rates affect back-month futures more than front-month futures, since the back- month contract has three months more of carry in its basis. As a rule of thumb, for a parallel change in funding rates: -1 x (change in funding rate) / 4 = change in calendar spread For example, if short-term rates increase by 25 basis points, the calendar spread is expected to decrease by approximately .0625: -1 x .25 / 4 = -.0625 (in decimal form, or -2/32nds) 3) Supply and demand pressures. The calendar spread may become richer or cheaper depending on the balance of long and short hedgers and investors who are rolling positions. Since late‑2025, the FSR has been actively deployed against Chinese companies across the rail, clean‑tech, and digital sectors, marking a clear shift toward enforcement (Exhibit 10). The April 2026 decision in the Lisbon metro case – where a Chinese rail supplier (CRRC) was effectively excluded – represents the first binding remedy under the FSR procurement tool and signals a more interventionist stance. More broadly, the pattern of cases suggests that the FSR is evolving into a complementary instrument to trade defence, targeting subsidised competitive distortions that manifest inside the EU rather than at the border. Taken together, these measures point to a clear intensification of EU trade defence policy vis‑à‑vis China, extending from border measures to in‑market regulation in an effort to contain the impact of potential subsidised excess capacity.

records.text: 14 May 2026 Europe Blog Deutsche Bank AG Page 6 amplifiers is currently less potent than it was during the post-pandemic inflation surge. As we have previously argued, the labour market is in a more ambiguous position today and large second -round inflation effects would likely need a stronger demand environment than the euro area is currently facing . If the drop in employment intentions in the European Commission survey signals a cooling of labour demand since the start of the Middle East conflict , maybe there will be less concern about passthrough. records.text: M Europe Insight 14 EGBs: The Waiting Game As discussed in the introduction, if energy prices rise further, in line with our baseline forecast, we would see initial pressure for EGB spreads to widen. However, we expect the Middle East conflict to normalize (albeit very slowly) and spreads should eventually tighten back. Exhibit 20 shows our 10y Italy-Germany forecast under all the macro scenarios. The bullish case for high yielders is realized in most of the alternative scenarios: an acceleration of the US economy, an AI dividend, or de-escalation in the Middle East would be positive for risky assets and EGB spread compression. The bearish case for high yielders is realized in the event that the conflict in the Middle East escalates. In this scenario, we have the 10y Italy-Germany spread widening as much as 145bp at the peak of the crisis. This might seem excessive given how tight Italy was trading before the Middle East conflict, but some historical context is needed - note that we still expect the spread widening to be contained compared to what we have seen in the post QE era, let alone during the sovereign crisis 15 years ago. We also highlight how the periphery spread beta to a credit spread proxy has decreased significantly since the launch of the PEPP and PSPP in March 2020 (Exhibit 21 ). records.text: Europe Economic Weekly | 15 May 2026 3 broad-based slowdown in Chinese exports to the US, EU imports from China still rose 11.6% yoy last year. Is trade diversion to blame for this? Not so fast – we look empirically and carefully at this in our main Europe piece. First, this trend did not start in April 2025; EU imports from China were well above pre-pandemic levels even before last year's tariffs hit. And yes, we estimate that post April 2025, Chinese exports to the US slowed by ca20-26% across HS2 manufacturing sectors. Yet there has been no statistically robust increase in China's export growth to the EU due to 2025 US tariff-induced trade rerouting. What are the key drivers then? EU imports from China being well above pre-pandemic trends even before 2025 suggests other structural forces are at play, including genuine comparative advantage, targeted domestic subsidies and vent-for-surplus behaviour (i.e., companies facing weakness in Chinese demand are forced to step up efforts to seek new destinations for their goods). We test the latter, whereby external markets absorb surplus domestic capacity. We find sectors with underperforming Chinese domestic demand systematically show stronger export volumes and significantly weaker unit value growth than other sectors in 2021- 26. This pattern holds when 2025 trade dynamics are excluded, consistent with a vent- for-surplus mechanism driven by excess capacity, not a tariff-induced diversion story. records.text: keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear CREDIT, COMMODITIES AND SUSTAINABILITY | CORPORATE MARKETS MONTHLY 3515/05/2026 Sustainability: Positioning for AI’s water constraints Making waves: The rapid growth of AI-driven digital infrastructure has created new – and sometimes underappreciated – pressures on global water resources. Water consumption in the AI supply chain is estimated to rise to around 1.2 trillion litres by 2030 from about 560 billion in 2023 (International Energy Agency, 2025). That would match the most recent estimate of annual water consumption in Estonia (World Population Review, 2026). Around two-thirds of water consumption in the AI ecosystem is currently for primary energy supply and electricity generation, and around a quarter for data- centre cooling. The rest is for the ultra-pure water needed in semiconductor and microchip manufacturing. Geographic constraints: Unlike electricity, access to which can be expanded through additional generation and transmission infrastructure, water availability is fundamentally constrained by geography, hydrology and climate. These structural constraints make scaling up water supply more difficult than expanding power capacity. Tighter regulation: The water stress issue is attracting global policy attention. Short-term real rates surged from around 0% to nearly 40% during 2025 amid election tensions and changes in the monetary framework, yet activity largely continued the weak trend already in place rather than collapsing as one might expect elsewhere in the region. We also think there is limited room for credit to expand meaningfully from the supply side. The main structural constraint is the lack of peso savings: total deposits in the banking system amount to only around 12% of GDP , down from an already low 24% in 2004 after two decades of high inflation and negative real rates. In the short run, this leaves banks with relatively little room to expand lending aggressively. Indeed, lending to the private sector already stands at roughly 67% of ARS deposits, up sharply from 33% in May 2024 and broadly back to the levels seen during 2015-19. At the same time, non-performing loans are elevated, particularly among households, where NPLs are at record highs, which probably limits banks' propensity to lend. Demand-side dynamics are not especially supportive either. While policy and deposit rates have fallen considerably, consumer borrowing rates have declined much less and remain close to the levels prevailing around the July 2025 monetary framework shift. records.text: US Economic Presentation15 May 2026 ab 37 Source: BEA, BLS, Haver, UBS What next? The expansion rests on narrow support, driven by AI underpinning the expansion. We are now at peak fiscal support to growth. We are also at peak tariff impact on inflation. Now we have higher energy prices as a new risk to the expansion, and little visibility into when the supply disruptions will be resolved. Plus, the labor market appears more vulnerable than appreciated. If the AI investment or support for equities falters, the expansion itself would be at risk. The FOMC will need to confront these risks too, with tensions in the mandate likely leading to tensions in the committee. The distribution of potential outcomes for monetary policy are widening (rates up and down), but we expect the FOMC would take some time before actually enacting rate hikes, and as a base case see the Fed funds at 3.25% - 3.5% by the end of 2026. We are bullish longer term and estimate that we are on the cusp of an acceleration in structural growth. Key question(s): Can the geopolitical disruptions, policy uncertainty and volatility get out of the way? records.text: US Rates Weekly 15 May 2026 Citi Research 8 In Figure 13, we report a simple year-to-date regression between SOFR/IORB and our simple front-end heuristic, private T-bill outstanding minus bank reserves. Effectively, as our heuristic falls, there is an increased chance that SOFR falls towards the RRP rate in a non-linear fashion. Or in other words, when there is too much liquidity, which itself is a moving target, money market funds can find themselves forced to lend closer to the RRP backstop. We think funding will remain relatively supportive for May and June but will turn more challenging in July as the Treasury looks to grow their TGA towards $1tn, which reduces reserves. This week, the Fed reduced their reserve management purchases (RMPs) down to $10bn/month, which was larger than the $20bn/month we expected. We do not think the Fed will reduce RMPs to zero for now, as they likely wanted to build a buffer on top of the Q4 2025 reserve levels. They presumably front-loaded this buffer ahead of the April 15 tax date. Going forward, we think they will want to maintain this buffer. Thus, the $10bn/month will help offset the growth in currency in circulation, which drains liquidity at roughly $6bn/month over the past year, and in bank deposits. The banking system’s demand for reserves will move higher as aggregate deposits goes up, since banks need to keep some cash on hand for liquidity purposes against those deposits. The scenario with the greatest upside for BEIs is one in which US demand surprises to the upside, inflation advances in Japan, and USD/JPY rises to 163. Even in this scenario, however, with inflation expected to slow in the latter half of 2027, the peak in BEIs would be only around 2.15%, suggesting limited upside from current levels. Conversely, in the demand-destruction scenario, which entails larger downside for BEIs, short-term inflationary pressure is the strongest, but concerns about future growth increase. Against a backdrop of a sharp decline in USD/JPY and deterioration in risk sentiment, BEIs would fall significantly. We expect BEIs to decline toward around 1.5% by mid-2027. Taking a weighted average based on the scenario probabilities assigned by our economists, BEIs are expected to remain broadly range-bound, which is our base scenario. An examination of risk/reward across these scenarios suggests that BEI upside is limited, but downside is also well supported.

records.text: US Credit Alpha Overview Risk assets keep rallying despite macro stress. Spread volatility is historically muted despite dangers from inflation and geopolitics. Strong earnings, high yields, and global supply support credit, but convergence risk is rising. Selective listening Risk assets and macro sentiment continue to diverge, operating almost in isolation. As of Wednesday's close, investment grade spreads were just 4bp off multi-decade tights, with high yield just 15bp back, and as of midday Thursday, the S&P 500 had broken through 7,500. In the background, bonds have sold off, as rising energy prices are driving inflation (and expectations) higher, the ceasefire in the Middle East continues to have a case of the hiccups, and average national gas prices have hit their highest levels since 2022. Markets, though, have clearly given more credence to the strong earnings season, with high yields drawing in fixed income demand (without concern for what caused them) and the potential for AI to unlock broad new growth streams for the global economy. This divergence is not new, but as markets become further misaligned, convergence risk between the two sides could be worrisome for frothy risk markets. Spread volatility has collapsed. Even with these risks popping up, over the past 20 trading days, high yield has traded in a 10bp range (262-272bp). Our view is that the market tends to fully price these flows in ex-post rather than ex-ante. " Since the 2033 reset date is 20 years prior to the effective maturity date, the economic incentive to extend is negated by the loss of S&P equity content at first call date (as long as the issuer remains IG rated), making this an even stronger structure for investors than a floored NC5/7. The SO 32NC7s — the only other NC7 in the market — is a floored structure. While the floor increases the likelihood of a call, it still carries extension risk, as it does not lose equity credit until year 12. This is a big reason, in our view, that the SO NC7-NC10 curve trades inverted, as most NC5-NC10 curves do. The coupon step-up in the VZ 32NC7 eliminates the extension risk and should drive a normalized curve over time, despite pricing inverted. See Figure 3 for a comparison between the two NC7s. In other words, step-up structures are designed as an extension risk vaccine while coupon floors are designed as pain killers in case of extension. As long as the issuer is IG rated at S&P , we rank extension risk in US corporate hybrids structures as follows (from lowest to highest): 30NC10 with coupon floor, 30NC10 (without coupon floor) or 30NC5/32NC7 with step-ups, 30NC5/32NC7 with coupon floor and then 30NC5/32NC7 (without coupon floor and without step-ups). Any fall in energy prices would, however, raise the likelihood that the PMI recovers again, which would work in the other direction. In any case, we are skeptical that energy prices will immediately fall close to pre-war levels and therefore upside inflation pressures are likely to remain. The ECB has also pointed to damaged production facilities, low storage levels and shipping bottlenecks as reasons for expecting a slow normalization of energy prices in case of a deal. In terms of the PMI, we expect it to nudge higher in May after having fallen sharply in March and April. This would provide some reassurance that growth is holding at a modest- ly positive level in May. We also expect the PMI to consoli- date the sharp increases in the output price index seen in April. records.text: Little Sign of Labor Market Mismatch So Far As AI adoption expands, there is growing concern that the type of workers the economy needs is changing faster than workers—especially young workers—are adapting, creating a mismatch problem. While industry- and state-level measures of job-worker mismatch remain subdued, they are imperfect tests of the claim that there are too many coders and not enough plumbers. We therefore introduce a new measure of occupation-level job openings using job opening data from LinkUp to investigate further. We find that the composition of US job openings has indeed shifted meaningfully since 2019: there are now 300k more openings for on-site service and production occupations such as healthcare, food preparation, and maintenance but 450k fewer openings for office occupations such as sales, computer and information services, and administrative support—areas where AI is already being deployed. It can provide greater energy efficiency ( ~1.4-1.8 PUE) and cooling capacity than air-cooled CRAC units, but less efficiency and capacity than other systems with centralized compressors. Its use of wet cooling towers leads to high water loss and requires water treatment to mitigate scaling, bacterial growth, and corrosion, adding complexity and cost. Where it is commonly used: These systems are typically deployed in mid-sized to large enterprise data centers that do not require high-density liquid cooling, already have cooling tower infrastructure or require higher thermal performance and energy efficiency than air- cooled CRACs can provide. How it works: Like air-cooled CRACs, water-cooled CRACs use a Direct Expansion (DX) refrigeration cycle to cool server room air. However, the heat absorbed by the refrigerant in the DX CRAC unit isn't transferred to an outdoor air-cooled condenser, but rather to a water-cooled condenser coil within the CRAC. They also adjust for Burnham's popularity, and accounting for that, estimate the by-election as yielding a narrow Labour win, with Labour at 39% and Reform at 36% (Exhibit 1 ). As a reminder, in the 2026 Gorton and Denton by-election, Greens won 41% of the vote, with Labour at 25% and Reform at 29%. While this seems a fair adjustment methodology, one should note, however, that Makerfield has fewer prospective Green voters than Gorton, as the two seats are demographically quite different. The funds rate can not do much to stop cost-push inflation, but it can risk making a weak labor demand too weak. The same goes for energy prices, a rising downside risk to the expansion. records.text: growing the price at the repo rate over the holding horizon, while subtracting the coupons received, adjusted for reinvestment, as well as the accrued interest at the forward date. For a TIPS bond, carry has an extra ingredient: inflation assumptions for future months. TIPS principal is indexed to CPI, so the forward price depends not just on repo rates and coupons, but also on where the market expects CPI to be at the forward date. We use daily CPI fixings values for the inflation assumption. The factors that contribute to carry calculation of a bond on a day-to-day basis are: 1. Price of the bond: Buying the bond when its price is high implies higher cost of financing, thus reducing the carry. Said differently, higher yield of a bond leads to higher carry and vice versa ( Exhibit 240 ). 2. Repo: All else equal, higher repo costs leads to lower carry. Repo cost is factored in financing the bond and reinvestment of the coupon payment back in the bond. 3. Inflation assumptions: As TIPS principal is linked to CPI, an assumption that inflation goes higher leads to higher principal amount and hence higher coupon payments. This leads to higher TIPS carry.

records.text: iquidity needs of banks and dealers are current- ly not being well served by the current market infrastructure, given the frictions and stigma that push banks toward holding a larger static reserve buffer than needed. Intraday repo changes that dynamic; instead of funding intraday peaks with reserves all day, banks can convert Treasury collateral into cash when needed and unwind shortly thereafter. The eco- nomic implications of intraday repo could also be meaningful; freed up reserves could be deployed into other areas that provide a higher ROI than IORB, and banks won’t have to pay up as much for intraday funding by funding that buffer overnight or long-term. Interestingly, intraday repo does not necessarily trigger the regulatory ratios that often lead to bal- ance sheet constraints in the traditional repo market. Because intraday repos are settled and unwound within the same day, they typically fall outside the end-of-day balance sheet snapshots that drive SLR, LCR, and related regulatory calculations. On the lending side, intraday repo allows those with excess, idle cash (e.g. corporates, MMFs, FHLBs, stable- coin issuers) to monetize those cash balances intraday, while still keeping their liquidity profile tight and predictable. records.text: Rockets and Feathers: Asymmetric Passthrough from Energy Shocks ECB officials are focused on passthrough effects from higher energy prices into underlying inflation, via indirect effects (through supply chains) and second-round effects (through wage bargaining). Our previous work shows that the likelihood of such passthrough depends importantly on the size of the shock, with larger energy price increases more likely to lead to persistent inflationary pressures. Past energy shocks also point to a potential asymmetry in the transmission of energy shocks. In particular, energy price increases tend to have stronger effects for underlying inflation than energy price declines. This asymmetry is often called “rocket and feather” pricing. Given the ongoing uncertainty around energy prices, such asymmetries in passthrough could have important implications for the inflation and policy outlook. Existing Evidence on Asymmetric Passthrough Several studies point to asymmetric transmission from energy prices to inflation. The IMF, for example, has documented uneven passthrough from headline inflation shocks to core inflation in the Euro area, with positive food and energy inflation shocks displaying a strong increasing relation with core inflation, whereas negative headline shocks have an insignificant relationship with core inflation (Exhibit 1, left). records.text: Diverging Hyperscaler Approaches to Water Use Hyperscaler data center cooling strategies are increasingly shaped by a multidimensional trade-off between energy consumption, direct (on-site) water use, and the indirect (upstream) water use and emissions associated with electricity generation. Within this framework, hyperscalers are beginning to diverge. Microsoft and Meta appear to be prioritizing low- or zero-water cooling architectures, accepting modest increases in electricity demand in exchange for reduced water exposure. By contrast, Google and Amazon have indicated they will continue to deploy evaporative cooling selectively where water risk is low. They frame evaporative cooling as a system-level optimization that can materially reduce electricity consumption and associated indirect water use and emissions, especially in hot climates or in regions where grid decarbonization is still evolving. That said, both companies emphasize that cooling system design remains region-specific, influenced not only by water availability, but also by climate, permitting risk, community acceptance, and grid carbon intensity. “When evaluating cooling technologies, we assess both water and energy usage to identify the most efficient method and minimize environmental and community impact. Liquid cooling addresses many of the challenges associated with power-dense AI servers by leveraging the fundamentally superior thermal properties of liquids—particularly water—relative to air. For a given temperature change: • Water carries roughly 3,500–4,000x more heat per unit volume than air; • Water’s thermal conductivity is ~20–30× higher than that of air; • Pumps are materially more energy-efficient at moving liquid than fans are at moving air. By bringing liquid closer to the heat source, typically through direct-to-chip cold plates, liquid cooling dramatically reduces thermal resistance between processors and the heat-rejection system. More recently, he has discussed carving specific spending (for defence) out of the fiscal rules, which would still amount to additional borrowing and an easier fiscal position. The backdrop for this is already a difficult fiscal outlook (with 1.6pp of GDP of tightening of the cyclically adjusted primary balance already factored in over the next three years) and one that had been made worse by recent rising gilt yields, which we calculate have taken around £7-10bn from the Chancellor's current c.£24bn of headroom. This means that Andy Burnham, like any potential leadership challenger, will have to walk a careful tightrope of delivering a message that maximises the chances of winning the leadership (and before that a potential by-election) and keeping financial markets onside so as to not see a deterioration of the fiscal position. By-election not a sure thing Current market odds have the chances of Labour winning the by-election in Makerfield at 4/6 (or 60%)2 . Labour won the seat with a majority of more than 5,000

Still, it adds to the pressure on the European economy; needless to say, the outlook remains dependent on the energy shock not intensifying further. Apart from the main macro forecasts, our mid-year outlook also contains a lot interesting analyses and deep dives on selected issues relevant for the European economy. We explore the strength of the consumer amid the real income shock, detail the upcoming wage negotiations across Europe and the expected pass- through from higher prices, and explain our expectations for EA inflation from the lessons we learnt in 2022-23. We will use the coming weeklies to present some of these findings in a condensed way. Next week we will start with what we know about European AI investments (spoiler: there is more to be seen than six months ago). Stay tuned (and if you don’t want to wait, again, the analysis can be found here).

records.text: Agency MBS Longer-term view: MBS basis likely to end the year wider from current levels Last week, we outlined our near-term positioning views. We expect MBS spreads to move sideways in the near term. Key near-term headwinds include the seasonal pickup in supply from originators and moderation in the pace of bank demand from March (based on recent H.8 data and the decline in CMO issuance). Although the recent rate back-up and spike in implied volatility have pushed MBS spreads wider, we believe the magnitude of widening should be limited by the GSE backstop and potential for stronger bank demand at wider spreads. Discount margins (DM) on GN 6.5% cap CMO floaters are only 5bp away from the March wides and could begin attracting some bank demand (Exhibit 1). Longer-term (with a year-end horizon), we continue to believe that spreads are likely to be wider from current levels. First, we do not expect the administration to scale-up the size of the GSE purchase program. Second, if the PSPA limits are not expanded or if GSEs complete their $200 billion purchases this year, the positive flow effect will not persist in 2027. Money managers would likely be the marginal buyers in 2027 and they may not be willing to purchase agency MBS at current tight spreads. Third, if the GSEs choose not to purchase $200 billion MBS this year but rather prefer to keep dry powder available for future periods, it would only accelerate the timing of spread widening. records.text: US | Josh Grasso(v) BCI, US High energy fuel prices have been affecting municipalities in various ways, but largely the net result has been negative for state residents, as well as some municipal sectors, particularly transportation. State oil revenues and gas consumption Higher oil prices are not entirely negative and should increase hiring. Oil-producing state and local municipalities should benefit if prices remain elevated long enough for them to start revising budgets and increasing employment. However, oil price increases now result in much smaller job gains than in the past, as producers have been striving for higher productivity or higher output with fewer rigs/workers. The main beneficiaries will likely be the largest oilfield services companies, where even a small uptick could result in large job increases for states such as Texas, Louisiana, Oklahoma and New Mexico. Smaller operations should benefit as well, given that even a marginal absolute increase in jobs should result in a large percentage increase, especially in New Mexico, North Dakota, Wyoming and Alaska. As noted above, this shift means that there is still room for Chinese FDI to the EU, but Brussels will likely be keen to keep this more targeted than in the past. From a timeline perspective, the IAA is expected to follow the standard legislative process over 2026-2027, with gradual implementation from 2027 onward, subject to sector-specific secondary legislation and guidelines. Some elements (particularly those linked to existing EU funding programs) could, however, be phased in earlier through delegated acts or conditionality attached to public support schemes. While framed as an industrial resilience tool, the initiative effectively introduces structural market‑access frictions for non‑EU producers, especially in sectors already characterised by global overcapacity. In that sense, “Made in Europe” complements traditional trade defence and FSR enforcement by shifting policy focus from border measures to in‑market preferential frameworks, with potentially significant implications for Chinese exporters.

This discount to rate differentials kicked off following the 'Liberation Day' volatility and has played an important role in explaining the USD’s weakness ever since. As discussed previously, compression or divergence in front-end rate differentials influences the USD both directly via changing rate differentials and indirectly via the cost of hedging. The more that US rates converge with foreign peers, the cheaper FX hedging costs become, which amplifies USD-negative flow (and vice versa). We think further compression in ECB-Fed rates, coupled with increased investor debate over the USD's long-run status, will lead to increased FX hedging flows, amplifying the USD's discount to the rates-implied fair value. That said, nothing lasts forever. We view the DXY move as a high-conviction, tradable, and economically significant decline – but a finite one. As investors approach 2027, we think the DXY likely bottoms and begins to rebound. First, US growth outperformance will ultimately prove an important 'magnet' for capital into the US, which ultimately creates a sustainable bottom for the DXY. US real GDP growth is expected to top the DM leaderboard, around 2.5% 4Q/4Q for both 2026 and 2027, which helps fuel a clear outperformance of US risk assets. LLC US Daily: Little Sign of Labor Market Mismatch So Far 14 May 2026 | 10:54AM EDT As AI adoption expands, there is growing concern that the type of workers the n economy needs is changing faster than workers—especially young workers—are adapting, creating a mismatch problem. While industry- and state-level measures of job-worker mismatch remain subdued, they are imperfect tests of the claim that there are too many coders and not enough plumbers. We therefore introduce a new measure of occupation-level job openings to investigate further. We find that the composition of US job openings has indeed shifted meaningfully n since 2019: there are now 300k more openings for on-site service and production occupations such as healthcare and food preparation but 450k fewer openings for office occupations such as sales, information services, and administrative support—areas where AI is already being deployed. Digging deeper, we find that occupations highly exposed to AI substitution have seen openings fall below pre-pandemic levels, while those exposed to AI augmentation or less exposed to AI have seen job openings fall more gradually to roughly their 2019 levels. So far, these trends have contributed to a decline in labor market mismatch in n recent years, in part because several occupations highly exposed to AI substitution where job openings have fallen started out with large labor shortages. Total BEV and PHEV penetration rose by about 2pp from end-2025 to 29% and HEV penetration by 4pp to 39%. Sales have been boosted by reinstated EV subsidies in major markets, a broader range of affordable models (especially thanks to expansion by Chinese carmakers) and a rush for manufacturers to meet CO2 emission targets. China’s EV exports to the EU in Q1 grew by 85% y/y for BEVs and 165% for PHEVs. records.text: Addressing Common Investor Misconceptions Based on our discussions with investors, we continue to sense meaningful confusion around several aspects of data center cooling and water use. In particular, investors frequently misunderstand: • The primary drivers of direct data center water consumption, with liquid cooling often— but incorrectly—identified as the main cause instead of evaporative cooling. • The role of air cooling, with a common assumption that air-based systems will be completely displaced by liquid cooling architectures. • The trajectory of immersion cooling, which is often viewed as the inevitable long-term cooling solution despite significant operational and ecosystem constraints. • The ongoing need for air-cooled chillers, even in liquid-cooled data center designs, leading some to conclude prematurely that chiller demand will structurally decline. We address each of these misconceptions in detail below. Liquid Cooling is NOT the Cause of Water Use Evaporative cooling, not liquid cooling, is the main cause of data center direct water use. In fact, liquid cooling can materially reduce on-site water use by limiting or avoiding reliance on evaporative heat-rejection systems. “Historically, most ongoing water usage has been for cooling servers to prevent overheating as they deliver cloud and AI services. Thus, any move in global yields should be at least partially mirrored in Trea- sury yields. Second, any evidence that labor markets are tightening would justify pricing in a more hawkish Fed path. The path is difficult — Andy Burnham’s victory in a leadership contest, let alone the by-election, should not be assumed. He requires approvals from the NEC before fighting for a seat that will be strongly contested by Reform. Only if he clears both these hurdles can he launch a leadership challenge. Instead, direct-to-chip liquid cooling is becoming the standard, with immersion remaining a niche solution constrained by operational, ecosystem, and regulatory factors Rear-Door and Side-Car Liquid Heat Exchangers: Bridge Solutions Rear-door and side-car liquid-cooled heat exchangers are rack-adjacent systems that transfer heat from hot server exhaust air into a liquid loop, reducing the burden on room-level air-cooling infrastructure. • Rear-door heat exchangers mount directly to the back of standard racks, cooling exhaust air as it exits the servers. • Side-car systems sit adjacent to racks and capture exhaust air via localized airflow or ducting. These approaches are attractive for retrofitting existing air-cooled facilities or supporting pockets of higher-density racks without a full redesign. However, they are best viewed as transitional solutions: while they materially extend the limits of air cooling, they cannot support the extreme rack-level power densities required by next-generation AI systems. Direct-to-Chip Liquid Cooling: the Hyperscale Standard Direct-to-chip (D2C) liquid cooling brings coolant into direct thermal contact with CPUs, GPUs, and AI accelerators via cold plates. records.text: persistent. Even in these markets, projects require municipal coordination, long-term offtake agreements, and upfront capital, which materially restrict scalability. A key constraint is temperature mismatch: data center waste heat is typically low-grade and unsuitable for direct use, often requiring industrial heat pumps to raise temperatures to levels compatible with district-heating networks. As discussed in our heat pump deep dive (Heat Pumps: Raising the Thermostat on Heating Decarbonization), this adds cost and electricity demand, making net emissions benefits highly dependent on local grid carbon intensity. The shift toward direct-to-chip liquid cooling modestly improves heat-reuse economics by enabling higher coolant return temperatures, which improve heat-pump efficiency. That said, even liquid-cooled data centers generally still require heat pumps for district-heating integration, and designing facilities around heat reuse can constrain cooling flexibility and siting optionality—key priorities for hyperscalers. Absorption (heat-driven) cooling is sometimes cited as a way to “use heat to create cooling. ” While technically feasible, its applicability to data centers is limited. Absorption chillers typically require higher-temperature heat than most data centers can reliably supply, are large and slow-responding, and are poorly suited to the rapid load variability and uptime requirements of hyperscale and AI facilities. Credit spreads peaked when the US introduced a grace period, the market had fully recovered by the end of May, but some (lower) tariffs were still in place and the market discussion remained obsessed with it through the entire summer. The parallels between this year’s military war and last year’s tariff war seem obvious. (1) President Trump introduces a shock that few market participants know how to analyse and hence they assume that the worst- case scenario is quite likely. (2) As a result, they cut risk, hedge up, and turn bearish on the macro-outlook. (3) Then the tail-risk fails to materialise, and investors are forced to cover aggressively. If that is the right playbook for now – and we think it is – then history suggests don’t fade the rebound until complacency, and therefore market vulnerability, is back in the market. Specifically, that means (1) investor positioning being back overweight/long, and (2) consensus growth expectations back up and bullish. We are not there yet (Fig. 1). The other takeaway is that credit has been protected by shock absorbers, mainly the fact that most credit trends are mid-cycle and few major imbalances have appeared. Fundamental trends are robust, Central Banks are broadly neutral, and the shocks to growth or inflation haven't been severe enough so far to challenge that view (Fig. 2). records.text: M Global Insight Morgan Stanley Research 129 Inflation-Linked Bonds United States In our probability-weighted baseline, we expect 5y and 10y breakevens to remain elevated at 2.60% and 2.40%, respectively, by the end of 2026, reflecting high energy prices and some energy shock passthrough to core. As energy prices settle lower and inflation stabilizes, we expect 5y and 10y breakevens to fall to 2.35% and 2.25%, respectively, by mid-2027. We see 10y real yields at 1.85% by 4Q26, rising to 1.95% by mid-2027, as a broadly unchanged Fed policy-rate path and the prospect of AI-driven productivity gains keep real yields elevated. We describe our frameworks for TIPS Breakevens and inflation forwards relative value. Japan Japan BEIs have risen on oil-driven inflation concerns, but we see limited upside well above 2% and downside also well supported. JGB linkers should remain firm into 2H26, helped by energy-led inflation, solid risk sentiment and resilient USD/ JPY. Supply/demand remains stable, valuations are no longer cheap, and shorter maturities look rich. Inflation carry should improve, supporting a buy-on-dips stance, especially if 10y BEIs fall into the 1.8% range.

But an avid reader may question why this is the case. After all, the European economy is less oil and energy intensive than the US. The answer lies on two main drivers. First, the US has become a net energy exporter in recent years, while Europe maintains an energy trade deficit of about 2% of GDP. This makes the direct negative impact on GDP larger to begin with in Europe, whereas an energy shock could be more redistributive than contractionary in the US. Second, despite Europe being a less oil and energy intensive economy, looking at the spending side shows a different picture. In Europe, energy expenditures (including taxes) are double those in the US, and the region is also more exposed to gas prices. The same picture shows in each region’s CPI composition, where the weight of oil in the Euro area is almost twice as in the US, with an even somewhat larger gap for energy overall. We therefore extend the analysis by testing the vent‑for‑surplus hypothesis in EU‑China trade dynamics. Under this mechanism, a domestic demand-driven decline in sectoral turnover leads to excess capacity that firms are keen to reallocate to foreign markets. Ceteris paribus, clearing surplus production abroad would be associated with lower prices. In trade data, this would show up as stronger export volumes accompanied by weaker unit value growth. To test this hypothesis, we first attempt to identify Chinese manufacturing sectors that displayed domestic demand underperformance. We follow the methodology set out in the ECB Economic Bulletin 1 (July 2025). records.text: Toll roads: Dangerous turns Toll roads, including bridges and tunnels, are among the municipal sectors most sensitive to gas prices. Outside of freight and business traffic, our credit card data give us a lens into consumer driving trends as it relates to toll roads. We use the Merchant Category Codes (MCCs) for "Tolls and Bridge Fees" (#4754), and count the number of transactions, as an approximation of trips and traffic volume, as opposed to spending, which is influenced by pricing changes. The largest merchants include the multi-states EZ Pass in the Northeast, the Florida SunPass, California's FasTrak, and the North Texas Tollway Authority (NTTA). Overall, toll transactions are up double digits y/y, and have even accelerated since the onset of the Iran war, contrary to what we may have expected, given the decline in implied fuel demand we are seeing from consumers. However, the largest state contributor is New York, which implemented congestion pricing last year and was hit by an outage in the EZ Pass system, effecting comps. Likewise, new roads in other states have either launched service or have transitioned to an entirely electronic toll system. We believe these fundamental changes are overwhelming any signal that higher fuel prices may be having a negative effect on consumer spending at toll facilities. FIGURE 19. Swap spreads have remained particularly resilient since commencement of the Iran/US conflict, further supporting our view that only limited fiscal-risk repricing has occurred in the gilt market. We also believe that historically elevated outright yield levels have encouraged demand for gilts on asset swap, especially at the front-end, and have limited selling pressure at the back end. Anecdotal evidence suggests that the market remains long. We do not find valuations compelling and remain agnostic on swap spreads, although lingering domestic uncertainty leaves spreads exposed to downside risk. • Repo. We introduce a GBP repo-spread model to explain and forecast the GBP three-month repo spread versus SONIA. The framework focuses on the main balance-sheet and collateral channels driving repo richness and cheapness: 1) the quantity of reserves, 2) gilt collateral scarcity, 3) the composition of BoE liquidity provision, and 4) the supply of near-cash collateral, such as T-bills. Overall, the model suggests repo spreads should remain broadly stable in the near term, extending the recent stabilization, with only limited cheapening further out. This would be the first and most sensitive core consumer price to higher energy costs. Domestic airfares have increased moderately in recent months (and were rising even before the oil shock). Annual increases in airfares also appear stronger given falling airfares this time last year. But international airfares remain surprisingly modest. After the jump in oil prices in 2022, airfares rose substantially within just a month or two. Airfares could still rise more the longer energy prices remain high. Of course, it is well-understood that the demand and labor market backdrop is very different now than four years ago. But the lack of substantial increases in airfares could still tell us something about how weaker demand is limiting the pass through of higher input costs to final consumer prices. records.text: United Kingdom Outlook What a week... Political developments have dominated this week. A clearer path to a leadership challenge against the PM has emerged but we expect this to take months to be resolved. While GDP data were strong for Q1, we expect slowing to come and we look to next week's inflation and labour market data. • Although no leadership contest has been triggered against Prime Minister Keir Starmer, the resignation of the Health Secretary Wes Streeting, and the ability of Andy Burnham to run in a by-election makes an impending leadership challenge highly likely. We anticipate more details on policy ideas from potential successors in coming weeks, and expect the whole process to take a number of months to reach resolution. • GDP growth was 0.6% q/q in Q1, although multiple factors suggest to us that underlying growth is weaker. We expect growth on a quarterly basis to weaken in the rest of the year. We now expect growth to average 1.0% y/y in 2026 (+0.1pp), and average 1.1% in 2027 (-0.1pp). • Deputy Governor Sarah Breeden gave a clear indication that she thinks the MPC has time to assess the current inflationary shock before needing to react, specifying that the June and July meetings were too soon, in contrast to market pricing. Next week, we get labour market data for March and inflation data for April, both of which we expect to show an easing. More broadly, high debt servicing costs likely reflect what the BoE and the Gilt market see as limited spare capacity to absorb additional material fiscal demand. This perceived resource constraint remains the key barrier to meaningfully expansionary fiscal policy in the near term. Govt. hiked duties on gold, silver imports India has significantly tightened its trade policy on precious metals, with the government raising the total import duty on gold and silver to 15% (from 6%) on May 13, 2026. This move mirrors the last major hike in July 2022, when duties were increased from 10.75% to 15% to curb a widening trade deficit and support the rupee. In 2022-23, the impact was immediate, gold import volumes fell a sharp 23%, after hav- ing increased by 35% in 2021-22. While official value dropped to $35 billion, this high-tariff regime also saw a dou- bling of gold seizures, signaling a spike in smuggling. In recent years, India's gold imports have evolved into a major external sector vulnerability, more than doubling from $35 billion in FY23 to a staggering record of $72 billion in FY26 (Figure 1). Primary Issuance in the Corporate Bond Market Primary issuance is a significant dimension of the corporate bond market. In US IG credit, new issues represented 14% of securities comprising the Bloomberg US Corporate Index between 2014 and 2025 annually on average. In Euro IG credit, new issues represented 17% of securities comprising the Bloomberg EuroAgg Corporate Index between 2019 and 2025 annually on average. When new issues are priced, it is generally done at a discount to similar outstanding bonds from the same issuer. The difference between their spreads – called the 'concession' – entices investors' demand, such that the new supply can be efficiently absorbed into the market. In addition, concessions are not reflected in the pricing of index constituents: bonds issued mid- month only join the indexes on the last day of the month of issuance. Concessions are thus not incorporated into index returns, indicating that they can be a source of outperformance for active bond investors. In 2015, we studied the magnitudes and determinants of concessions in our white paper Concessions in Corporate Bond Issuance: Magnitude, Determinants, and Post-Issuance Dynamics (23 January 2015). We see higher services inflation as second-round effects feed through, likely around 4.1-4.4% over the next 12 months. This is primarily driven by insurance and financial services inflation. Medical inflation has also remained elevated and is likely to show up in the April print again. Higher fuel costs should put upward pressure on items such as restaurants and accommodation in coming months. Housing inflation is also picking up and is likely to be a pain point for the June CPI print. Rising transport and food prices could lead the unions to make higher wage demands to insulate workers from the increasing cost of living. We have seen evidence of wage compression in the private sector, while public sector evidence is mixed. Government wage agreements are set at around 4%, while public companies such as Eskom and Transnet have agreements close to 7%. Food inflation a risk for early 2027 Food inflation is still moderate thanks to a good harvest in the 2025/26 farming season, but could rise in early 2027. Dans Global Outlook Printemps 2026 : Se projeter au- delà de la guerre du 24 avril, nous avons construit notre scénario de base sur l'hypothèse que le conflit allait se poursuivre encore quelque temps avant qu'un accord ne soit conclu, conduisant à la poursuite de tensions sur les prix du pétrole avant une normalisation au-dessus du niveau d'avant la guerre. En termes concrets, nous prévoyons que les prix du Brent devraient évoluer autour de 110 $/baril au deuxième trimestre, avec un pic à 140 $. Le pétrole s'est comporté jusqu'à présent de manière globalement conforme à cette hypothèse, bien que le risque de prix supérieurs aux prévisions ait augmenté, dans la mesure où les discussions actuelles ne montrent toujours aucun signe de résolution rapide. Pas de récession mondiale: selon notre scénario de base, nous nous attendons à un ralentissement important sur l'activité et à une augmentation de l'inflation par rapport à nos projections d'avant guerre. Cependant, nous pensons que l'économie mondiale évitera la récession. Le conflit a éclaté à un moment où celle-ci témoignait d’une forte résilience: essor de l’intelligence artificielle, plans de relance budgétaires et bilans solides constituent un véritable amortisseur face au choc pétrolier. BoJ rate-hike pricing continues not to be a driver of the JPY: In constructing our USD/ JPY forecast, we have not incorporated the BoJ’s rate-hike path as a key driver. As discussed in "Japan Macro Strategy: Watching Geopolitical Risk and the Growth Impact", with JPY weakness and higher oil prices raising concerns that the BoJ may be falling behind the curve, the rates market is increasingly being priced with close reference to the FX level. In our view, unless the BoJ raises rates to around 1.5% – the level that many market participants regard as the terminal rate – concerns that the BoJ is behind the curve are unlikely to fade. Put differently, unless the BoJ hikes toward roughly 1.5%, the impact of BoJ rate-hike pricing on the FX market is likely to remain very limited. FX Intervention: We think the risk of FX intervention could act as a constraint on speculative JPY short positioning. GS trading desk estimates show that retail trading volumes have risen by 28% since mid-April and a basket of retail favorite stocks (GSXURFAV) has rallied by 29% over the same period. The recent replacement of pattern day trader rules with less stringent margin requirements increases the likelihood that retail trading activity will rise further. We estimate retail traders hold $12 trillion of equity assets in self-directed n brokerage accounts, amounting to approximately 10% of total US corporate equity market value. Retail traders are a subset of US households, which directly and indirectly own the majority of the $111 trillion US corporate equity market. Retail trading activity has recently accounted for roughly 20% of total US n equity trading volumes. This is up from 15% a decade ago but below the peak of 24% in 2021. Specialized market makers known as wholesalers execute the majority of retail order flow. As a result, institutional investors typically interact with only a fraction of retail trading activity. Retail trading activity has increased during recent equity market n drawdowns. Retail volumes in index-linked ETFs rose during the equity market selloffs in 2020, 2022, and 2025. As a result, banks hold fixed reserve buffers to insure against intraday liquidity needs. After all, reserves are immediately monetizable for payments and settle- ment purposes. They are also stable in value, carry no operational risk if offsetting trades fail, have no interest rate risk, and require no selling of securities to monetize. More- over, there are frictions and stigma in the repo markets and Fed liquidity tools, respectively, that make contingent liquidity sources less usable. Even as banks have grown increasingly sensitive to intraday liquidity needs, they have simultaneously shifted toward secured fund- ing as the preferred mechanism for covering cash shortfalls, while moving away from unse- cured alternatives such as fed funds and short-dated commercial paper.
