records.text: 7 LFP dominates: Recent years’ technological breakthroughs have allowed lithium- iron-phosphate batteries to narrow the gap in energy density to ternary batteries, which have historically been preferred because their higher energy density allows longer driving ranges for the same battery mass. LFP batteries already account for over 50% of global passenger EV battery demand, according to BloombergNEF. Coupled with fast charging technology, which compensates for the shorter driving range, LFP batteries should continue to take market share. For example, CATL unveiled its third-generation Shenxing battery in April, which it said charges from 10% to 90% in only 6 minutes 27 seconds. The battery, first announced in 2024, has an energy density of 205Wh/kg – surpassing 200Wh/kg for the first time. Moreover, as cobalt prices continue to rise after the Democratic Republic of Congo implemented strict export quotas on the metal, automakers are more likely to shift to the cheaper LFP cathodes to reduce costs. New technologies finding their way: Sodium-ion batteries are gaining momentum as a cheaper and more cold-resistant alternative to lithium-ion batteries. CATL has announced plans to mass-produce its Naxtra sodium ion batteries (energy density of 175Wh/kg), to be delivered in Q4 2026 to power the Changan Nevo A06. BYD began building its first sodium-ion battery plant in January 2024, and other automakers experimenting with sodium-ion batteries include JAC Motors, Chery and Volkswagen.

records.text: enters is evaporative cooling, which we detailed in section Cooling is Critical to Data Center Operations. Evaporative cooling can deliver high cooling capacity with relatively low electricity use, particularly in hot or power-constrained regions. It reduces reliance on refrigeration-based cooling systems that depend on energy-intensive mechanical compressors and fan-cooled condensers, enabling data centers to allocate more electrical capacity to compute, lower operating costs, and reduce emissions. However, these energy benefits come at the expense of higher on-site water use, even if evaporative cooling may reduce indirect water consumption associated with thermoelectric power generation, depending on the local grid mix. “Water is mainly used in two ways: evaporative cooling and humidification. The evaporative cooling system converts water into vapor to lower the temperature when the outside air is too hot, while the humidification process maintains the humidity level if the air is too dry.” — Meta: Simulator-based reinforcement learning for data center cooling optimization So how does liquid cooling reduce water use? Liquids have far greater heat capacity and thermal conductivity than air, and direct-to-chip and immersion cooling systems remove heat precisely at the source, allowing liquid-cooled data centers to operate at much higher supply coolant temperatures while still maintaining sufficient cooling performance. records.text: As rack densities move beyond roughly 30–40 kW per rack, air-only cooling faces compounding constraints: • Airflow requirements rise non-linearly, demanding dramatically higher cubic meters per minute. • Fan power consumption increases sharply, eroding overall energy efficiency and adversely affecting PUE. • Acoustic noise and vibration increase, which can impact equipment reliability and serviceability. • Thermal gradients worsen, raising the risk of hot spots and reducing operational resilience. • Physical space constraints emerge, as larger fans, ducts, and plenums consume valuable white space. These limitations are now colliding directly with AI hardware realities. NVIDIA’s Blackwell-based systems operate at approximately 120–150 kW per rack, well beyond the practical limits of air-only cooling. Looking ahead, Rubin-class ultra-scale systems are expected to push rack power densities toward several hundred kilowatts, effectively rendering air cooling infeasible as the primary thermal solution. records.text: Euro Area Viewpoint | 14 May 2026 3 Structural or cyclical beyond 2025 record year? China-EU trade dynamics were eye-catching in 2025, with the trade deficit widening by 16%. On average last year, the EU import value from China rose 11.6% yoy, the import volume was up 14.3%, while the aggregated EU import unit value from China declined by ca 2% (Exhibit 3). Looking at trends by sector, our China Economics team (see report: China Viewpoint: Will Europe remain a key destination for China’s exports amid US tariff shocks? 19 November 2025) noted that machinery and electronic equipment, small packages (de- minimis), and autos contributed most of the robust 2025 growth in EU imports from China, explained by sector-specific drivers. Machinery and electrical equipment imports were partly cyclical, in contrast with double-digit growth in Chinese auto exports as a result of a more structural trend driven by Chinese EV makers’ comparative advantage in tech-advancement and cost efficiency. They attributed tariff-induced trade diversion away from the US and into Europe to certain consumer goods exports such as de-minimis, toys, and textiles. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 13 We have added a simulation and fair value for the wildcard option embedded in UXY ( Exhibit 23 and Exhibit 24 ). We incorporated five years of observed late-day (3pm-6pm ET) price movements in the UXY CTD to simulate late-day CTD price performance across 100k cycles. For UXY, we estimate fair value of the wildcard as 1.6 ticks. We drew some inspiration for the simulation from a methodology published by the Montreal Exchange. Accounting for the wildcard option, the front contract is 0.4 tick cheap. The back contract is then cheaper than the front by a meaningful amount, which leaves us mildly bearish on the roll from an optionality point of view, as the back contract has room to richen. records.text: of cooling method largely depends on the climate of the datacenter region.” — Microsoft: Modern Datacenter Cooling, 2023 How it works: In an adiabatic cooling system, ambient air passes through wetted media or a fine water spray. As a portion of the water evaporates, it absorbs heat from the air, lowering the air’s dry-bulb temperature. This pre-cooled air is then used either directly, to cool IT equipment (direct evaporative cooling), or indirectly, to improve heat rejection across a heat exchanger— such as a dry cooler or air-cooled condenser—without increasing humidity inside the data center (indirect evaporative cooling). Adiabatic cooling doesn't use much electricity (no energy to power a chiller), but require more water than free-air cooling. MFST's existing Arizona data centers use direct evaporative cooling and don't use water for cooling when temperatures are below 29.4 degrees Celsius, reducing cooling water use to less than 40% percent of the year. With adiabatic cooling, the data center cooling system can operate in dry mode most of the year. Adiabatic assist can be activated during periods of elevated ambient temperatures to preserve cooling capacity and improve energy efficiency. This operating mode allows facilities to achieve peak-condition performance with only episodic water use, materially reducing overall water consumption relative to conventional wet cooling towers. records.text: tion without moving to a scarce reserves regime by providing a market-based contingent liquidity source that redistributes cash only when needed, rather than requiring the system to hold fixed reserves all day to insure against intraday timing risk. The primary impact should be a tighter upper tail and lower day-to-day volatility with respect to repo pricing. Because today’s repo market is predominately a morning market, bottlenecks emerge when intermediation capacity is constrained, increasing the probability that banks and dealers will have to pay up to get funded. Intraday repo would reduce that pressure point in the morning, allowing banks and dealers to borrow on demand, which should dampen intraday squeezes that would otherwise force market participants to pay up for overnight funding. Over time, this could modestly lower SOFR levels, widening SOFR/FF basis. From a policy perspective, this might allow the Fed to shrink the Fed balance sheet without going back to a scarce reserves regime. For contracts with negligible embedded option values, the relative value of the calendar spread can be determined by comparing the implied repo rate (IRR) of the calendar spread to the forward three-month funding rate. The relevant three-month Euro future is generally used as a proxy for the forward funding rate. The calendar spread IRR is the breakeven funding rate for going long the calendar spread, taking delivery in the front month and making delivery in the back month contract. If the calendar IRR is historically low compared to the three-month forward rate for a particular market, the calendar spread may be considered rich. For contracts where delivery options in the futures are valuable, such as U.S. Treasury bond futures, a simple IRR analysis is inadequate because it overlooks the potential impact of switches in the cheapest-to- deliver bond. records.text: M Global Insight 172 First, we think Japanese lifers’ FX hedging demand is likely to remain limited. Looking at Japanese lifers’ FY2026 investment plans, their stance on foreign bonds has become more cautious than in the last fiscal year. Only around two lifers plan to add to foreign bond holdings, and most firms are basically making decisions subject to the level of interest rates and FX. Exhibit 305 shows our forecasts for 3m USD/JPY FX hedge costs based on our forecasts for US and Japanese policy rates. For 2026, the forecast is broadly in line with market pricing, but we expect FX hedging costs to decline meaningfully in 2027. In this mid-year outlook, the resumption of Fed rate cuts has been pushed back to March and June 2027 (from January and March 2027 previously), while markets are pricing in rate cuts through 2027. Our forecast for the BoJ’s rate-hike path is more gradual than market pricing, as we expect the BoJ to pause after the June hike until another hike in April 2027. The 3m USD/JPY FX hedge cost can be calculated from 3m SOFR-OIS, 3m TONA-OIS, and the 3m SOFR/TONA basis. What is needed for the estimation is policy-rate expectations rather than the policy-rate path itself, and we have therefore adjusted the calculation so that policy-rate expectations move around the timing of Fed rate cuts and BoJ rate hikes. The remaining now-cooled condenser water returns to the chillers to repeat the cycle. This multi-loop system provides high thermal efficiency and scalability, but it does involve water consumption due to evaporation at the cooling towers. 'Free cooling' optional enhancement: The system is often paired with water-side economizers when ambient temperatures are low enough for extended periods to enable free cooling for a substantial portion of the year. records.text: On Iran, President Trump said the US and China share a common goal of ending the Iran war, while Beijing struck a measured tone in urging further diplomacy13 . The Chinese delegation's official messaging was brief, noting that the two countries exchanged views on the Middle East . E15 can be tens of cents less per gallon than E0 or E10. The starting mix is 40% baseline, 15% US aggregate demand, 10% AI productivity, 15% global oil-led recession, and 20% permanent oil premium. Oil tails keep yields cheap to forwards in 2Q26, with 2y/10y at 4.05%/4.45%, about 22bp/18bp above forwards. As baseline probability rises to 100% by 4Q27, the Fed midpoint falls to 3.125%, 2y/10y end 2027 at 3.45%/4.15%, about 48bp/33bp below forwards, and 2s10s steepens to 70bp. The inflation mix limits the long-end rally: 5y/10y breakevens decline from 2.60%/2.40% at end-2026 to 2.35%/2.25% by mid-2027, while 10y real yields rise to 1.95%. Scenario skew: The UST bear case is US aggregate demand upside: stronger wealth effects and animal spirits lift growth above baseline, the Fed hikes to 4.625%, the 10y reaches 5.15%, the 30y rises to 5.50%, and 2s10s inverts to -50bp by 2Q27. The UST bull case is now a global oil-led recession, not a mild domestic recession: crude above $150/bbl triggers demand destruction, the Fed cuts to 1.625%, the 10y troughs at 3.30%, and 2s10s steepens toward 165-170bp. Moody’s calcu- lates PADR by dividing program assets by total bonds outstanding plus accrued interest, after adjusting for intangible accounting entries such as deferred costs, loan loss reserves, and bond and loan discounts. To maintain a score consistent with an invest- ment-grade rating, programs are expected to maintain at least a 1.00 PADR. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 15 May 2026 11:25:06 ET │ 18 pages US Economics Weekly Little to shift market pricing in the next month CITI'S TAKE Markets are focused on scenarios where sticky inflation prevents Fed officials from lowering rates again and are increasingly looking to scenarios where the next move in policy rates is a hike. Details of April CPI and PPI data this week were either expectedly strong due to measurement quirks or unsurprising, and leave us tracking 0.26%MoM core PCE inflation in April. May PCE inflation will again be uncomfortably strong due to rising equity prices, suggesting there will be little to change market pricing in the next month. But Atlanta Fed wage data this week shows wage growth continuing to slow in a loosening labor market. The current demand and labor market backdrop is not one that suggests persistent inflationary pressure. We expect market pricing to shift back towards cuts in the summer months with cooler inflation and labor market data. records.text: Studies show that energy price shocks tend to pass through to underlying n inflation asymmetrically: rising energy prices push core inflation up much more than falling prices pull it down. This “rocket and feather” pattern matters for the ECB because it implies that renewed increases in energy prices could create persistent inflation pressure, while a decline in energy prices may offer only limited relief. Research highlights three main reasons for this asymmetry: firms protect margins n more aggressively when costs rise than when they fall (given the possibility of bankruptcy), the “menu” cost of lowering prices tends to be higher with positive trend inflation, and wages and prices are sticky on the downside. Together, these mechanisms help explain why inflation can become more persistent after an energy spike than after an equivalent decline. We provide fresh statistical evidence on this uneven passthrough behaviour in n the Euro area. We start with a simple top-down perspective using quarterly data from 1999-2025. We confirm that positive food and energy price shocks have significant passthrough effects into core inflation, while the passthrough of negative non-core shocks is small and insignificant. We show that this finding is robust to considering a broader set of data. And this excludes other upstream water uses, such as the semiconductor supply chain (see separate Semis' thirst for water: A shifting global picture report on semiconductor supply chain water risk). Importantly, data center water withdrawals—the total volume taken from rivers, lakes, groundwater, or municipal systems—can greatly exceed water consumption, which reflects only the portion lost to evaporation or otherwise removed from the local watershed. On a global scale, the International Energy Agency (IEA) estimates that data centers worldwide—across cooling, electricity generation, and the semiconductor supply chain—account for roughly 5.2 trillion liters of annual water withdrawals.7 While much of this water is returned, it is often discharged at higher temperatures or with altered chemistry, creating material environmental, regulatory, and cost burdens—particularly in water-stressed regions—and driving growing interest in water reuse and alternative sourcing (see Water Tech: Complementing Cooling-System Design section on complementary water tech opportunities). BNEF reports slight upticks in battery prices in China in 2026, with LFP and NMC prices rising around 11% after years of decline. However, we see two main factors cushioning the pass-through effect. ▪ Overcapacity of cathode manufacturing, mainly in China, perpetuates a buyers’ market, leaving manufacturers with limited bargaining power to raise prices. ▪ Most Tier 1 cathode manufacturers are vertically integrated with downstream BESS or EV manufacturers, allowing them to take on compressed margins. Constant efficiency gains could also help to offset the increase in input costs. Even with increased battery costs, there were continued EV price discounts amid intense competition, with 10% BYD price cuts in China in March, the highest in two years. Therefore, we do not expect current high battery metal prices to result in a material increase in EV prices, and any price increase will more likely be due to increased demand. records.text: extract heat into a dedicated liquid loop. This heated liquid passes through a heat exchanger or Coolant Distribution Unit (CDU), which transfers the heat to a facility water loop. The warm facility water is then pumped to water-cooled chillers, which remove the heat via a refrigeration cycle and transfer it to a secondary condenser water loop. The condenser water is routed to wet cooling towers, where heat is rejected into the atmosphere through evaporative cooling: ambient air flows over the water, and a portion of the water evaporates, carrying away heat. 'Free cooling' optional enhancement: The system is often paired with water-side economizers when ambient temperatures are low enough for extended periods to enable free cooling for a substantial portion of the year. This enables the system to bypass the mechanical water-cooled chillers and use the cooling towers directly to reject heat, improving energy efficiency and reducing wear on the mechanical chillers. 13 May 2026 38 Barclays | Thematic Investing

records.text: 8 Fig. 12: Since the start of 2026, lithium prices have surged nearly 90% and cobalt prices are up 8% Surge in cost of raw materials: Lithium prices have reached a record-high USD24/kg, up from around USD10/kg at the end of 2025, on the back of bullish sentiment surrounding demand for battery energy storage systems and ongoing supply concerns. China’s export BESS orders rose by 144% y/y in 2025 to 366GWh, according to the China Energy Storage Alliance. The energy capacity of global BESS installations grew 65% to 111GW/296GWh in 2025, led by China and the US. The bullwhip effect of demand amplifying as it moves up the value stream likely led to the boom in lithium prices as cathode manufacturers overproduced. Meanwhile, delayed shipments from the DRC and depleting inventories have sent cobalt prices grinding upwards to USD26/lb, though upside in Q1 was capped by weak EV sales, especially in the US, where ternary batteries dominate. We expect battery metal prices to remain supported in the near term, especially as the Middle East conflict promotes EVs and BESS globally, further fuelling bullish sentiment. In the longer term, though, overproduction should eventually turn into underproduction due to inventories, and fading supply risks could see prices fall as the market remains fundamentally oversupplied. Pass-through to battery prices cushioned: Higher raw-material prices have a direct impact on battery pack prices. BNEF reports slight upticks in battery prices in China in 2026

Handle with care Last week’s local election results increased UK political volatility, with PM Starmer potentially facing a formal leadership challenge. Long-end Gilts remained relatively resilient amid the news flow, likely helped by the broader DM curve. 10y cross-market spreads widened relative to last Friday’s close, with more resilience emerging in the second half of the week. Gilts also held up relatively well against Sonia, including at the long end of the curve. From the rates market perspective, fiscal policy trajectory in the case of potential leadership change will be key. A centrist outcome would likely be perceived as a continuity trade, implying adherence to fiscal rules with pressures met within the existing framework. A left-leaning candidate would likely raise concerns around fiscal discipline and higher borrowing, although market sensitivity to the matter may act as a limiting factor. Overall, a break from fiscal rules is not assured, we think. The high level of UK implied vol’ reflects political uncertainty overlayed upon global uncertainty, entangled with the UK market’s structural fragility, we would say. records.text: Introduction of step-ups: A structural innovation that could be a game-changer for the US corporate hybrid market The 32NC7 step-up structure is a first of its kind for the US corporate hybrids market. Since Moody's methodology change in 2024, there was originally the innovation of standardized 30NC5s and 30NC10s, next came the emergence of the coupon floor from Dominion (D), then SO's 32NC7 hybrid, and now, the introduction of step-up features in VZ 32NC7 to ensure S&P's equity content loss at first call dates. This structure with step-ups (25bp five years after the first call date + 75bp 20 years after the first call date) is in line with typical European corporate hybrids and could potentially be a game-changer for the US corporate hybrids market. How does this differ from floors? We view this 32NC7 hybrid with step-ups as a stronger structure for investors than a floored NC5 or NC7. Although the floored structures significantly increase the chance of a call at the call/reset date for a 30NC5 or 32NC7, there is still some extension risk, given that the bonds do not lose equity content at S&P until 20 years prior to the maturity date, ie, at the 10y point for a 30NC10 or 12y point for a 32NC7. The step-up feature, in contrast, aligns a cumulative step-up of 100bp 20 years after the first call date. For VZ, that is +25bp in 2038, +75bp in 2053, which by definition makes 2053 the "effective maturity date. " Since the 2033 reset date is 20 years prior to the effective maturity

Futures contracts theoretically represent a 6% coupon bond with maturity varying based on contract. In reality, owning a UST future represents a claim on one bond inside a basket of bonds, while being short represents the obligation to deliver one of those bonds. The particular bond is chosen by the short, which chooses to deliver the cheapest-to- deliver (CTD) bond. records.text: ts. Markets are pricing ~100bps of RBNZ hikes in 2026, more than any other G10 central bank, but we see a strong case to remain on hold and look through the energy spike. Inflation largely reflects supply-side forces that are independent of RBNZ policy, medium-term expectations remain anchored, spare capacity is widening, and financial conditions are already restrictive. However, we also see a 30-40% likelihood the RBNZ opts to front-load hikes towards 3% as insurance against second round effects. Hikes could start as soon as 27 May, although at least waiting for 2Q CPI (July 21) seems prudent. Front-loading also recognizes that monetary policy operates with long and variable lags, requiring pre-emptive action if inflation is expected to remain above target for an extended period. However, they would also imply a high sacrifice ratio, amplifying demand destruction and slack for only marginal progress on inflation, in our view. If the RBNZ does hike in 2026, we would expect easing to follow in 2027. For another, oil shocks affect inflation immediately via gas prices, while spending only slows with a lag. Gas accounts for less than 2% of PCE spending, so consumers have leeway to absorb a gas shock for a few months. But the longer the shock lasts, the more likely it is that they will make substantial cuts to discretionary outlays. This could then weigh on labor demand, with an additional lag. Bottom line: the jury is still out Our conclusion is that the facts on the ground don’t let us distinguish yet between reflation and stagflation. The true test of consumer and labor resilience might still be ahead of us. Markets pricing of nearly a full hike by mid-2027 seems reasonable given the latest data flow. We view this as a balance between a base case of an extended hold (the appropriate policy response to stagflation), with substantial risks of a hiking cycle (reflation) and smaller risks of cuts (if stagflation gives way to recession). This provides very high energy efficiency (~1.1-1.3 PUE), but lower efficiency than liquid cooling systems employing wet tower systems in high ambient temperatures. Where it is commonly used: This architecture is well-suited for data centers with high-density servers that exceed the capabilities of traditional air cooling, but where water usage must be minimized or where simplicity and ease of deployment are priorities. records.text: M Europe Insight 30 Main views: • Front End. We believe front-end rates remain too elevated relative to: 1) our economists’ baseline views and scenarios; 2) the BoE’s conditional Bank Rate paths, after taking into account current energy-market valuations; and 3) both economists’ consensus and market participants’ consensus, as shown in the May MaPS survey. We present supporting evidence in the first section of our Mid-Year Outlook. In our view, the gap largely reflects a meaningful front-end risk premium. We therefore recommend positioning for a lower trough rate and entering a long SFIM7 position. • Long End & Curve. With intermediate- and long-end yields close to multi- year highs, we assess valuations through a cross-market lens and analyze embedded term premium in a dedicated section of this publication. We find only modest evidence of an increase in term premium. Our cross-market analysis suggests that only part of this move can be attributed to idiosyncratic factors related to fiscal risk and political uncertainty. The analysis further supports our view that front-end risk premium has been the dominant factor behind higher yields and the UK’s cross-market underperformance. Combining our bullish front-end view with limited evidence of a material term-premium increase at the long end, and a still- uncertain domestic backdrop, we recommend initiating 10s20s SONIA steepeners. • ASWs. We reached this conclusion by finding the probability combinations (Cepeda versus opposition victory) that lead us into an expected value of rally/sell-off equaling our excess premium estimation (-70bp, Figure 2). Excess premium denotes the portion of the ACM premium estimation that standard macro variables cannot explain. Our current excess premium estimation is -70bp; in other words, the observed ACM premium is 70bp lower than it should be if only macro variables were at play. US Rates Strategy: While markets have gradually been pricing the risk of a rate hike in 2027, it seems unprepared for the scenario we describe above. In a 1999 like playbook, where “insurance cuts” were reversed, hikes could be more front-loaded (starting in December 2026) and also in a cluster (three hikes back to back), as opposed to a shallow buildup to a hike that markets seem to be expecting. We think the options market offers an attractive structure to play for this scenario. We suggest a SFRH7 a/a+40bp 1x1.5 put spread – a trade that has a maximum payout at 40bp higher where the market prices 1 -2 additional hikes by the March 2027 FOMC meeting, similar to our scenario above. The cost of the trade is 4.9bp, making for a max payout ratio of ~8.1 : 1. The key risk to the trade is that the market prices a total of more than 5.5 hikes by March (which would likely entail 50bp hikes – highly unlikely in our view). Morgan, Cotality As a reminder, CES prepayments have multiple drivers, including CES to CES refinancings, first and second lien consolidation, and to a smaller extent, curtailments. The general rate rally we’ve seen over the last year would have driven a sizeable volume of CES to CES refinancings, particularly for loans with more proactive servicing. More borrowers who have taken out CES loans recently appear to be refinancing to reduce their monthly pay- ments. We see this above in the more significant dispersion in prepayment speeds by WAC in 2025 vintage loans versus 2024 vintage loans, with the 10-11 WAC loans prepaying almost 10c faster than 7-8 WAC loans. Borrowers may also be extracting more equity; loan sizes have been increasing in recent vintages along with the second lien LTV . While we do not have a way to explicitly identify the reason for full payoffs (the majority of loans are cashout refinancings), we can segment out the portion of prepayments attributed to curtailments. Small local government entities in Texas had been creating PFCs that were providing tax exemptions for properties bought or built in completely different parts of the state. After the Legislature tightened the rules on PFCs, developers shifted their atten- tion to HFCs, which had fewer regulations, leading to the emergence of "traveling HFCs." Similar to the "traveling PFC" scenario, HFCs based in small cities and counties across Texas established deals with developers building properties in larger cities like Houston or Dallas. In exchange for a fee, they would take nominal ownership of the properties to render them exempt from property taxes. The cities and counties where these “traveling HFC/PFC” properties were located were not aware of these deals and never approved them. A missing element of the syndicate datasets is that they do not record the identities of the comparables against which the concession is calculated. These identities cannot be inferred as the determination process is not fully rule-based.2 Consequently, we cannot observe the dynamics of the syndicate concession in the days immediately following the pricing date. To address this, we construct a second concession dataset using new issues from the Bloomberg US and EuroAgg Corporate Indexes (henceforth, the 'Bloomberg Matched Subset' datasets). For each issue, we use an algorithm to select the closest comparable bond by a consistent criteria: an outstanding bond from the same issuer, with the same seniority and credit rating, and having the closest time to maturity. We calculate the concession as the ask spread of the new issue minus the bid spread of the comparable and adjust it for their maturity difference using the spread curve of the issuer.3 Finally, we compare our Bloomberg-based calculation with the syndicate's concessions to ensure they align. For now, we expect the ongoing decline in the stock of BoE reserves to have limited impact on 1Yx1Y SONIA/ SOFRR basis. BoE reserve balances have fallen by around £20bn since the start of this year to around £630bn, although the pace of decline has slowed over the past few months given the ongoing increase in participation in the BoE’s STR and ILTR facilities, with total STR and ILTR usage around £167bn (as of early May). As reserves decline further, they will eventually stabilise around the PMRR (Preferred Minimum Range of Reserves). This is currently esti- mated by the BoE as £385-540bn and as the level of reserves continues its decline towards the top of the PMRR range then increased usage of BoE repo-facilities should limit a further linear decline in reserves and also prevent further narrowing of the front-end basis. We stay neutral on a 1Yx1Y SONIA/SOFR basis. As AI-driven capacity expands, water permitting timelines are increasingly rivaling—or exceeding—grid interconnection timelines, fundamentally altering project sequencing and financing risk. Several high-profile projects in recent years have been delayed, downsized, or withdrawn following community opposition tied to water use, particularly in drought-prone regions of the Southwest and fast-growing areas of the Southeast. State-level legislative activity is accelerating with multiple states introducing or advancing requirements for water-use disclosure, separate water permitting tracks for data centers, and enhanced local review authority. Minnesota is among the first states to adopt explicit, data center-specific water-permitting requirements. Similar frameworks are emerging or under active consideration in states such as Illinois, Virginia, Arizona, and Nevada, with additional momentum building through local and incentive-linked regulation in New York, New Jersey, and parts of Texas. Importantly, regulatory pressure is shifting toward the local level. Even where state governments seek to preserve data center investment, municipalities are increasingly using zoning, moratoria, and conditional use approvals to exert control over water-intensive projects. records.text: Google Google's water withdrawal increased 27% year-over-year to nearly 42 billion liters in 2024 for its owned and operated data centers. This is inline with the 27% growth in 2024 electricity demand. While Google does not explicitly report a standalone WUE metric, our analysis—based on Google’s disclosed electricity consumption and water withdrawal data—implies an effective WUE of over ~1.3 L/kWh in 2024, materially higher than its hyperscaler peers. Google has stated that it will continue to deploy evaporative cooling in low water-risk regions, emphasizing that its “climate-conscious cooling strategy” seeks to balance access to carbon-free electricity with responsibly sourced water. Google notes that water-based cooling can materially reduce electricity consumption and associated emissions, particularly where grid decarbonization is still in progress, making evaporative cooling an attractive option when water risk is low. In 2024, 72% of Google’s freshwater withdrawals came from sources categorized as low or medium risk, with 14% from medium-scarcity regions and 14% from high-scarcity regions. In regions facing high water stress, Google has stated that it will avoid evaporative cooling altogether. For example, Google opted to deploy air-cooled designs at data centers in Mesa, Arizona; Canelones, Uruguay; and Waltham Cross, United Kingdom, after determining that local water sources faced elevated depletion and scarcity risk. We start by comparing curve behaviour across markets using a simple “transmission” measure: the ratio between daily changes in 10y10y forwards and daily changes in 1y1y forwards. Intuitively, this captures how much of a front-end move is transmitted into the long end of the curve. Higher values indicate a more parallel repricing, while lower values point to a more front-end-led move. To focus on the underlying regime rather than day-to-day noise, we compute a 252- day rolling median of this daily transmission ratio. records.text: 9 Sources: Bloomberg, BNP Paribas Aluminium prices spike following Gulf smelter production losses: The war- related closure the Strait of Hormuz, combined with Iranian attacks on smelters operated by Aluminium Bahrain (Alba) and Emirates Global Aluminium, has left the global aluminium market facing extreme shortages over the next 12–18 months. We expect a deficit of about 2.5–3 Mt this year, driven not only by Gulf losses but also China’s self-imposed production cap of 45mt/year, a slower-than-expected ramp-up in Indonesia capacity, and the closure of South 32’s Mozal smelter. As detailed overleaf, we do not see Chinese output filling the output gap. LME 3-month aluminium prices have risen by c.18% since the start of the year. More importantly for the physical market, aluminium premiums in Europe and Asia have jumped by 61% and 106%, respectively, since the current Middle East conflict started. Aluminium intensity of use in BEVs is typically three times more than comparable ICE vehicles, leaving the auto sector facing significant input cost implications. All-in aluminium costs (LME cash price plus regional premium) for all major auto-producing regions are up by 25–30% so far this year. US-based auto producers face the most significant aluminium input cost issues due to the impact of section 232 aluminium import duties. This provides very high energy efficiency (~1.1-1.3 PUE), but lower efficiency than liquid cooling systems employing wet towers systems in high ambient temperatures. There is no water loss given it employs closed-loop water systems. Where it is commonly used: This is an emerging approach in high energy-density data centers in water-scarce regions or when water sustainability is a strategic priority. It enables the use of liquid cooling without relying on evaporative cooling towers. How it works: Servers are equipped with direct liquid cooling systems—such as cold plates or immersion—that extract heat into a dedicated liquid loop. This heated liquid passes through a heat exchanger or Coolant Distribution Unit (CDU), which transfers the heat to a facility water loop. The warm facility water is then pumped to water-cooled chillers, which remove the heat via a refrigeration cycle and transfer it to a secondary condenser water loop. Case in point, the recent RDMICH issuance was excluded from the 144A For Life friendly Bloomberg Global Agg and US Universal indices, whereas it was included in the ICE indices that had previously excluded Beignet (RPLDCI) for this same reason. It is our understanding that the more recent RDMICH bond had more investors involved in the primary process than RPLDCI and thus reason for different index providers to draw this line at a different point in the sand, but this shows the frailty of this criteria altogether. Our view is that when there is public disclosure pointing to limited syndica- tion, this should be supplemented with some sort of objective criteria . Those criteria could be spread related. For example, if a bond issued with limited syndication tightens more than say 5% of its issuance spread over the first five days then it should be excluded; if not, it should be included, so long as its secondary market volumes are in line with similar size/rating broadly syndicated, registered securities. While higher energy prices and commodity investment provide some support to the economy, they have not materially changed the broader structural backdrop due to export capacity limits. Canada remains underexposed to the sectors currently driving global trade growth — particularly AI, electronics, and data infrastructure — while remaining concentrated in resources and lower-complexity manufacturing. This keeps CAD from appreciating against USD directly and performing better on crosses. CAD remains range-bound into 2027. Increased infrastructure spending, energy investment, and FDI tied to critical minerals and upstream commodity supply chains could provide medium-term support to growth and the currency, but domestic growth only improves modestly and consumption remains weak. CAD could only perform better on the crosses if growth spillovers remain supportive and trade uncertainty fades. Risks to our view: The main upside risk is a stronger-than-expected global growth and commodity cycle that lifts Canadian investment and exports. A faster or cleaner USMCA resolution could also reduce uncertainty sufficiently to support investment flows and improve confidence around Canadian growth. The downside risk is that uncertainty persists while Canada continues to underperform in the fastest-growing segments of global trade, reinforcing CAD’s increasingly cyclical and risk-sensitive profile.

records.text: iciency of a data center’s operations. WUE measures the direct, on-site water efficiency of data center operations. It is calculated by dividing the annual volume of water withdrawn on-site (primarily for cooling) by annual IT energy consumption, typically expressed in liters per kilowatt-hour (L/kWh). Lower WUE values indicate greater water efficiency. Average WUE varies significantly by geography and cooling approach. Facilities relying heavily on evaporative cooling tend to exhibit much higher WUEs, as discussed in section Liquid Cooling is NOT the Cause of Data Center Water Use, while air-cooled or closed-loop liquid-cooled designs can achieve materially lower values, particularly in cooler climates. For example, Alibaba reports an average data center WUE of 1.144 L/kWh in FY2025, reflecting a blend of 1.8 L/kWh for evaporative-cooled facilities and 0.33 L/kWh for non-evaporative-cooled sites.15 Similarly, Equinix reports a 2024 average WUE of 0.95 L/kWh, which is skewed higher by a 1.144 L/kWh WUE for its evaporative-cooled data centers.16 As with PUE, it is essential to distinguish between average and peak WUE. During hot periods or drought conditions, direct water use can spike sharply as evaporative systems operate more intensively. The announcement includes "initial price thoughts, " which represent the spread range within which the deal is likely to be priced. In the US (Europe), the spread range is set relative to a Treasury bond (Euro mid-swap rate) within the same maturity bucket, is based on market conditions at that time, and is updated as investors begin to submit orders.1 After some time, a final "indicative price range" is communicated and investors' orders become "firm. " The deal is priced near market close, with the price typically falling within the indicative range. The date of these activities marks the pricing date. A couple of business days later, the new issue is delivered to buyers and interest accrual begins. This sets the issuance date. Between the pricing and issuance date, the new issue can trade on a when- issued basis. records.text: US Economic Presentation15 May 2026 ab 16 Source: BLS, Haver, UBS • Like the broader economic expansion, the labor market expansion is narrow. Excluding health care and social assistance, nonfarm payroll employment has been declining -20K jobs per month for the eight months ending in April. Work weeks look low, and slack. • Job growth underlying the unemployment rate has been below the so-called break-even, even the estimates done correctly. Layoffs and job losses are not that low. • Residual seasonality, near zero net immigration, and weak labor demand likely remain in 2026. records.text: Evolution of online and what consumers are paying up for For their part, retailers are increasingly looking for ways to increase consumer engagement. This is translating not only into greater use of agentic commerce but also continued evolution in the speed of delivery. In this vein, we think it is instructive to look at what Amazon and Walmart are doing to drive demand. Speed of delivery matters: Baseline expectations around speed of delivery continue to shift faster with Walmart noting that a 'significant' number of its orders are being fulfilled in under half an hour as consumers opt for delivery times as short as one hour. In the last FYE, it highlighted that its fast delivery option (under three hours) rose over 60%. Such expedited options come with a higher incremental cost, which is being assumed given the convenience it offers. The company has previously highlighted that its store base gives it the ability to serve 95% of the US population within three hours. Grocery as a traffic driver: Amazon has been aggressively adding perishable offerings to its delivery options via Prime. The company has been seeing an uplift from shoppers adding perishable items to their baskets given that the option is available in 2300 cities and towns. Positioning/Hedging: Recent APRA data show Australian superannuation funds have reduced notional FX derivative positions, which represents a potential AUD-positive factor if it continues. AUD futures and options positioning seems to have diverged from spot positioning, which remains short. Our options-based positioning metric (MSOPAUDU Index) sits around the 78th percentile, and CFTC data show a rise in net non-commercial AUD positions. However, our franchise flows show that investors have been selling AUD, leaving room for longs to build before crowding becomes a constraint. The key risk to our bullish AUD view is a swifter-than-expected deceleration in Australian growth and in the labor market, which would reduce AUD's carry profile and attractiveness.

We think the momentum in Samurai issuance should be discounted to some degree. European names often route proceeds through USD even when ultimately swapping into EUR, which indirectly creates widening pressure on the SOFR/TONA basis. Although US IG credit spreads and European IG credit spreads still remain tight, we expect gradual widening ahead. In that environment, we expect Samurai bond issuance momentum to increase gradually with a broader issuer base. Yankee bond issuance (USD-denominated bonds issued for the purpose of swapping proceeds into JPY) has been running above the past 10-year average (see Exhibit 314 ), but has been broadly in line with the 2025 pace. The North West is one of the wettest parts of England, with rainfall frequently above long-term averages and catchments often classified as “above normal” providing a structurally more secure water resource base than the water-stressed South and East. This matters as data centers remain reliant on reliable water access for cooling, even as efficiency improves. In our UK Water sector deep dive, we identified UU as the name with the largest capex step-up potential from AMP8 (2025-30) to AMP9 (2030-35), amongst the three listed names. This is driven by the wet weather increasing CSO investments needs and by UU's assets likely having the largest MEAV (replacement costs). At the end of April, UU submitted another £2.5bn in capex needs via a re-opener for AMP8, increasing the period's investment programme to £11.5bn, and raised £800m to fund the growth. The market clearly viewed the raise as a strong growth accelerator with the stock rising c.12% on announcement day. We flag that this re-opener was only the first of five within the AMP8 period. We see a strong growth profile ahead—part of which is incremental data center demand converting it into higher regulated asset growth and returns—paired with the cheapest infrastructure valuation in the sector. records.text: Retail traders in the equity ownership landscape Following a decline in early 2026, retail trading activity has inflected higher alongside the recent equity market rally. GS Global Banking & Markets estimates of retail trading volumes show a 28% increase in retail trading activity since mid-April. Mirroring this increase, a basket of stocks popular with retail traders (GSXURFAV) has rallied by 29% over the same period. See Exhibit 25 for the current constituents of GSXURFAV with the largest recent retail share of trading volumes. The recent replacement of pattern day trader rules with less stringent margin requirements increases the likelihood that retail trading activity will rise further. Retail traders are a subset of US households, which are the largest owner of the US equity market. We define retail investors as individuals making self-directed trading decisions in brokerage accounts. The Fed’s latest Financial Accounts of the United States data (Z.1) show that US households are the largest owner of corporate equities. Of the $111 trillion value of corporate equity assets, 40% is directly held by households. Including indirect ownership via retirement accounts, mutual funds, and ETFs, households own the majority of the US corporate equity market. Morgan Securities plc Fabio Bassi AC (44-20) 7134-1989 fabio.bassi@jpmorgan.com Global Markets Strategy 15 May 2026 J P M O R G A N We are now rounding out the 11th week of the Iran conflict and there seems to be limited progress on negotiations between the US and Iran, driving oil prices up 7.6% over the past week. Notably, since the beginning of March, Hormuz transit remains muted and our commodity team states that the depletion of oil inventories should pressure the Strait of Hormuz to reopen as it will incentivize both parties to come back to the negotiating table. Using a June reopening in their models, the commodity team revises the 2Q/3Q/4Q 2026 average quarterly forecast to $103, $104, $98/bbl, implying a 2026 average of $96/bbl. In contrast, Brent forwards are suggesting a pronounced downward price pressure with September and December 2026 Brent contracts at $97/ bbl and $88.7/bbl respectively. On the macro side, the effects of the energy shock are feeding through to global inflation, with the aggregate April CPI report pointing to another 0.4% jump to 3.5%oya, about 1% above pre-conflict. This week, inflation data in the US (April CPI and PPI) surprised to the upside, contributing to the full dis-inversion of the US money market curve, which is now pricing 60% probability of a 25bp hike in Dec26, and the market is now pricing ~30bp of hikes by June 2027 at the time of writing, more hawkish than our economists’ call of one hike in September next year. It looks more like a delayed policy repricing, with 2s10s carrying more signal than the 10y outright. In the global oil-led recession, the Fed cuts aggressively, the 10y moves toward the low- 3% area, and 2s10s steepens sharply. In US aggregate demand, the Fed hikes, the 10y trades above 5%, and 2s10s can invert again. Our baseline lands in the middle, with the market first respecting the tails and then giving more weight to the modal outcome. Inflation markets explain why the long end does not rally more. Breakevens stay elevated into end-2026 as energy lifts headline inflation and passes through to core, then decline in 2027 as energy settles. Real yields remain high by post-GFC standards. A still-restrictive Fed, better productivity, and fiscal supply make it hard for 10y real yields to fall much. Put differently, nominal UST performance comes more from lower inflation compensation and lower expected policy rates than from a collapse in real yields. Debt management matters too. For another, oil shocks affect inflation immediately via gas prices, while spending only slows with a lag. Gas accounts for less than 2% of PCE spending, so consumers have leeway to absorb a gas shock for a few months. But the longer the shock lasts, the more likely it is that they will make substantial cuts to discretionary outlays. This could then weigh on labor demand, with an additional lag. Bottom line: the jury is still out Our conclusion is that the facts on the ground don’t let us distinguish yet between reflation and stagflation. The true test of consumer and labor resilience might still be ahead of us. Markets pricing of nearly a full hike by mid-2027 seems reasonable given the latest data flow. We view this as a balance between a base case of an extended hold (the appropriate policy response to stagflation), with substantial risks of a hiking cycle (reflation) and smaller risks of cuts (if stagflation gives way to recession). For what it’s worth, we are still some ways from making hikes our base case. The bar for labor is much higher when it comes to hiking rather than staying on hold. records.text: ssured China that their relationship was "going to be better than ever before" and hailed Xi as a "great leader" . However, as Trump left Beijing on Friday there was little tangible progress from the two-day talks. There were no formal announcements of new contracts for US companies or regulatory changes for their operations in China. A potential purchase of 200 Boeing planes was mentioned by Trump, but without further detail, and the subsequent drop in Boeing stock points to investors' disappointment. On geopolitics, there was agreement on the need for a rapid reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, but no indication of a common approach. China made no commitment to put pressure on Iran, even though Trump considered lifting the sanctions on China's purchases of Iranian oil. At the same time, Xi communicated an assertive stance on Taiwan, including a warning of potential "conflict" with the US. Trump did not make any concession on the US language regarding Taiwan (ie, "opposed to" versus "not supportive of" Taiwanese independence), but for now also held back on deciding on the pending $14bn arms sale to Taiwan. More broadly, the meeting may have succeeded in establishing a sense of stability and continued mutual non-aggression. The concept of "new constructive strategic stability" introduced by Xi supposedly aims at keeping "competition within proper limits" . records.text: FIGURE 16. 1y1y CPI swaps Source: Barclays Research The shape of the Rbob, WTI and Brent futures curves implies near-term inflation, but forward deflation in energy prices. At the time of writing, the WTI futures curve implied crude back below $80/b (a ~20% decline from spot) as early as Q1 27, and back below $70/b by 2029. If taken literally, this backwardation implies the opposite of sustained energy price inflation and runs counter to fears of a more sustained and renewed inflation process (we discussed this topic in more detail in Seriously, but not literally, April 30, 2026). Put together, there is a clear argument for a meaningful inflation impulse resulting from higher near-term energy prices, but uncertainty is pervasive and the dynamics get more complicated, as investors need to the weigh the combination of persistence risks, backwardation in commodity curves and the possibility of demand destruction weighing on consumer spending. Indeed, even as Barclays' economists recently raised their near-term inflation forecast and pushed back their rate cut call to March 2027 amid a higher inflation profile, they now forecast sub-2% headline inflation in H2 27 for both CPI and PCE. As noted above, this shift means that there is still room for Chinese FDI to the EU, but Brussels will likely be keen to keep this more targeted than in the past. From a timeline perspective, the IAA is expected to follow the standard legislative process over 2026-2027, with gradual implementation from 2027 onward, subject to sector-specific secondary legislation and guidelines. Some elements (particularly those linked to existing EU funding programs) could, however, be phased in earlier through delegated acts or conditionality attached to public support schemes. While framed as an industrial resilience tool, the initiative effectively introduces structural market‑access frictions for non‑EU producers, especially in sectors already characterised by global overcapacity. In that sense, “Made in Europe” complements traditional trade defence and FSR enforcement by shifting policy focus from border measures to in‑market preferential frameworks, with potentially significant implications for Chinese exporters.

Last year there was a view that inflation would be close to target once tariffs have rolled off the y/y rate. Some of this optimism was due to continued housing disinflation. Some analysts also argued that financial services inflation (due to the portfolio management component, which moves with stocks with a 1-2m lag) would normalize after a couple of outsized gains last year. These arguments feel a lot more tenuous now. After yesterday’s import price data, we estimate that core PCE will come in at 3.3% y/y (0.28% m/m) in April. Tariffs are still likely to start rolling off y/y core PCE in 2H ’26, but that effect should be at least partially offset by pass-through of the oil shock. Further, some of the increase in goods prices that was being attributed to tariffs now appears to be due to demand for AI inputs. So this inflation is likely to be stickier, and it’s having a much bigger effect on PCE inflation (the Fed’s target) than CPI (Exhibit 6, see report: Not a good wedge for the Fed). For the Fed, markets have aligned with our call for a Fed rate hike next year, and the latest developments raise risks of an earlier move. ECB & BoJ to hike in June; BoE less clear There are still four weeks until the ECB’s June policy meet- ing. Incoming commentary supports a hike but emphasizes data dependence. A deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz could alter the calculus, but our commodities analysts expect oil prices to stay high for a while, and natural gas prices to rise, regardless. We expect next week’s flash PMI to edge up after large falls in March-April, with output prices staying high. All of this points to a June rate hike and one more thereafter. The ECB will also view an initial 25bp hike as a relatively modest move that leaves its policy rate in its neutral range. The BoE has set a higher bar for rate hikes than the ECB, reflecting the UK’s weaker labor market. Despite this, growth indicators have surprised positively, with 1Q GDP up 2.5% annualized and April PMI showing resilience. Having said that, fiscal pressures are high even in this scenario. There is likely to be pressure to provide support in response to the energy shock (we expect targeted temporary support to low- income households costing low single digit billions) along with public services and defence spending pressures, which may increase further given Labour losses. But these pressures are likely to be met by higher taxes or near- term borrowing followed by medium term tightening (i.e. within the confines of fiscal rules). Streeting has previously suggested aligning capital gains tax with income tax and reforming inheritance tax but overall, he is unlikely to advocate big tax hikes. He has also previously suggested funding defence pressures with potential welfare savings. On other policy areas, Streeting has suggested support for rejoining the EU customs union. We believe that the DA is unlikely to shy away from any process that would cause embarrassment for the ruling party ahead of the upcoming polls. This raises key questions about the structural versus cyclical forces driving Chinese exports to Europe: What is the extent of tariff-related trade rerouting? How much depends on genuine comparative advantage (e.g. productivity gains and technological advancements)? Are Chinese domestic subsidies playing any meaningful role? More structurally, are there signs of vent-for-surplus behaviour amid longer-term changes in Chinese domestic demand? Conversely, is there a structural shift in EU demand with respect to specific trade goods/sectors? There are definitely several factors at play. Focusing on China-EU trade flows, we examine: (1) evidence of 2025 US tariff‑induced trade re‑routing; and (2) the role of the vent-for-surplus hypothesis, before and after the 2025 US tariff wave. 1 The empirical literature on the 2018-19 US-China trade war consistently documents a large and causal decline in Chinese exports to the US, driven by tariff increases and concentrated in directly targeted sectors. Product‑level and customs‑data analyses show a sharp contraction in bilateral trade flows, accompanied by significant reallocation of sourcing away from China. A final leg of the DXY's cyclical selloff: We think the DXY remains in a tradable, cyclical downtrend that began in early 2025. We expect 2y rate differentials on a DXY-weighted basis to compress about 20bp between the US and the RoW, which reduces the DXY's rates-implied 'fair value' by about -1.5%. But ultimately, we expect the DXY's decline to outpace this for two key reasons. First, robust risk appetite thanks to upside equity earnings revisions should boost cyclical currencies and weigh on the DXY at the margin. As discussed above, relative measures of Gilt performance, such as swap spreads and long-end curve shape, indicate these factors are already improving. And while global dynamics are contributing to higher Gilt yields, we expect to see lower yields in most major markets over time. As our European economists have argued, Gilt yields are high relative to the UK’s fiscal fundamentals and rates remain well above equilibrium levels. This points to lower Gilt yields over time. For 2026, we continue to think that macro outcomes on inflation and BoE policy will remain the key drivers for Gilt yields. Our baseline remains that the BoE will be on hold through 2026, before cutting in 2027, and as a result we continue to see 10y Gilt yields at 4.40% at end-2026. To cross-check the extent of long-end risk-premium pressure, we use a simple fair- value residual framework that separates global from UK-specific factors. We estimate the relationship between 10y (see Exhibit 131 ) and 20y (see Exhibit 132 ) SONIA swaps and 1y1y SONIA over the past year, and compare the resulting residuals with equivalent residuals in the SOFR and Euribor markets. We then define the UK-specific component as the SONIA residual less the average of the SOFR and Euribor residuals. This gives us a proxy for the part of the UK long-end move that cannot be explained by either domestic front-end repricing or the common global rates move. On this measure, the past month points to a UK-specific risk premium of around 10bp in 10y SONIA swaps and 12bp in 20y SONIA swaps. We would not over-interpret this as a pure fiscal premium. The residual can reflect several overlapping factors: domestic political uncertainty, fiscal concerns, inflation-risk premium, liquidity and positioning. Wage growth remains on trend Australia’s wage price index printed at 0.8%q/q sa for the third consecutive quarter in 1Q, consistent with J.P. Morgan and consensus forecasts. The annual rate ticked lower to 3.3%oya, but remains within the range of the past few years. The underlying mix of wage growth was more interesting with private sector wages running commensurate with head- line, while the public sector slowed to 0.5%q/q sa, about half 2025’s average quarterly run rate. The magnitude of this deceleration is unusual and seems to be a function of fewer public sector employees receiving wage increases in 1Q, with just 21% of employees reporting a pay bump, below the long- run average of 27%. There could also be lingering issues around the seasonal adjustment process given the swings in timing/magnitude of wage contracts since 2022. We look at the role played by entry levels when predicting future €, $ and £ swap rates over different horizons since 2022 and find that the level of the curve is the most accurate to predict, especially 3m- and 6m- ahead. Its predictability drops across currencies when initial forward rates are also included as rhs variables. Finally, we find that the front-end cross-market spreads are more predictable than longer tenors, with €-£ more accurate than €-$. Predicting tomorrow’s price using today’s. Legal support to grant additional certainty A missing piece in the puzzle before the third stage was launched last week was related to the rule of law as investors continued to seek certainty and legal protection before com- mitting to long-term projects. The Sheinbaum administration seems to understand private investors’ skepticism after the approval of the 2024 judicial reform and last week released the rules of the game for the Strategic Investment Plan. These bylaws state that whenever a conflict related to the economic or technical aspects of a contract arises, alternative dispute resolution mechanisms should be prioritized. It also lays out guidelines to establish an arbitration committee aimed at ensuring fairness. While in our view this enhanced legal framework is a step in the right direction to address rule-of-law concerns, the pro- cess has shortcomings that are unlikely to dispel broader wor- ries. For starters, arbitration can only be used as a resolution mechanism if both parties agree to it or if the contract explic- itly provides for it. In addition, conflicts related to the legal validity of any revocation of authorization—or other acts by the authority—can only be resolved via federal tribunals. records.text: M Global Insight 96 Alternate scenarios Consistent with the rest of our global rates forecasts, our bull and bear scenarios for yields on Canadian government bonds align with two alternative scenarios from our economists: a US aggregate demand upside case and a global oil-led recession scenario. Our baseline reflects the probability-weighted outcome between these paths, where the BoC remains on hold through 2026 before markets price normalizing policy in 2027. In the US aggregate demand scenario, stronger US growth spillovers support Canadian exports, investment, and fiscal-sensitive sectors sooner than in our base case. Improved growth prospects and firmer domestic activity push investors to reprice BoC normalization earlier and more aggressively, sending the 2-year GoC yield above 4.50% by end-2027 and the 10-year yield toward 5.50% as markets increasingly price a move back toward the midpoint of neutral. In the global oil-led recession scenario, weaker global demand dominates the positive terms-of-trade effects from higher energy prices and materially weakens the Canadian growth outlook. In this scenario, front-end yields lead the decline as markets price a prolonged period near the lower end of neutral and slower normalization from the BoC. The bull case for bonds sees 10-year GoC yields falling toward 3.25% by end-2027 as investors contemplate the lasting effects of weaker global growth on Canada’s recovery outlook. records.text: weakly to falling ones (Exhibit 1, right). Why the Asymmetry? Uneven passthrough could reflect several factors. First, asymmetric firm markup adjustment. When input costs rise, firms are forced to adjust prices upward to protect their profit margins given the constraint of bankruptcy. But when costs fall, firms might retain prices to expand margins, especially when they have market power. Second, the cost of changing prices (“menu costs”) could play a role. Given the cost of changing prices—both physical “menu costs” and the desire to avoid negative reactions to frequent price changes—firms may absorb small cost decreases rather than incur these broader adjustment costs with positive trend inflation. Third, the asymmetry could reflect downward nominal stickiness in prices and wages. When a positive energy shock erodes purchasing power, workers are likely to demand higher wages. Conversely, firms find it very difficult to cut nominal wages when their costs fall, meaning cost savings are not fully passed on through lower labour costs. New Evidence We provide fresh statistical evidence on this passthrough behaviour in the Euro area. We start with a simple top-down perspective, similar to the IMF and Danish national central bank. In particular, we use a statistical (vector autoregressive) model to estimate the effect of non-core (food and energy) inflation on subsequent core inflation, controlling for long-term inflation expectations and labour market slack. We start by comparing curve behaviour across markets using a simple “transmission” measure: the ratio between daily changes in 10y10y forwards and daily changes in 1y1y forwards. Intuitively, this captures how much of a front-end move is transmitted into the long end of the curve. Higher values indicate a more parallel repricing, while lower values point to a more front-end-led move. To focus on the underlying regime rather than day-to-day noise, we compute a 252- day rolling median of this daily transmission ratio. Our positioning data suggest NOK longs have been the most consistently popular of any G10 currency, with NOK/EUR long positioning at one point reaching its record high. NOK should gain but lag SEK: The net result is that we think NOK’s appeal will continue to carry the currency forward, with EUR/NOK projected to fall to 10.60 by year end, but ultimately NOK may lag gains from other currencies like SEK that have more capacity to ‘catch up’. With markets at the moment primarily oriented toward carry and risk appetite, NOK’s gains are understandable, but we think later on this year markets can reorient toward a focus on cyclical global growth, which sees NOK’s peer, SEK, catch up. Key risks to the view: NOK’s tight links to energy, risk appetite, and carry demand create risks to the currency should these forces evaporate, naturally. Given NOK’s popularity, a meaningful shift in market narrative toward defensive assets and safe havens could see NOK underperform more meaningfully than usual. Increased energy prices leading to larger transfers to the GPFG could also put downward pressure on NOK in the absence of NOK demand on the other side of the ledger. On the positive side, we remain highly attentive to any changes in government policy around drawdowns of the GPFG; given that all fund assets are invested externally, greater consumption of fund assets to finance domestic expenditure could present a meaningfully positive, long-term NOK flow.

records.text: GBP: Pressures coming together. UK political newsflow has picked up following last n week’s local elections and, as is often the case, a rise in political uncertainty has been accompanied by FX underperformance. Heading into this week, we saw relatively little risk premium in the currency, with EUR/GBP moving closely in line with our GSBEER model of cyclical fundamentals. That has changed in recent days, with the cross now incorporating about 1ppt of fiscal premium according to this model, but the newly reintroduced premium is still light compared to most of last year when it regularly traded about 2% above its fitted value (Exhibit 3). We think that represents a reasonable near-term target at least until there is more clarity on the policy plans. What would follow a leadership transition, and whether it would see any material shift in fiscal policy, also remains far from clear. records.text: jectives. In practice, most modern data centers employ hybrid cooling architectures, combining multiple technologies to optimize performance, efficiency, and resilience. What does water use have to do with data center cooling? The primary source of direct (on-site) data center water use is evaporative cooling—not liquid cooling itself. While liquid cooling systems do use water-based coolants, they typically operate in closed-loop configurations; once initially filled, the coolant is continuously recirculated and is not consumed during normal operations. As we detail in section Liquid Cooling is NOT the Cause of Water Use, liquid cooling can actually reduce water use by mitigating evaporative cooling needs. Evaporative cooling, by contrast, is a long-standing HVAC technique used in both commercial buildings and data centers. In evaporative systems, warm air is passed through wetted media or fine water sprays, causing a portion of the water to evaporate. This phase change from liquid to vapor absorbs heat (via the latent heat of vaporization), thereby lowering the air’s dry-bulb temperature. This process is analogous to human perspiration—as sweat evaporates, it absorbs heat and cools the body. The water vapor is then exhausted to the atmosphere, resulting in net water consumption, while the cooled air can be supplied to IT or heat-rejection equipment with significantly less reliance on energy-intensive mechanical compressors and fan-cooled condensers. Primary metrics for data center water & electricity use Source: Barclays Research Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) measures non-IT energy efficiency. PUE measures the non-IT energy overhead required to support data center operations, rather than the efficiency of the IT equipment itself. It is calculated by dividing total annual data center energy consumption (IT plus non-IT) by annual IT-equipment energy consumption. Non-IT energy includes cooling systems, electrical distribution losses, lighting, and other facility infrastructure, with cooling typically representing the largest share. A PUE closer to 1.0x indicates greater efficiency. For example, a PUE of 1.5x implies that for every 1 kWh consumed by IT equipment, an additional 0.5 kWh is used for non-IT loads— meaning roughly one-third of total facility energy consumption is non-IT . While the industry-wide average PUE remains above ~1.5x, according to the Uptime Institute, this reflects a simple average that includes a large installed base of older enterprise and colocation data centers.13 In contrast, hyperscalers, which now represent a growing share of global data center capacity, consistently report average PUEs in the ~1.1–1.2x range, driven by scale advantages, purpose-built facilities, optimized cooling architectures, and increasing adoption of liquid-cooling technologies. On the lending side, intraday repo allows those with excess, idle cash (e.g. corporates, MMFs, FHLBs, stablecoin issuers) to monetize those cash balances intraday, while still keeping their liquidity profile tight and predictable. Transparency into this nascent market is limited. Based on conversations, intraday repo volumes are less than $10bn, which is de minimus in the context of a $3tn overnight Treasury repo market. Growth in this market will take time, and we suspect adoption will grow alongside familiarity with blockchain, similar to the trajectory seen in stablecoins and tokenized MMFs. Moreover, to the extent banks have been borrowing overnight repo to fund a fixed intraday buffer, intraday repo could cannibalize some overnight repo demand. The more important dynamic to watch is whether the product unlocks new lender capacity from participants previously unwilling to lend overnight, which would be net additive to system liquidity. Computer Room Air Handler (CRAH) + air-cooled chiller system illustration CRAH Unit Warm DC Air Cool DC Air Warm Water Cool Water Warm Air Cool Outside AirAir-cooled Chiller Source: Barclays Research CRAH + Water-cooled Chiller + Wet Cooling Tower This configuration is similar to the Computer Room Air Handler (CRAH) + air-cooled chiller setup but uses water-cooled chillers and wet cooling towers to reject heat more efficiently via evaporative cooling. This provides very high energy efficiency (~1.1-1.4 PUE), but very high water loss. Where it is commonly used: This architecture is widely deployed in large enterprise, colocation, and hyperscale data centers where maximum cooling capacity and energy efficiency are required, in regions with high ambient temperatures and low humidity, and where water sustainability is not a limiting factor. How it works:CRAH units inside the data center hall circulate warm server room air across chilled-water coils, absorbing heat into a chilled water loop. This chilled water is supplied by remote water-cooled chillers, which function as large refrigeration systems. Inside the chiller, heat from the chilled water is transferred to a separate condenser water loop via a heat exchanger. The warmed condenser water is then pumped to wet cooling towers, where heat is rejected into the atmosphere through evaporative cooling: ambient air flows over the water, and a portion of the water evaporates, carrying away heat. According to the BBC, the NEC will allow Burnham to contest this coming by-election. We assume the local Labour party in Makerfield will accept him as their candidate, should the NEC allow him to stand. For the February 2026 Gorton and Denton by-election, the NEC reached the decision on Burnham's candidacy 24 hours after he asked for the permission to stand. The by-election was organised one month after the previous MP stood down. Hence, it looks like we should know if Burnham will stand in the coming days, and that the by-election is likely to be held by the end of June or early July. And we have been emphasizing that moves in Dollar crosses understate terms of trade dynamics compared to near-neighbor crosses like NOK/SEK, AUD/NZD, and BRL/CLP , which have moved much further. We attribute part of the broad Dollar’s more muted response to this conflict to the fact that its impact has fallen most severely on less central US trading partners and those with heavily-managed currencies— particularly in Asia. Indeed, we find that Asia FX returns have tracked terms of trade moves less closely than elsewhere in EM and the G10 (Exhibit 6). Besides more stringent currency management, this also reflects that commodity terms of trade do not capture the recent boost from higher‑value tech exports, overstating the deterioration for the likes of KRW, TWD, and CNY; we find that incorporating tech exports alongside commodity terms of trade better explains recent Asia FX performance (Exhibit 7). More broadly, we find FX returns over shorter horizons have tracked less well with changes in terms of trade than they have over the entirety of the conflict period. This seems in part due to the fact commodity exporters like AUD have seen asymmetric outperformance on days when energy prices increase. The slowdown was mostly observed in the market-rate segment ("recursos livres"), with new credit growing 4.1% in real terms, from 11.2%, while earmarked credit growth (which is typically subsidized and includes lines for housing, agriculture and the national development bank, BNDES) accelerated in the period, up 4.8% in the 12 months ending in March, from 3.4% a year earlier. The longer it doesn’t show evidence of cracks due to tariffs, Iran and AI-related layoffs, the more likely it is that downside risks have waned. The April jobs report was solid, with good news on payrolls and some disappointment in wage inflation and the Household Survey (see report: April jobs: we give it a B+). Jobless claims are still benign. Booming corporate earnings also underpin the case for reflation. Per our equity strategists, 1Q EPS is running at 26% y/y, with nearly 90% of the S&P 500 having reported. This is the strongest growth rate since 2021. Earnings are being led (but not exclusively driven) by AI demand. Strong corporate profits boost the case for consumer resilience (via equity wealth effects) and reduce any urgency around layoffs. The case for stagflation A counter to this optimism is that inflation has already started to weigh on activity, but the impact has been obscured by fiscal stimulus. In late February, we were expecting nearly 3% annualized real spending growth (6% nominal) in 1H ’26. We are now tracking 2.3% real spending as discussed above, with inflation substantially above our pre-war forecasts. That is stagflation, in a very mild sense. records.text: 10 Europe Economic Weekly | 15 May 2026 There are a lot of moving parts in this print. Another leg up in weekly fuel prices is likely to cause a rise in energy inflation from 4.9% to 6.2%y/y, but a 6.7%m/m fall in gas prices (due to Budget measures) is likely to moderate the rise. Core inflation is likely to fall from 3.1% to 2.7%, with a drop in services inflation to 3.5%. This is driven by the impact of NICs dropping out of the annual calculation for services and water bills/ vehicle duty rising less than last year. This is likely to cause a big slowdown in services inflation. We expect core goods to rise from 0.8% to 1.1% as clothing inflation picks up. Food inflation is likely to be flat at 3.7%. But inflation is set to rise in H2 once the gas price impact of the conflict starts showing up in the July price cap and indirect effects materialize, especially in food prices. We expect the unemployment rate to be flat at 4.9% in the three months to March, while we expect payrolls to fall by 10K in April. So far, evidence is for a minor reduction in hiring activity in March and not a sharp slowdown. Private wage growth should fall slightly from 3.2% to 3.1% but with a firming up of monthly wage increases (0.3%m/m seasonally adjusted).
