records.text: Cayla Seder 13 May 2026 1 Insights Classification: Complimentary Material Developed Markets Strategy Weekly : T here’s no going back ? KEY THEMES THIS WEEK: Infront, behind and beside the curve. We are at a unique point of divergence in developed market central bank policy: some are signalling a slowdown in hiking cycles, others are preparing to begin, and a few remain on hold. As always, the outlook remains data-dependent. April US CPI surprised to the upside, and sustained supply disruptions could further exacerbate inflation pressures ahead, which makes the risk of higher inflation later an omnipresent force in market thinking. Although we have yet to get April data for the bulk of the G10, PriceStats data indicate online prices were by and large far from normal, which could keep pressure on banks that have yet to hike rates. Policy divergence is increasingly evident. Central banks such as the RBA have been tightening for months, while others, including the BoC, have yet to begin their hiking cycles. This backdrop informs our positioning, with a shift from long CADCHF to short AUDCAD. More broadly, market pricing has returned to peak hawkish expectations for the BoE, RBNZ, ECB, BoJ, and BoC. In contrast, the Fed is beginning to appear behind the curve, yet markets remain reluctant to price hikes into 2026—even as core inflation has risen to 2.8% YoY, its highest since September 2025. Japan BOJ QT likely to stay the course. The BoJ will release its quarterly bond market n survey this upcoming week, ahead of the bond market group meetings on May 21 and 22. At these meetings, the BoJ seeks market participants’ views on the pace of QT. This feedback will be a key input for the Bank’s balance sheet policy review at the June monetary policy meeting and help inform any potential changes. During its previous review of balance sheet policy at the June 2025 MPM, the BoJ noted that “in the case of a rapid rise in long-term interest rates, the Bank will make nimble responses by, for example, increasing the amount of JGB purchases.” Despite a sizable increase in long-term rates since then, the pace of QT has proceeded as planned. Most recently, in April, the BoJ implemented its scheduled moderation of purchase reductions from ¥400bn to ¥200bn per quarter. With funding markets showing no obvious signs of volatility and swap spreads relatively flat on the year, our economists do not anticipate a change to the QT path in June. Further, while a shift could provide some relief along the supply/demand dimension specifically, it would not address the main source of JGB volatility this year, which we think reflects domestic macro risks stemming in part from the BOJ’s gradual approach to rate hike

What Mr. Huang was signaling, in our view, is not the elimination of chillers altogether, but rather that chillers will not be required in all regions or at all times. In reality, chillers remain essential in hotter climates, during peak seasonal temperatures, and for redundancy and load-balancing purposes, even in liquid-cooled data centers. Liquid cooling reduces the frequency and intensity with which chillers must operate, but does not eliminate the need for mechanical cooling across an annual operating profile. Importantly, as data center operators shift away from evaporative cooling, this transition is likely to favor air-cooled over traditional water-cooled chiller plants, reinforcing the ongoing relevance of air-cooled chillers in modern and future data center designs. records.text: Mexico - Banxico meeting minutes: On May 21 Banco de México will publish the minutes of the May 7 meeting, in which the majority of the board decided to cut the reference rate by 25bp to 6.50%. While the decision was widely expected, the 3-2 decision was tighter than the 4-1 we had anticipated. Deputy Governor Galia Borja decided to dissent for the second consecutive time, voting to leave the interest rate unchanged. We had expected that she would vote in favor of reducing the rate, based on the comments made in an interview published in the newspaper El Economista on April 24. In that interview, Deputy Governor Borja stated that in the March decision the board “…had limited information to accurately assess the implications of the shock, its magnitude, and its duration… ” . However, she also had noted that more recently “…it appears that tensions are easing, there is an intention on both sides to find a solution, and markets have priced in a less pessimistic scenario… ” . Likewise, the fact that the federal government is absorbing the shock from fuel prices—both gasoline, a directly and indirectly significant component of the National Consumer Price Index, and diesel, which powers close to 60 percent of product transportation in the country—should help reduce concerns about a larger inflationary shock. records.text: To give a sense of scale, mechanically, were retail gasoline prices to rise from $4.5/gallon to $5.0/gallon and stay there, at a high that would be an 11.1% increase on 3.68% of the basket, implying a +41bp impulse to the CPI price index, all else equal (if anything, this is likely an understatement, given that the weight in the basket would likely rise). To go one step further, the inflation and rates markets can take their cue from commodity markets, specifically gasoline futures (ie, Rbob futures), which have informational content as to the forward path for gasoline, and have a more natural correlation to retail gasoline prices than crude oil. After all, consumers buy gallons of gas, not barrels of oil. The second channel is what is broadly referred to as second-order effects, which capture not only potential spillovers into core inflation (eg, via jet fuel into airline fares, discussed in more detail here), but also potential pass-through into food via higher fertilizer prices and/or diesel (which matters for shipping and transportation, as discussed here). The second-order channel is much more sensitive to how long prices stay elevated, whether inflation expectations begin to shift due to higher energy prices, and whether wages begin to accelerate. After all, it is hard to get a wage price spiral without wage growth. We find that: • Underperforming demand sectors exhibit a significantly more negative time pattern in unit value growth, pointing to stronger price compression relative to others. Our estimates indicate progressively stronger price compression in the “weak” bucket, by ca 3.5% per year. For export values, the differential slope for weak sectors is positive but not statistically significant. Notably, these sectors show relative and statistically significant outperformance in import volumes. Taken together, the results are consistent with surplus being absorbed through both a price and quantity adjustment (Exhibit 8). • Truncating the sample into a pre‑tariff window, underperforming demand sectors continue to show greater price compression and evidence of relatively stronger volumes when the tariff period is excluded. If anything, the coefficients have a higher magnitude in absolute terms. This suggests that the “venting” mechanism has been occurring independently of tariff‑driven trade dynamics, with even stronger price compression/volume resilience pre the 2025 tariff wave. Short post‑Apr 2025 windows are statistically uninformative given the limited number of observations. To address this, we test for a structural change in pricing dynamics around 2025 using a piecewise-linear trend specification with HS2 fixed effects and year dummies.

The energy shock presents downside risks to economic growth and likely fiscal revenues. It is still too early to be confident on the damage to fiscal revenues. For now, we know that the temporary fuel levy relief (April to June) is costing a total of R17.2 billion. The Treasury plans to cut spending to keep the cost deficit neutral. The impact of slower economic growth on fiscal revenues is still less clear. National Treasury assumes nominal GDP growth of 5.6% in 26/27, which now appears on the higher side. We don’t think it will exceed 5% this year. Perhaps some of the commodity- linked revenues could offset revenue shortfalls associated with lower growth. June fiscal data (corporate tax take) is likely to provide initial guidance on revenue performance. The expenditure side is likely to be well contained. The wage agreements are locked in at 3.4% for fiscal 26/27. Social grants received a similar CPI-linked adjustment. Debt servicing costs could increase given higher bond yields following the energy shock. Nevertheless, the Treasury is likely to stick with its guidance on issuance – keep local fixed rate bond supply unchanged and access the international markets during the fiscal year to seek $2-3billion issuance.

records.text: M Global Insight Morgan Stanley Research 147 Short-Duration Strategy United States More than ample reserve balances in the financial system, ongoing Fed reserve management purchases, and Treasury cash management buybacks have dampened conditions in short-term funding markets. As additional proposals on bank regulation are finalized later this year, this should keep soft conditions in funding markets in place - a bullish factor for Treasury performance against relative to SOFR swaps and funding-related spreads. Abundant cash availability and fluid dealer intermediation should keep funding markets well equipped to absorb a pick-up in demand for UST collateral as bill supply is set to ramp up. Japan We continue to expect flattening pressure on the short- to medium-term XCCY basis curve. While we think Japanese lifers’ appetite for foreign bond investment is likely to remain limited for the time being, gradual demand for JPY assets among overseas investors should keep the front end broadly flat to slightly tighter. Further out the curve, moderate widening in US and European credit spreads, issuance trends in Samurai and Yankee bonds, and receiving demand in XCCY basis swaps related to the $550 billion in US-bound investments and loans should drive curve flattening. We continue to recommend a 1y1y/1y4y SOFR/TONA basis flattener.

records.text: Cooling requirements have also changed the sequencing and scope of construction work. Direct-to-chip liquid cooling and rear-door heat exchangers require tighter integration between structural design, mechanical systems, and fit-out than legacy designs, reducing modularity at the building shell stage. At the same time, water availability, heat rejection and energy efficiency constraints are influencing site selection and plot utilisation, particularly in Europe where permitting and sustainability thresholds are more stringent. This has increased demand for specialist contractors able to manage complex MEP packages, early design involvement, and phased delivery aligned with power and cooling availability rather than simple “build then fit” models. All of this combined with ever more rigorous performance requirements (in terms of uptime, capacity and energy efficiency) mean that data centers need to be constructed to withstand more demanding conditions, including higher load-bearing requirements, greater vibration control, enhanced fire resistance as well as more stringent thermal management, all with significantly reduced margins for error. These tighter requirements naturally entail more complex building processes and thus increase the potential for contractors to add-value by increasing the design and engineering requirements, which benefits contractors that are able to deliver these projects, particularly at the larger (multi-GW campus) end of the market. records.text: ility water is then pumped to water-cooled chillers, which remove the heat via a refrigeration cycle and transfer it to a secondary condenser water loop. Instead of using wet cooling towers, the condenser water is routed to outdoor dry coolers—large air-to-water heat exchangers with fans that blow ambient air across finned coils to dissipate heat into the atmosphere. Because dry coolers rely solely on sensible heat transfer, they consume no water under normal operation. Alternative option: To enhance performance during high ambient temperatures, some systems incorporate adiabatic assist: a fine mist of water is sprayed onto the coils to improve heat rejection. This feature uses only a small fraction of the water required by traditional wet cooling towers and is activated only during peak thermal conditions. Adiabatic cooling optional enhancement: The system is often paired with adiabatic cooling. The data center cooling system can operate in dry mode most of the year, with adiabatic assist activating during higher ambient temperatures to maintain cooling capacity while using only a fraction of the water required by traditional wet cooling towers. Free Cooling Using Economizers In temperate climates or during cooler winter months in hotter climates, the outside is often cool enough to efficiency be used to absorb heat from the servers and reject the heat outside of the data center simply using fans. If the Option-Adjusted Basis Net of Carry (OABNOC) is lower for the front month than for the back month contract, the calendar spread is considered rich. 2) Changes in short-term funding rates. An increase in funding rates generally causes futures prices to rise relative to cash prices, since it decreases the carry basis. Thus the calendar spread reflects changes in the shape of the short end of the yield curve: for example, if four-month funding rates rise while one-month rates remain the same, the calendar spread would be expected to fall. Changes in funding rates affect back-month futures more than front-month futures, since the back- month contract has three months more of carry in its basis. As a rule of thumb, for a parallel change in funding rates: -1 x (change in funding rate) / 4 = change in calendar spread For example, if short-term rates increase by 25 basis points, the calendar spread is expected to decrease by approximately .0625: -1 x .25 / 4 = -.0625 (in decimal form, or -2/32nds) 3) Supply and demand pressures. The calendar spread may become richer or cheaper depending on the balance of long and short hedgers and investors who are rolling positions. records.text: 6 Euro Area Viewpoint | 14 May 2026 2026; we also run specifications that exclude the 2025 tariff wave. Again, we include year fixed effects. We find that: • Underperforming demand sectors exhibit a significantly more negative time pattern in unit value growth, pointing to stronger price compression relative to others. Our estimates indicate progressively stronger price compression in the “weak” bucket, by ca 3.5% per year. For export values, the differential slope for weak sectors is positive but not statistically significant. Notably, these sectors show relative and statistically significant outperformance in import volumes. Taken together, the results are consistent with surplus being absorbed through both a price and quantity adjustment (Exhibit 8). • Truncating the sample into a pre‑tariff window, underperforming demand sectors continue to show greater price compression and evidence of relatively stronger volumes when the tariff period is excluded. If anything, the coefficients have a higher magnitude in absolute terms. This suggests that the “venting” mechanism has been occurring independently of tariff‑driven trade dynamics, with even stronger price compression/volume resilience pre the 2025 tariff wave. Short post‑Apr 2025 windows are statistically uninformative given the limited number of observations. To address this, we test for a structural change in pricing dynamics around 2025 using a piecewise-linear trend specification with HS2 fixed effects and year dummies.

But we do not think upcoming data will support the chance for rate hikes, especially as markets pricing 50bp of hikes this year will imply a tightening of financial conditions before officials ever even decided to raise rates. Some officials suggested a risk of less excess supply and a faster tightening of the output gap, but this would look like a much smaller risk after the increase in the unemployment rate in April. records.text: Assuming fuel prices remain elevated and airlines raise ticket prices and cut capacity, small and medium-sized airports, especially in tourist-heavy markets, would be most affected, particularly those that have greater exposure to low-cost airlines. Airports have very strong cost-recovery mechanisms, so we do not expect widespread credit stress, but rather a retreat in more discretionary travel. Our analysis of most major US airports found that Toledo, Fort Lauderdale, Myrtle Beach, Asheville and Orlando have the highest exposure to low-cost carriers (which include JetBlue, Allegiant, Frontier, the now bankrupt Spirit and several smaller airlines). When we plot airport spreads going back to 2022, we see that both small and large airport spreads have barely widened, as investors continue to overweight the sector (Figure 25). The richness of smaller airports is especially surprising, as they trade just slightly wider than large airports at the moment. In our view, investors should be a bit more cautious on the sector's prospects, given its rich valuations. FIGURE 25. records.text: In Israel, April CPI stayed broadly unchanged in annual terms at 1.9% y/y (in line with our forecast and slightly below the 2.0% y/y Bloomberg consensus) and picked up by 0.8pp to 1.2% m/m. Base effects, strong shekel and emergency measures for most of April (that interrupted normal economic activity and required population to stay close to shelters) were the main drivers of contained price growth. Higher gasoline prices and the travel abroad component added pressure, while lower prices in new rental contracts partially offset that. We expect inflation to remain within the target range, allowing the BoI to resume the easing cycle. Although we currently see space for two 25bp cuts in H2 26, a downside surprise in GDP alongside further strengthening of the shekel would increase the balance of risks in favor of an earlier cut at the end of May. In Egypt, inflation slowed in April despite higher energy prices and a weaker currency. This reinforces our view that the CBE will remain on hold at the upcoming meeting, while likely maintaining a wait-and-see stance and looking through near-term inflation volatility before resuming the easing cycle later in the year. There are, however, some outliers. In South Africa, April CPI (due 20 May) will be the first to reflect the impact of higher oil prices. We believe front-end rates remain too elevated relative to: 1) our economists’ baseline views and scenarios; 2) the BoE’s conditional Bank Rate paths, after taking into account current energy-market valuations; and 3) both economists’ consensus and market participants’ consensus, as shown in the May MaPS survey. We present supporting evidence in the first section of our Mid-Year Outlook. In our view, the gap largely reflects a meaningful front-end risk premium. We therefore recommend positioning for a lower trough rate and entering a long SFIM7 position. • Long End & Curve. With intermediate- and long-end yields close to multi- year highs, we assess valuations through a cross-market lens and analyze embedded term premium in a dedicated section of this publication. We find only modest evidence of an increase in term premium. Our cross-market analysis suggests that only part of this move can be attributed to idiosyncratic factors related to fiscal risk and political uncertainty. The analysis further supports our view that front-end risk premium has been the dominant factor behind higher yields and the UK’s cross-market underperformance. Combining our bullish front-end view with limited evidence of a material term-premium increase at the long end, and a still- uncertain domestic backdrop, we recommend initiating 10s20s SONIA steepeners. • ASWs. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 15 May 2026 3 Therefore, while energy intensity has declined globally over time, and that should make the global economy more resilient to oil shocks, the US remains a more energy intensive economy compared to Europe. Why are growth and inflation harder hit in Europe, then? Europe is a net energy importer while the US has become a net exporter Two main factors are to blame, in our view. On the activity side, the Euro area is structurally a net energy importer, with an energy trade deficit of close to 2% of GDP that peaked at c 4% of GDP after the war in Ukraine erupted. In contrast, while the US was a net energy importer of similar magnitude compared to Europe until around 2010, the shale boom has led the US to become a net energy exporter (Exhibit 3). This is a key factor underlying the harder hit on GDP in the Euro area vs the US. The first order impact of an energy price shock is larger when it is a clearly negative terms of trade shock. In the US, in turn, whereas the oil price shock hits the consumer, the economy overall is much more cushioned as the energy sector somewhat compensates for the relatively weaker consumer picture. In other words, the shock is more distributive in the US, but less harmful to the economy overall. Energy expenditures and CPI weights in Europe far outpace the US Last but not least, the spending side of the equation delivers an even clearer picture, and higher taxes are likely partly to blame. This suggests that downstream firms are still struggling to pass higher input costs further along the value chain. Within upstream sectors, PPI for oil and gas extraction surged to 29% y/y in April, the strongest reading since late 2022. Higher oil prices also spilled over into coal, with PPI for coal mining and washing turning positive for the first time since mid-2024. While CPI inflation rose by 0.2pp to 1.2% y/y in April, we think this modest pickup in headline inflation mainly reflected energy-driven supply-side constraints rather than demand-led reflation or second-round effects. We estimate the contribution from energy to headline CPI rose by about 0.5pp in April, compared with only a 0.2pp increase in headline CPI inflation. This implies that, excluding energy, underlying CPI inflation actually softened in April. Consistent with this view, several major CPI components continued to decline, including housing rents (April: -0.6% y/y vs -0.5% in March), automobiles (-1.2% vs -1.1%), and household goods and services (1.4% vs 1.5%). Moreover, core CPI remained subdued at 1.1–1.2% in March April following the Middle East conflict, compared with an average of 1.3% in January–February. Over the same period, services CPI was broadly flat at 0.8–0.9%, slightly below its pre-conflict average of 0.9%, underscoring still-weak domestic demand. 1

Our baseline scenario, which our global economics team describes as “de-escalation”, sees oil prices declining towards USD90/bbl in 4Q26 and settling around USD80/bbl in 2027. This is broadly consistent with an A/B-type energy outcome in the BoE’s April MPR framework, rather than a persistent Scenario C shock. For the UK, this still implies a difficult policy mix: weak real disposable income growth weighing on consumption, GDP growth remaining below potential, and headline inflation peaking at around 3.4% in 2Q26. Against this backdrop, we expect the BoE to remain on a prolonged hold, albeit with a tightening bias over the next couple of meetings, as policymakers assess the impact of oil supply disruptions and the timing of any reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. LLC Shaun Zhou Shaun.Zhou@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-3348 United States | Calm Before the Storm Expect calm in the short-term The rates volatility market has transitioned from the disorderly repricing seen during the March-April geopolitical shock into a much calmer regime. Realized volatility has declined materially across the curve, dealer positioning has rebuilt toward a long gamma configuration ( Exhibit 320 ), and short-expiry implied volatility has largely retraced back toward pre-conflict levels ( Exhibit 319 ). At first glance, this normalization appears surprising given the persistence of geopolitical uncertainty and the unresolved nature of the underlying energy shock. In our view, however, the current low-volatility environment is internally consistent with the macro backdrop. The market has found a temporary balance. That balance rests primarily on developments in the oil market. Inventory draws, increased US crude exports, and reduced Chinese imports have collectively helped stabilize physical energy markets. Observable inventories absorbed a substantial portion of the initial disruption, while temporary adjustments in trade flows reduced immediate spot tightness. The result has been a compression in near-term uncertainty and a narrowing of trading ranges across rates markets. To cross-check the extent of long-end risk-premium pressure, we use a simple fair- value residual framework that separates global from UK-specific factors. We estimate the relationship between 10y (see Exhibit 73 ) and 20y (see Exhibit 74 ) SONIA swaps and 1y1y SONIA over the past year, and compare the resulting residuals with equivalent residuals in the SOFR and Euribor markets. We then define the UK-specific component as the SONIA residual less the average of the SOFR and Euribor residuals. This gives us a proxy for the part of the UK long-end move that cannot be explained by either domestic front-end repricing or the common global rates move. On this measure, the past month points to a UK-specific risk premium of around 10bp in 10y SONIA swaps and 12bp in 20y SONIA swaps. We would not over-interpret this as a pure fiscal premium. The residual can reflect several overlapping factors: domestic political uncertainty, fiscal concerns, inflation-risk premium, liquidity and positioning. While there is no single federal water-use cap specific to data centers, water access, disclosure, and permitting are increasingly becoming binding constraints, particularly for large AI-oriented campuses. A central challenge is that water rights and permitting frameworks vary materially by state. In Western states operating under prior-appropriation regimes (e.g., Arizona, Nevada, Colorado), new large water users face elevated curtailment risk during droughts and must navigate seniority-based systems that can undermine long-term operational certainty. In Eastern states governed by riparian or “reasonable use” doctrines (e.g., Virginia, Georgia, the Carolinas), permitting is formally more flexible but increasingly subject to public opposition, infrastructure strain, and environmental review, particularly where groundwater withdrawals or evaporative cooling are involved. As see n in 2022, these second -round effects can fuel a more persistent inflation shock. Figure 6 shows the PMI output prices coefficients obtained by re-estimating the baseline regression separately for each regime. This approach gives us a clearer visualisation of how the strength of the passthrough differs across regimes. Passthrough from survey price data to inflation is nearly 7 times larger when the labour market is tight. Supply chain stress can also trigger a higher passthrough (4x) while the relative impact of financial conditions is smaller (2x). When we apply the same approach to the “perfect storm” scenario (Figure 7), the passthrough is also amplified, although confidence bands are wide because we only have a handful of episodes when all three stress periods prevailed (e.g. Jun-07, Nov-20 to Jan-22 and Mar-26). For the fifth payment, Romania has to meet about 28 milestones, and the main ones are: unified wage bill in the public sector (critical delay, could be worth EUR0.8bn or more), digitalisation of tax authority to improve tax collection (critical delay), reforms in SOEs (critical delay) and reforming the National Integrity Agency. These are to a large extent political and we think most of the required legislation will be approved, espe- cially the unified wage bill. Romania also needs to fulfill 151 milestones for the sixth payment, and while the legislation does not appear complicat- ed (and thus political risks are low), actual work on projects has been delayed. Decarbonisation is blocked as the decom- missioning of coal is stalled on lack of an alternative energy source; the Government Cloud is under severe technical delay, the construction of railway and metro infrastructure faces execution delays and the new 27 hospitals are mostly in early or middle stages of construction. It is unclear what may be finalised by end-August 2026. Disregarding the political situation, there is a high risk of failure to meet milestones for the sixth tranche owing to execution of works; this could result in Romania losing a significant portion of the RRF funds, including grants. records.text: Delayed reaction in Gilt premium. Despite an increase in political uncertainty on n Monday and Tuesday, it took a global sell-off to shift Gilt risk premium higher late in the week. The UK curve steepened and our FX strategists’ proxy for the political risk premium in Sterling — the gap between actual and GSBEER model-implied EUR/GBP performance — has risen. But overall, stress on UK assets has been more modest than in recent comparable periods. Our measure of the term premium also remains contained, and when we apply our spillover framework to the term premium, we find that the UK has not been contributing to upward pressure on global rates until very recently (Exhibit 7). This is consistent with the stability up until this week in Gilt swap spreads and 10s30s curve vs other G4 markets since last year’s budget. Although political uncertainty will keep the market focused on fiscal policy, it is possible that some of the drivers of UK term premium, namely BoE QT and the rise in duration-adjusted free float, have started to moderate. That said, we expect relief to come from the front-end of the Gilt curve vs the belly, where the term premium will remain stable but sticky. Only a little help from higher T-bill issuance. In this respect, we continue to view two 25bp hikes, at the June and September meetings, as a robust policy choice across a wide range of outcomes, provided the inflation outlook remains characterised by a mid-sized, not overly persistent deviation above target. As Chief Economist Lane noted this week, “the optimal response might be smaller for an exogenous supply disruption than for a demand shock, but there are several reasons why an active response may be required” , including the risk that current inflation feeds into subsequent wage and price- setting dynamics, that negative real rates amplify the inflationary impulse, that even temporary inflation shocks can affect the formation of expectations, and that a material deviation from target unaccompanied by a policy response would pose communication risks for the central bank. With this in mind, recent ECB communication suggests that concerns around the growth outlook could place a cap on the extent of policy tightening should the energy and inflation outlook evolve towards more unfavourable configurations. In such a scenario, we think a majority of GC members would become increasingly attentive to growth-inflation trade-offs and may favour a more gradual and limited – but also more persistent – tightening cycle. 15 May 2026 21 Barclays | Global Economics Weekly: Leaders meet and bonds shriek

records.text: US Outlook Into the fire Kevin Warsh was confirmed as Fed chair this week, taking the helm from Powell, who will remain as a governor. Warsh will inherit a hot seat, with cost pressures now becoming quite apparent and little indication that demand is cracking amid robust AI-related capex and resilient consumer spending. • April inflation estimates came in a fair bit firmer than expected, even after accounting for a measurement quirk for rent inflation. Core CPI inflation was 0.38% m/m (3.3% y/y), and source data translate to core PCE at about 0.27% m/m (3.3% y/y). Measures from the PPI and import prices were considerably firmer, suggesting intensifying cost pressures in the pipeline. • Activity and spending remained resilient through April, despite purchasing power pressures from the Iran conflict. The retail sales control group exceeded expectations, with upward revisions to prior months, placing consumers on track for a real spending gain exceeding 2% q/q saar in Q2. Industrial production also exceeded expectations, led by strong utilities and AI capex demand. • Cost pressures and a resilient economy will complicate the task of Kevin Warsh, the incoming Fed chair, who is likely to see continued pressure from the president to ease the policy rate. Even if Warsh were inclined to cut the policy rate, which we doubt, communications indicate that a consensus of FOMC voters see two-sided risks to the funds rate. One explanation is continued robust demand, particularly at the front end. At the long end, positioning still appears net long spreads, but relatively attractive valuations and optimism around a potentially swift resolution of the conflict seem to have limited any meaningful reduction in positions or initiation of shorts. The performance of iota spreads, shown in Exhibit 134 , points in the same direction: spreads have broadly tightened, with little evidence that a liquidity or fiscal premium has increased materially since 27 February. This resilience is a double-edged sword. On the one hand, current pricing does not suggest that the market is assigning a high probability to a material shift in fiscal policy. On the other hand, the combination of supported ASW valuations and still-long positioning creates downside risk if political uncertainty or fiscal concerns intensify. In that scenario, investors could begin to unwind long spread positions or initiate shorts. To gauge the potential downside, we look back at the post-October 2024 Budget episode. records.text: 2 US Economic Weekly | 15 May 2026 Stagflation or reflation? Aditya Bhave BofAS aditya.bhave@bofa.com • The economy is being buffeted by a plethora of supply and demand shocks. The tails of the economic and Fed policy distribution are fat. • Inflation is clearly a problem. But are we experiencing stagflation or reflation? Resilient spending and booming earnings point to reflation. • But we think the jury is still out. With the fiscal tailwind fading, the true test of consumer and labor resilience might still be ahead of us. The labor market would have to start tightening for reflation and rate hikes to become our base case. Crucible of confusion There probably isn’t any historical precedent for the plethora of shocks buffeting the US economy. On the supply side, we are facing three negative shocks – Iran, tariffs & immigration policy – and a positive one – AI. There is uncertainty about when and how much each shock will impact activity and inflation. The economy is also experiencing two positive demand shocks: fiscal stimulus from the OBBB and AI investment demand. Moreover, the World Cup is starting in a few weeks. Its effects on spending, inflation and employment should be mostly transitory. But the resulting distortions to the data could make it hard to get a clean read on the underlying state of the economy until late summer. It is closest to Scenario B through much of 2027, before moving materially lower and converging towards Scenario A-like levels by the end of the horizon (see Exhibit 64 ). Taken together, futures are consistent with de-escalation and gradual normalisation, rather than a persistent Scenario C-style energy shock. Oil shows more near-term persistence than Scenario A, but converges towards Scenario A-like levels further out. UK nat gas also embeds more near-term persistence than Scenario A, particularly through 2027, but remains far below the BoE’s Scenario C assumptions throughout.
